statement: In healthy adults tested the morning after an evening of heavy drinking, with blood alcohol back near zero, the morning after compared with a day without alcohol or with placebo is associated with poorer short-term and long-term memory, sustained attention and reaction speed: pooled standardized differences of about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation (short-term memory g = 0.64, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.13, five studies; long-term memory 0.59, 0.01 to 1.17, four studies; sustained attention 0.47, 0.07 to 0.87, four studies; reaction speed 0.66, 0.31 to 1.00, five studies), with no pooled effect on divided attention, mixed results for working memory, and no clear effect in single studies of problem solving, management simulations or examination scores (Gunn et al., 2018). Each estimate pools a few small studies with moderate to high heterogeneity (I2 36% to 84%); sleep was rarely controlled, nobody could be blinded, naturalistic studies with more drinking found impairment more often than laboratory studies, and the review did not separate people who felt hungover from those who did not, so the finding describes the morning after heavy drinking rather than hangover symptoms as such. A later simulator study found slower responses on a divided-attention task during a drive the morning after a night of social drinking, including in drivers with no alcohol left in their breath (Alford et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: The morning after heavy drinking, even with no alcohol left in the blood, people in studies remembered less, kept their attention less well and reacted more slowly than on a day without alcohol, by a medium amount on average. The studies were small, often did not control sleep, and could not hide from people whether they had been drinking, so how big the effect really is remains uncertain.
population: Healthy adults, mostly young (students and cadets in several studies), tested the morning after an evening of heavy drinking in 19 controlled laboratory and naturalistic studies from 1970 to 2016 summarized in one systematic review; and 52 young drivers in one later simulator study
exposure: An evening of heavy drinking, given in the laboratory or chosen by participants in naturalistic studies, with the hangover confirmed by questionnaire and blood alcohol near zero at testing (study amounts are on the study cards)
comparator: The same people on a morning after no alcohol or placebo, or a separate group without a hangover
outcome: Next-morning performance on memory, attention, reaction-time, working-memory and executive tasks
magnitude: Hedges' g, positive meaning worse after drinking: short-term memory 0.64 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.13; 5 studies; I2 73%); long-term memory 0.59 (0.01 to 1.17; 4 studies; I2 84%); sustained attention 0.47 (0.07 to 0.87; 4 studies; I2 50%); reaction speed 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00; 5 studies; I2 36%); divided attention, 4 studies, no detectable effect (no estimate reported); working memory and executive tasks not pooled. Later simulator study: divided-attention response time slower the morning after drinking, d = 0.55 in 52 drivers and 0.69 in the 26 with zero breath alcohol (authors' effect sizes, no intervals).

evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

risk_of_bias.note: The pooled memory and reaction-speed estimates rest mainly on naturalistic, non-randomized within-person comparisons; testing could not be blinded, task order was not always randomized, sleep was rarely controlled, and the review is of critically low confidence (model not stated, no assessment of blinding or confounding).

inconsistency.note: I2 of 50% to 84% for three of the four pooled domains; naturalistic studies tended to find impairment where laboratory studies did not, an explanation proposed but not tested.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the morning after heavy drinking in healthy adults, as studied; it does not claim effects of hangover symptoms as such.

imprecision.note: Four or five small studies per estimate; the long-term memory interval reaches down to 0.01, and divided attention has no estimate.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed; small positive studies dominate, and several null studies were excluded by the strict inclusion criteria or are not accounted for among the exclusions.

grade.reasoning: Started low because the pooled estimates for memory and reaction speed come mainly from naturalistic comparisons in which people chose their drinking nights; the randomized placebo-controlled laboratory studies within the review mostly found smaller or no effects. Downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision and suspected publication bias, which leaves very low certainty; starting high for the laboratory studies would give the same result after these downgrades. Status replicated: impairment was found by at least two independent groups in each pooled domain (for example McKinney and Coyle, Grange and colleagues, Howland and Rohsenow), with null results mainly in small laboratory studies at lower amounts; the direction of every pooled estimate is the same. The later simulator study adds one consistent observation on response speed but used a different task from those pooled.

statement: In young drivers tested in a driving simulator the morning after a night of social drinking that they chose themselves, the morning after drinking compared with the same drivers after a night without alcohol is associated with poorer driving on a short simulated commute through town and country, including in drivers with no alcohol left in their breath: in 52 drivers, eight of 15 driving measures were worse, among them slower responses to a divided-attention task (d = 0.55), more time off the road (d = 0.68), more lane excursions (d = 0.58), more centre-line crossings (d = 0.36), faster driving (d = 0.42) and more tickets for violations (d = 0.34), with similar effects in the 26 whose breath alcohol was zero, while lane-keeping variability and speed variability did not differ, and collisions differed in the analysis of variance (p = 0.04) but not in the paired comparison; in the 26 with some alcohol still in their breath, collisions also rose (d = 0.74) (Alford et al., 2020). A systematic review found that two of three earlier naturalistic driving studies reported poorer vehicle control the morning after heavy drinking and one found no change in speed; they were too different to pool (Gunn et al., 2018). Drinking amounts and sleep were not recorded and drivers knew their condition, so the effect of alcohol cannot be separated from a short night; the authors' comparison with driving at 0.05 to 0.08% blood alcohol rests on another study and was not tested in theirs, and the faster driving they attribute to residual alcohol was already present in that group on the alcohol-free morning (editors' reading). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a driving simulator, young drivers drove worse the morning after a night out drinking than after a night without alcohol, even when a breath test showed no alcohol: they reacted more slowly, drove faster, left their lane and the road more often and got more tickets. Drivers with some alcohol still in their breath also had more crashes. Sleep was not measured, so part of the effect may come from a short night.
population: Young drivers aged 18 to 25 with 1 to 6 years of driving experience who drink socially and report regular hangovers (52 in one UK simulator study); and the participants of three earlier naturalistic driving studies summarized in a systematic review
exposure: The morning after a self-chosen night of social drinking, with breath alcohol zero (26 drivers) or still measurable (26 drivers) before driving
comparator: The same drivers on a morning after a night without alcohol
outcome: Simulated driving: divided-attention responses, vehicle control (speed, lane keeping, time off road, lane excursions, centre-line crossings) and violations (collisions, speed-limit exceedances, tickets)
magnitude: All 52 drivers, morning after drinking against alcohol-free morning (authors' Cohen's d, no intervals): divided-attention response time d = 0.55, missed responses 0.30, incorrect responses 0.21; mean speed 0.42; centre-line crossings 0.36; time off road 0.68; lane excursions 0.58; tickets 0.34; no significant difference in lane-keeping variability, speed variability, mean lane position, speed-limit exceedances or collisions. Zero breath alcohol (26): response time 0.69, speed 0.40, centre-line crossings 0.48, time off road 0.61, lane excursions 0.64. Residual breath alcohol (26): response time 0.50, speed 0.45, time off road 0.72, lane excursions 0.51, collisions 0.74. Workload rated higher after drinking (d = 0.99).

The authors attribute the residual group's faster driving, more speed-limit exceedances and more tickets to residual alcohol, but that group also drove faster, exceeded limits more and got more tickets on the alcohol-free morning (34.3 against 29.1 mph; 10.4 against 7.0 exceedances; 1.0 against 0.6 tickets), so these group differences cannot be attributed to residual alcohol (editors' note).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st, 6th and 8th paragraphs; Results › 3 (opening paragraph)
evidence.extracted: Drinking was unobserved and amounts are not reported (some participants could not recall them); sleep was not recorded, and the authors note that sleep loss may be a significant component of hangover effects on next-day performance. Their statement that the impairment is equivalent to driving at or above 0.05-0.08% blood alcohol cites another study's simulated highway test (ref 21); no alcohol benchmark was run in this study.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

evidence.locator: Results › 'Real-life' simulations, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of three naturalistic studies of driving the morning after heavy drinking, two found poorer control of the vehicle (deviation from a set course; Laurell and Törnros, 1983; Verster et al., 2014) and one found no next-day effect on speed (Törnros and Laurell, 1991); differences in method prevented pooling.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

risk_of_bias.note: Naturalistic within-person comparison: drinking nights self-chosen, amounts and sleep unrecorded, drivers and experimenters aware of condition, three unregistered studies combined; the earlier studies are seen only through a review and cannot be appraised here.

inconsistency.note: The direction is consistent across studies, but the measures differ: weaving increased on a long highway drive in one earlier study, while on this short urban route weaving did not change and lane excursions and time off road did.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for simulated driving in young drivers, as studied; real-road crash risk is not claimed.

imprecision.note: No intervals are reported; with 52 drivers in a within-person design, effects of the reported size are unlikely to be chance, but the size is uncertain.

grade.reasoning: Observational within-person evidence starts low and is downgraded once for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated: poorer vehicle control the morning after drinking was reported by this study and by at least one independent earlier group (Laurell and Törnros, 1983), with Verster et al. (2014) sharing an author with Alford et al.; only this study separated drivers with zero from those with residual breath alcohol. The claim does not repeat the authors' equivalence with a legal blood alcohol limit or their residual-alcohol speeding finding, which the data do not support.

statement: In healthy Japanese men aged 20 to 50 with the fully active form of the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, drinking water in between drinks while drinking sake, compared with the same sake without the extra water in another session, did not detectably change breath alcohol or acetaldehyde, or any of six symptom ratings the next morning (headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, flushing and feeling exhilarated), in a randomized crossover trial of 13 men; scores on a short speed-of-processing test were lower with water right after drinking, when several men felt bloated, and slightly but not significantly higher the next morning (Imai et al., 2026). Evidence is insufficient to say whether water during drinking changes hangover: the trial was small and open-label, reported no effect sizes or intervals, used no hangover scale, could detect only a very large effect, and was funded by the brewer of the sake used; because the amount of alcohol was fixed, it could not test whether water helps in real life by leading people to drink less or more slowly. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial with 13 men, drinking water between drinks did not change how much alcohol was in their breath or how they felt the next morning, compared with drinking the same alcohol without the water. The trial was too small to rule out a modest benefit, and it could not test whether water helps by making people drink less.
population: 13 healthy Japanese men aged 20 to 50 with the fully active ALDH2 genotype, studied in one clinical trial unit
exposure: Water drunk in between drinks during a supervised session of drinking sake (study amounts are on the study card)
comparator: The same men drinking the same sake without the added water in another session
outcome: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde; next-morning symptom ratings (headache, nausea, concentration, sleepiness, facial flushing, feeling exhilarated); Digit Symbol Substitution Test
magnitude: No numerical estimates or intervals reported. Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde: no significant difference at any time. Six symptom ratings: no significant difference at any time. Digit Symbol Substitution Test, change from the pre-drinking score: lower with water right after drinking (p = 0.01) and higher with water at the first two next-morning tests (p = 0.05 and 0.08, called not significant by the authors). The authors put power at barely 0.8 for an effect size of 1 (one-sided).

evidence.extracted: Breath ethanol and acetaldehyde did not differ significantly between the water and no-water sessions at any time after drinking; acetaldehyde point estimates were slightly higher with water shortly after drinking, and the curves were almost identical by the next morning.

risk_of_bias.note: Open label with self-rated symptoms, per-protocol analysis after one exclusion tied to the water condition, randomization not described, and no numerical results; card overall high risk, although the expected bias would favour water rather than the null.

inconsistency.note: Single study.

indirectness.note: Men only, one genotype, one drink, one fixed amount of alcohol and a very large amount of water; the real-life question (does water help when people drink as they choose) was not tested.

imprecision.note: 13 participants, no intervals, power only for a very large effect.

grade.reasoning: A randomized crossover trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and twice for imprecision, giving very low. The relation is insufficient evidence rather than no detectable change, because no interval excludes a meaningful benefit (METHODS 6.3). Single study. The authors' suggestion that water may help in daily life by limiting how much people drink is not a finding of this trial.

statement: In healthy young adults, mostly university students, who drank beer in a laboratory to the same level of intoxication and then had a supervised night in bed, beer with added caffeine compared with the same beer without caffeine did not detectably change next-morning hangover severity (Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 against 1.45, d = 0.13) or the share with any hangover (61% against 69%), nor self-reported time to fall asleep, time asleep or morning sleepiness, in a randomized comparison of 28 and 36 people; the caffeine group rated its sleep quality better (d = 0.64), mainly because of morning alertness items (Rohsenow et al., 2014). Evidence is insufficient to say whether caffeine changes hangover: the intervals include a moderate difference either way (editors' calculation: any hangover from 32 percentage points lower to 15 higher with caffeine), sleep was self-reported, energy drinks and other amounts were not tested, and the study is a later analysis of a trial designed for driving outcomes. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, beer with added caffeine did not change the next-morning hangover compared with the same beer without caffeine, and people did not report sleeping less. The study was small, so a moderate effect either way cannot be ruled out, and energy drinks were not tested.
population: 64 healthy adults aged 21 to 30 (89% university students) without drinking problems, in a laboratory study in Boston
exposure: Beer with added caffeine, at the concentration of a commercial caffeinated beer, drunk to a set level of intoxication (amounts are on the study card)
comparator: A randomized group drinking the same beer without caffeine to the same level
outcome: Next-morning Acute Hangover Scale (severity and any hangover); self-reported sleep quality, time to fall asleep and time asleep; Stanford Sleepiness Scale
magnitude: Caffeinated against non-caffeinated beer: Acute Hangover Scale 1.34 (SD 0.84) against 1.45 (0.89), d = 0.13 (editors' 95% CI for d −0.63 to 0.38); any hangover 60.7% against 69.4%, h = 0.19 (editors' risk difference −8.7 percentage points, 95% CI −32 to 15); sleep quality 4.45 against 4.16, d = 0.64 (95% CI of the difference 0.057 to 0.517), better with caffeine; time to fall asleep d = 0.28, time asleep d = 0.21, sleepiness d = 0.23, none significant.

The authors' statement that people who believe caffeine affects hangover are misinformed goes beyond these data. Single study.

statement: In healthy young adults at a German university who drank beer and white wine under medical supervision to the same level of intoxication, drinking beer before wine compared with wine before beer (each person tried both orders in a randomized crossover trial) does not detectably change next-day hangover severity: the difference between groups was −0.68 points on the 0 to 56 Acute Hangover Scale (P = 0.71; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 3.0), which rules out a difference as large as the 8 points the trial was planned to detect but not a smaller one; participants who drank only beer or only wine on different days did not differ either (Köchling et al., 2019). In exploratory analyses, vomiting and feeling very drunk went with worse hangovers, and women reported worse hangovers than men, although the paper's Discussion says it found no difference between women and men. The trial used one lager and one white wine, was open-label and analysed only completers (90 of 105). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, the order of beer and wine made no detectable difference to the next day's hangover: beer before wine and wine before beer felt about the same. What went with worse hangovers was vomiting and feeling very drunk.
population: 90 healthy adults aged 19 to 40 (half women) at a German university, excluding people of East Asian origin, who completed both sessions
exposure: Beer then white wine in one session, drunk to a set level of intoxication under medical supervision (drinks and amounts are on the study card)
comparator: The same people drinking wine then beer in another session; in a control group, beer only against wine only on different days
outcome: Next-day Acute Hangover Scale score (eight symptoms, 0 to 56)
magnitude: Within-person difference between orders: −0.32 (SD 7.63) in the group that drank beer then wine first against 0.36 (SD 6.82) in the group that drank wine then beer first, P = 0.71; editors' approximate 95% CI for the difference −4.4 to 3.0 points; planned meaningful difference 8 points (14% of the scale). Control group: no difference between beer-only and wine-only days (P > 0.05). Women reported more severe hangovers than men (P = 0.009; data not shown).

statement: In young adults aged 21 to 24 in a Los Angeles cohort who had drunk alcohol in the past month, having ever used hangover remedy pills (such as dihydromyricetin), compared with never having used them, is associated with more alcohol-related problems and heavier drinking on drinking days: 2.3 points higher on a 0 to 40 problem scale (95% CI 0.8 to 3.8), about a quarter more drinks per drinking day (rate ratio 1.24, 1.02 to 1.49) and almost twice as many symptoms of alcohol use disorder in the past year (rate ratio 1.86, 1.18 to 3.02), but not with more drinking days or binge-drinking days; only 42 of 1312 (3.2%) had ever used such pills, while 18.9% had heard of them and 8.6% believed they work (Han et al., 2024). The survey was cross-sectional, so it cannot say whether the pills lead people to drink more or heavier drinking leads people to try the pills, and it asked only whether people had ever used pills. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Few young adults in one Los Angeles survey had ever used hangover pills (about 3 in 100). Those who had reported more drinking problems and more drinks on the days they drank, but the survey cannot tell whether the pills led to heavier drinking or heavier drinkers tried the pills.
population: 1312 past-month drinkers aged 21 to 24 in a school-based cohort in Los Angeles, surveyed in 2021
exposure: Ever having used hangover remedy pills (for example dihydromyricetin), self-reported
comparator: Past-month drinkers in the same survey who had never used them
outcome: Modified AUDIT problem score; drinks per drinking day; drinking days and binge-drinking days in the past month; count of alcohol-related problems
magnitude: Adjusted for sociodemographic factors and depressive symptoms: modified AUDIT difference 2.29 (95% CI 0.82 to 3.76) on a 0 to 40 scale; drinks per drinking day rate ratio 1.24 (1.02 to 1.49); alcohol-related problems rate ratio 1.86 (1.18 to 3.02), also adjusted for drinking frequency and intensity; drinking days 1.19 (0.94 to 1.51) and binge days 1.40 (0.91 to 2.23), not significant. Prevalence: ever used 3.2% (42 of 1312), heard of 18.9%, believe they work 8.6%.

statement: In people who drink alcohol, mostly people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification centres, a short course of paracetamol (acetaminophen) at usual doses compared with placebo does not detectably raise the liver enzyme ALT at an early measurement in five randomized trials of 901 people (pooled difference about 0.1 units per litre, 95% CI about −1.3 to 1.5, editors' recalculation; the paper prints a standardized difference as if it were in units per litre), and no trial reported liver failure or death; three trials that measured later found modest ALT rises with longer use, mostly just after stopping, which had gone in the one trial that checked (Rumack et al., 2012). No trial tested paracetamol taken for a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking; no events among 551 treated people cannot rule out rare serious liver injury (upper 95% limit about 5 in 1,000, editors' calculation); and the review was funded by a paracetamol maker, which reviewed the manuscript, the authors' employer had contracts with paracetamol makers, its authors wrote all five pooled trials, and it did not assess the trials' risk of bias. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In trials with people who drink, mostly heavy drinkers who had just stopped, a short course of paracetamol at usual doses did not raise a liver blood test compared with a dummy pill, and nobody had liver failure. Small rises appeared in some trials when people took it for longer. No trial looked at paracetamol for a hangover after one night of drinking, and the review was paid for by a paracetamol maker whose researchers ran the trials.
population: People who drink alcohol in five randomized trials (551 on paracetamol, 350 on placebo): mostly people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification centres (four trials) and moderate drinkers who kept drinking (one trial)
exposure: A short course of paracetamol (acetaminophen) at usual doses (doses and durations are on the study card)
comparator: Placebo
outcome: Change in serum ALT from baseline at an early measurement; ALT at later measurements; liver dysfunction, liver failure and death
magnitude: Pooled difference in mean change in ALT (paracetamol minus placebo): printed as 0.0 (95% CI −0.2 to 0.1) and labelled IU/L, which matches a standardized difference (editors' recalculation −0.04, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.10); in IU/L about 0.1 (95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; editors' calculation). Later, unpooled: ALT higher with paracetamol by 12.6 and 8.4 IU/L in two trials just after the end of a course, and by 18.7 IU/L (8.1 at the lower dose) in a third, gone at that trial's last measurement. Liver dysfunction, failure or death: none reported (upper 95% limit about 0.5% for 551 treated people; editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1; Figure 2 legend
evidence.extracted: Five trials (551 on acetaminophen, 350 on placebo) were pooled with a fixed-effect model: the difference in mean change in ALT is printed as 0.0 IU/L (-0.2 to 0.1; labelled '97% CI' in the Results and '95%CI' in the Abstract), Q = 1.7, I2 = 0. Recalculated from Table 1, these figures are a standardized difference (-0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.10), as the forest-plot legend says; in IU/L the pooled difference is 0.09 (95% CI -1.27 to 1.46) (editors' calculation).
evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

evidence.locator: Results, 1st, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Abstract › Main Results
evidence.extracted: No randomized trial, included or excluded, reported liver dysfunction, liver failure or death; AST, INR, bilirubin and glutathione S-transferase changes were similar between groups where reported, apart from a rise in INR in people taking warfarin.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

evidence.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: At later, unpooled measurements ALT was higher with acetaminophen than placebo by 12.6 IU/L (Dart 2010) and 8.4 IU/L (Heard 2007, statistically significant), mostly just after the end of dosing, and by 18.7 and 8.1 IU/L at the higher and lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra 2007; Table 2's means give 18.3 for the higher dose), with no difference at that trial's last measurement.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Four of the six included trials (four of the five pooled) enrolled people with heavy drinking admitted to detoxification, who started acetaminophen soon after their last drink and had no alcohol during the trial; one enrolled moderate drinkers who kept drinking. In two pooled trials dosing had ended before the pooled measurement.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Footnotes › Financial disclosure; References 6 to 10
evidence.extracted: The protocol was not registered and no assessment of bias in the trials was done. The review was funded by an investigator-initiated grant from McNeil Consumer Healthcare to Denver Health; the sponsors are stated to have had no role in design, performance, analysis or authorship, but the sponsor reviewed the final manuscript. Five authors are Denver Health employees, and Denver Health has contracts with McNeil and Cadence (acetaminophen makers) and Cumberland (IV acetylcysteine maker); one author consulted for McNeil on behalf of Denver Health and testified for McNeil in 2010 litigation; review authors are authors of all five pooled trials.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 110 (first reader)

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized trials with an objective laboratory outcome, but the review assessed no risk of bias, searched published trials only, and is of critically low confidence; the trials share authors and partly a funder with the review.

inconsistency.note: No heterogeneity (I2 = 0).

indirectness.note: Mostly recently abstinent people in detoxification, ALT as a surrogate at one early measurement; not paracetamol taken for a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking.

imprecision.note: The interval for the ALT difference (about −1.3 to 1.5 IU/L) excludes clinically meaningful rises; rare serious injury is not addressed by this outcome, as the claim states.

publication_bias.note: Not downgraded: no sign of missing trials, but only published trials from largely one group were sought, and a five-trial funnel plot cannot show much.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving low. 'Does not detectably change' is used for the early ALT measurement because the recalculated interval excludes meaningful rises; the claim does not extend this to rare serious liver injury, to longer use, or to use during a hangover. Status replicated by the same team: the five pooled trials agree but share investigators with each other and with the review. Placed in section 6 with the other interaction claims; it answers the day-after question about the safety of a common hangover medicine.

statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; figures second-hand, no systematic search or appraisal), alcohol helps healthy people fall asleep, but in people with alcohol use disorder sleep is disturbed during drinking and for a long time after stopping: cited studies found clinical insomnia in 35 to 70% of people with the disorder against about 15 to 30% of the general population; longer time to fall asleep and shorter sleep during drinking and through the first weeks and months of abstinence; less deep (slow-wave) sleep that may take months to years to recover; a rebound of REM (dreaming) sleep after stopping, though findings conflict; and broken sleep from the first nights of abstinence to a year or more. Self-reported insomnia early in abstinence predicted relapse in several studies, and a long time to fall asleep did in two of three, with mixed results for other sleep measures. The review's own summary table marks the early-abstinence changes for alcohol as uncertain. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of sleep research says alcohol can help you fall asleep at first, but people who drink heavily for a long time sleep badly, and their sleep can stay poor for months after they stop. Bad sleep after stopping was linked with starting to drink again. These are second-hand findings from a review that did not check study quality.
population: People with alcohol use disorder in studies cited by a narrative review; healthy people for the acute effect
exposure: Regular heavy drinking and abstinence after it
comparator: Healthy sleepers, the general population, or the same people at other times, as in the cited studies
outcome: Insomnia, sleep latency, total sleep, slow-wave and REM sleep, sleep fragmentation, relapse
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized: clinical insomnia 35 to 70% in alcohol use disorder against about 15 to 30% in the general population; reduced total sleep at 2 to 4 weeks of abstinence in several studies; slow-wave sleep recovering over months to years; fragmentation found up to one to two years after stopping.

statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; second-hand, without appraisal), medicines tried for sleep problems in people stopping or cutting down alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioids had mixed results, and better sleep did not reliably mean less drug use. For alcohol, gabapentin gave largely positive results in studies; quetiapine improved waking at night and insomnia in one placebo-controlled trial, with mixed effects on drinking; and trazodone improved sleep measures but in a large placebo-controlled trial was linked with less abstinence during treatment and more drinking after it. For cannabis withdrawal, zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved some sleep measures, but none clearly reduced relapse. For cocaine, modafinil normalized deep sleep in one study from the senior author's laboratory. For opioids, trazodone did not improve sleep in methadone maintenance, and amitriptyline and lorazepam did not differ for withdrawal insomnia in 27 people. Benzodiazepines are often avoided with alcohol because of dependence and overdose risk. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: A review of sleep research says that sleep medicines given to people stopping alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioids sometimes improved sleep, but that did not reliably help them stay off the drug. In one large trial, people stopping alcohol who took trazodone slept better but drank more. These are second-hand findings from a review that did not check study quality.
population: People with alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioid use disorders in early abstinence or treatment, in trials cited by a narrative review
exposure: Medicines for sleep (gabapentin, quetiapine, trazodone, zolpidem, mirtazapine, modafinil, amitriptyline and others)
comparator: Placebo or another medicine, as in the cited trials
outcome: Sleep measures and relapse or drug use
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized; no effect sizes given. Trazodone in alcohol use disorder: better sleep quality but less abstinence during treatment and more drinking after it in a large placebo-controlled trial; amitriptyline against lorazepam in 27 people with opioid-withdrawal insomnia: no difference on most measures.

statement: In adults who drink, mostly young adults and students with mild-to-moderate hangovers, the day of a hangover compared with a sober day or with their usual mood is associated with worse mood (more anxiety, low mood, stress and irritability, and less alertness and contentment) in most of the quantitative studies, with guilt described in interviews and linked with how bad the hangover was, in a systematic review of 22 studies with 6152 participants (Rothman et al., 2026). The review gives no effect sizes, so how much worse is unknown; in the largest survey (1837 students) anxiety and depression were the least reported and least severe hangover symptoms, one smaller study found no change in tension-anxiety, and another found none in people who rarely get hangovers. The studies cannot separate the hangover itself from lost sleep, regret about the night or mood before drinking. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: On the day of a hangover, most studies found that people felt more anxious, low or guilty than on a sober day, but none measured how big the change is.
population: Healthy adults who drink alcohol, mostly young adults and students (57% women; mean age about 26), in 22 studies published from 1980 to 2024
exposure: The day after drinking with a hangover (after a usual night out, after drinking in a laboratory, or a recently reported hangover)
comparator: The same people on a sober or alcohol-free day, their baseline mood, or respondents with milder hangovers
outcome: Self-rated negative affect (anxiety, low mood or depression, stress, guilt, irritability, emotion regulation) and positive mood or alertness
magnitude: Direction only: worse mood during hangover in most of 19 quantitative studies; no study-level or pooled effect sizes or intervals are reported. Exceptions: in the largest survey (n = 1837) anxiety and depression were the least reported and least severe symptoms, while regret and apathy were moderate; one study found no significant effect on tension-anxiety; one found no change in anxiety or depression in people who rarely get hangovers.

risk_of_bias.note: Mostly naturalistic within-person and cross-sectional studies rated moderate to serious (ROBINS-I); mood self-rated by people who knew they were hungover; synthesis by counting significant results; one sample appears to be counted twice (card reporting issues).

inconsistency.note: Direction consistent in most studies; the exceptions concern anxiety in particular and are stated in the claim.

indirectness.note: Young adults and students reporting their own hangovers are the people the question is about; severe hangovers and older adults are under-represented.

imprecision.note: No study-level or pooled effect sizes or intervals at all, so the size of the change cannot be judged.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Most primary studies are observational (naturalistic within-person or cross-sectional), so the evidence starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and for imprecision (no magnitudes), which gives very low. Status replicated: worse mood during hangover appears in many studies from independent groups (UK, US, the Netherlands, Australia). The claim is about the direction of the association only; its size and whether the hangover itself causes it are unknown.

statement: In adults who drink, whether any remedy or way of coping reduces anxiety or low mood during a hangover was not tested in any of the 22 studies of a systematic review, which included no intervention study, and its authors call for one (Rothman et al., 2026). In three interview studies (109 young adults, mostly students, in Norway and the United Kingdom), people said that sharing the hangover with friends who had also been drinking eased their distress, which they traced mainly to regret about what they had done while drunk, gaps in memory and a wasted day; in one cross-sectional survey, people with more resilience reported less severe hangovers and people who used avoidant coping reported more severe ones. Evidence is insufficient to say whether any strategy changes how people feel during a hangover. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Nobody has tested anything that eases the worry or low mood of a hangover; in interviews, young people said that talking it over with friends helped.
population: Adults who drink: three interview studies of young adults, mostly students (66, 23 and 20 participants), and one cross-sectional survey of 648 respondents (described inconsistently in the review), within a systematic review
exposure: Ways of coping with a hangover: sharing it with friends (as described in interviews); resilience and coping style (measured in one survey)
comparator: No comparison group: interview accounts, and correlations across survey respondents
outcome: Anxiety, low mood, guilt and other distress during a hangover; hangover severity
magnitude: No intervention tested. Interview themes in all three studies: distress linked to behaviour while drunk, memory gaps and a wasted day; sharing the experience with friends eased it. One survey: resilience correlated with less severe and avoidant coping with more severe hangovers (coefficients not given in the review).

evidence.extracted: Across the three interview studies, people described sadness, guilt, regret, shame, worry and embarrassment during hangovers, prompted mostly by behaviour while drunk that clashed with their beliefs, catastrophic thinking and a sense of a wasted day; they said that bonding with friends and sharing the unpleasantness of the hangover helped ease these feelings.

statement: In healthy adults in sleep-laboratory studies, drinking alcohol in the hours before bed, compared with the same people on a night without alcohol, reduces REM (dreaming) sleep that night: the first REM period came about 18 minutes later (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1) and REM sleep was about 11 minutes shorter (95% CI 1.8 to 20.8) or 2.8% less of sleep (1.7 to 3.9), and the delay and the loss of REM minutes were larger after more alcohol, in a meta-analysis of 27 mostly crossover studies (Gardiner et al., 2025, journal pre-proof). The prediction intervals include no change, so results varied between studies; 11 of the 27 studies were at high risk of bias, most were small, and nearly all gave alcohol shortly before bed. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In sleep-lab studies, drinking before bed delayed and shortened dream (REM) sleep that night, and more so after more alcohol.
population: Healthy adults aged 18 to 70, mostly young (12 studies men only, 4 women only, 11 mixed), in 27 sleep-laboratory studies published from 1966 to 2022
exposure: A measured amount of alcohol drunk before bed, nearly always shortly before bedtime (study amounts and timings on the study card)
comparator: The same people on a night without alcohol (placebo or no alcohol); separate control groups in two studies
outcome: REM sleep onset latency; REM sleep duration and proportion of the night (polysomnography)
magnitude: REM onset latency +18.0 min (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1; prediction interval -18.8 to 54.8), k = 29 effect sizes, n = 212, p = 0.001, larger with more alcohol (p = 0.024). REM duration -11.3 min (-20.8 to -1.8; prediction interval -37.2 to 14.6), k = 13, n = 96, p = 0.026, larger with more alcohol (p = 0.009). REM proportion -2.8% (-3.9 to -1.7; prediction interval -6.1 to 0.5), k = 32, n = 255, p < 0.001, not detectably moderated by amount (p = 0.424) or timing (p = 0.664).

statement: In healthy adults in sleep-laboratory studies, drinking alcohol in the hours before bed, compared with the same people on a night without alcohol, did not detectably shorten the time taken to fall asleep on average (2.0 minutes shorter, 95% CI 4.3 shorter to 0.2 longer), although in the dose analysis it was shorter after larger amounts, and evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes total sleep time (10.1 minutes less, 95% CI 24.6 less to 4.4 more; prediction interval 71.5 minutes less to 51.3 more), waking during the night or sleep efficiency, in a meta-analysis of 27 mostly crossover studies (Gardiner et al., 2025, journal pre-proof). In three of five studies people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol. Most studies did not hold time in bed constant, and nearly all gave alcohol shortly before bed. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.

statement: In adults followed in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death (published 1981 to 2021, mostly from North America, Europe and Australia), drinking a little (about 1.3 to 25 g of ethanol a day, from one 10-g drink a week to about two drinks a day) compared with not drinking: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of dying from any cause, and the question is disputed. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them, people who drank a little died at lower rates: in a 2006 pooled analysis of 34 cohorts (1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths), against each study's lowest-intake category (no drinking with former drinkers left out in 30 of 56 curves; people who said they did not drink, 12 curves, or drank only occasionally, 14, with former drinkers not left out), the death rate was lowest at 6 g a day, about half a drink (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.83, from a fixed-effect model whose interval does not reflect the differences between studies), and stayed lower up to 42 g a day; in 87 and then 107 cohorts (up to 4,838,825 people and 425,564 deaths), in most of which the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking or drank occasionally, the relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90, and 0.83 to 0.88). These analyses give relative risks only, so the difference cannot be given as a number out of 100 (editors' observation). The difference shrinks or disappears with stricter comparison groups and with adjustment for study characteristics: people who had stopped drinking (some, the authors suggest, because of illness) died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38); against occasional drinkers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment), while abstainers had a higher one with limited adjustment (1.19, 1.12 to 1.27) but not after adjustment (1.04, 0.94 to 1.16); after adjustment for study characteristics (among them age, sex, smoking control and how each study defined its non-drinkers) the estimate was 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107; in the 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk it was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), about the same point estimate as in the 41 cohorts whose non-drinkers included both former and occasional drinkers (0.91, 0.83 to 1.00) but less precise; and in the 6 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger, followed beyond 55 and compared with people who had never drunk, 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 studies of older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers. Even in 2006, adjusted curves whose comparison group, by the authors' coding, did not include light or former drinkers (27 curves) showed a smaller reduction at the lowest point (16% against 23% in 21 curves whose comparison group did) that ended at 30 rather than 52 g a day. The 2016, 2023 and 2024 analyses are by one research group and reuse the same cohorts; the 6-study estimate rests on studies the article does not name and allows anything from a 13% lower to an 11% higher death rate (editors' arithmetic); and genetic studies, which avoid the non-drinker comparison, concern heart disease and diabetes rather than deaths from all causes (see the answers on the heart). None of these designs can show whether drinking a little itself makes people live longer or shorter. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In many large studies, people who drank a little (up to about two drinks a day, under 25 grams of alcohol) died at slightly lower rates than people who did not drink. But in most of these studies the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill, and people who drank now and then. When people who drank a little were compared with occasional drinkers, or with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference, though the few studies that made the strictest comparison cannot rule out a small gain or a small loss. Allowing for differences between the studies also shrank the gap. These studies cannot show whether a little alcohol itself helps, harms or makes no difference to how long people live, and researchers disagree.
population: Adults in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death from any cause published from 1981 to 2021, pooled in a 2006 meta-analysis (34 cohorts to December 2005) and in three analyses by one research group (87 cohorts to 2014; 107 to July 2021; subgroups of the 107); mostly from North America, Europe and Australia, with some from Asia; drinking reported at the start of each study

risk_of_bias.note: The comparison groups of most cohorts include former and/or occasional drinkers; drinking was self-reported, mostly once; each cohort adjusted for different confounders; the 2016 and 2023 adjusted estimates are study-level (ecological) models calculated at unstated covariate values; all four reviews are rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_di_castelnuovo_2006, sc_stockwell_2016, sc_zhao_2023, sc_stockwell_2024).

inconsistency.note: Estimates run from 0.81 to 1.04 depending on the comparison group and study features, which the abstainer biases partly explain; within categories heterogeneity remains large (I2 61% to 84% in 2016, above 85.87% in 2023; in 2006 the deviance fell from 879.4 to 154.0 with random effects).

indirectness.note: Death from any cause is measured directly; cohorts are mostly from high-income countries and middle-aged at entry, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: The estimates against study-defined non-drinkers are precise, but those least exposed to the biases are not: 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) from 6 studies, 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06) from 13, and 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) after adjustment, each compatible with a meaningful reduction and with no difference or an increase.

publication_bias.note: Egger tests found no evidence in 2016 and 2023; not assessed in 2006 or for the 2024 subgroups.

dose_response.note: The lower rate is a dip at low intake, not a gradient.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding and former drinkers in the comparison groups would more plausibly create than hide a lower death rate; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether drinking a little changes the risk of dying: the lower death rate against study-defined non-drinkers is consistent, but whether it reflects alcohol or the make-up of the comparison groups is disputed, and the estimates least exposed to the biases are too imprecise to show either a benefit or its absence. Overlapping evidence: Stockwell et al. (2016), Zhao et al. (2023) and Stockwell et al. (2024) are one group's analyses of largely the same cohorts (the 87 are among the 107, and the 2024 subgroups are drawn from the 107), and Di Castelnuovo et al. (2006) shares many cohorts with them, so their agreement on the unadjusted pattern is counted once, not as independent replication. Genetic (Mendelian randomization) studies are observational too: using gene variants linked to drinking addresses some confounding, but effects of the variants through other routes (pleiotropy), weak instruments, selection (for example analyses split by drinking status) and the inability of most to show a curve at low intake remain; here they are cited only second-hand, through the review the GBD 2020 authors cite, and for heart disease and diabetes, not deaths, so they do not change this rating and are rated in the answers on the heart. The editorial (Chikritzhs et al., 2015) frames the debate and is not counted as evidence. Status contested: credible evidence and critiques point both ways (METHODS §6.4, §7).

debate.question: Do people who drink a little live longer because of the alcohol, or is the lower death rate seen in many studies explained by who the non-drinkers are?
debate.evidence_yes: Pooled cohort studies consistently find lower death rates in people who drink a little than in non-drinkers as the studies defined them. In 34 cohorts with over a million people (Di Castelnuovo et al., 2006; sc_di_castelnuovo_2006; funded by the Italian research ministry, no financial disclosures reported), the pooled curve was lowest at 6 g a day (relative risk 0.81, 0.80 to 0.83); the reduction held in curves adjusted at least for age (17%) and for social status and diet as well (18%), and in curves whose comparison group, by the authors' coding, did not include light or former drinkers (16% at 5 g a day); within the same studies, adjustment moved the lowest point only from 19% to 16% lower, from which the authors argue that unmeasured confounding as strong as the measured kind would still leave more than 10%. In 87 and 107 cohorts the pooled relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (Stockwell et al., 2016, sc_stockwell_2016; Stockwell et al., 2024, sc_stockwell_2024), and after adjustment for study characteristics the point estimates stayed below 1 (0.97, 0.88 to 1.07, in 2016; 0.93, 0.85 to 1.01, P = .07, in Zhao et al., 2023, sc_zhao_2023), and in 2023 taking the study characteristics out of the model one at a time mostly lowered the estimate again (Zhao et al., 2023); the estimate in 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk (0.90, 0.76 to 1.06) was about the same as in 41 cohorts whose non-drinkers included both former and occasional drinkers (0.91), only less precise (Stockwell et al., 2016). A pooled analysis of individual data from many cohorts reproduced the U-shaped curve for deaths from any cause when never and former drinkers were included (Wood et al., 2018; sc_wood_2018; values in an appendix not read). The lower rate fits observational findings for the heart: in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 review, ischaemic heart disease was the one condition whose risk was significantly lower at low intake (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men at 0.83 standard drinks of 10 g a day and 0.82 in women at 0.92; GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; sc_griswold_2018); the heart findings, observational and genetic, are rated in the answers on the heart.
debate.evidence_no: How much lower the death rate looks depends on who is in the comparison group, as the abstainer-bias argument predicts. Of 87 cohorts, 65 counted people who had stopped drinking among their non-drinkers and 50 counted occasional drinkers; only 13 compared with people who had never drunk (Stockwell et al., 2016; funded by the US National Institutes of Health; no statement of the authors' interests). People who had stopped drinking died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38), and the 2006 authors note that former drinkers may have stopped because of health problems. Against occasional drinkers instead of abstainers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment). Adjusting for study characteristics moved the estimate from 0.86 to 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts, and from 0.85 to 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107 (Zhao et al., 2023; partly funded by the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction through a Health Canada grant for Canada's guidance on alcohol and health). In the 6 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger, followed beyond 55 and compared with people who had never drunk, the relative risk was 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), or 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without allowing for differences between studies, against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 studies of older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers (Stockwell et al., 2024; partly funded by the same centre under a contract for that guidance; three authors declare earlier funding from government alcohol monopolies, and two travel support from an organization that advocates against alcohol use). Even in 2006, curves whose comparison group, by the authors' coding, did not include light or former drinkers showed a smaller reduction that ended at a lower intake (30 against 52 g a day). Genetic studies avoid the non-drinker comparison: by a review that the Global Burden of Disease 2020 authors cite, 67% of such studies of heart and blood-vessel disease and 75% of those of diabetes found no association with alcohol (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022; sc_bryazka_2022). A 2015 editorial by six authors, three of whom wrote the 2016 review, argued on these grounds that the case for protection was so undermined that the field was due for repositioning, and that guidelines and burden estimates should assume no protection (Chikritzhs et al., 2015; sc_chikritzhs_2015; no interests declared).
debate.neither_can_show: Whether alcohol itself makes any difference: every study is observational, drinking was mostly reported once at the start, and people who never drink differ from people who drink in more than drinking (in the one analysis that compared them, in sex, ethnicity, smoking and diabetes; Wood et al., 2018), so even the strictest comparison cannot separate alcohol from the reasons people do not drink; cohorts recruited younger also contribute deaths at other ages and from other causes (editors' observation). The adjusted estimates of 2016 and 2023 come from models of study characteristics, not of people, calculated at covariate values the papers do not state, and the 2023 estimate moved lower when most single characteristics were taken out of its model. The decisive 6-study subgroup is not named in the article, its participants and deaths are not counted, no measure of disagreement between its studies is given, and its difference from the older cohorts is not tested in the article (editors' calculation from the printed intervals: ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.34, p of about .03). The four analyses share most of their cohorts (the 87 cohorts of 2016 are among the 107 of 2023 and 2024, all by one group), so their agreement is not independent, and all four rate critically low on a standard checklist for reviews (AMSTAR 2: for example single-database or English-only searches and no list of excluded studies). The genetic studies concern heart disease and diabetes, not deaths from all causes, and only five of 24 tested a curved relation that could show an effect at low intake. No source read gives death rates out of 100 or 1,000 for people who drink a little and people who do not.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the cohort studies read, people who drink a little die at somewhat lower rates than non-drinkers as most studies define them (relative risks of about 0.81 to 0.86, that is 14% to 19% lower), and pooled analyses of many cohorts consistently find that pattern, though the cohorts differ significantly among themselves (Di Castelnuovo et al., 2006; Stockwell et al., 2016; Stockwell et al., 2024). But it is largest where the non-drinkers include people who stopped drinking or drink occasionally (Di Castelnuovo et al., 2006; Stockwell et al., 2024), and it shrinks to no clear difference where the comparison is with occasional drinkers or with people who never drank, above all in cohorts recruited younger (Stockwell et al., 2016; Stockwell et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023); those estimates are few and imprecise, so neither a small benefit nor a small harm can be ruled out. The editors therefore do not read these studies as showing that drinking a little makes people live longer, nor as showing that it shortens life: the designs read cannot tell. Both sides' main estimates agree that people who had stopped drinking (Stockwell et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2023), and people drinking 45 g a day or more (1.12 to 1.44 in the 2016 analysis; Stockwell et al., 2016), died at higher rates than abstainers (see the answer on the amount at which drinking starts to shorten life).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A pooled analysis of individual data from cohorts that record drinking from early adulthood and repeatedly, with people who never drank and stable occasional drinkers as separate comparison groups and former drinkers counted at the amounts they used to drink, reporting death rates out of 1,000 under an adjustment set fixed in advance; genetic studies of deaths from all causes able to show the shape of the curve at low intake; or a long-term randomized trial of drinking a little against not drinking. None of the sources read reports these.

statement: In the world's population aged 15 and older, as modelled in two Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analyses, the second an update of the first that keeps 17 of its curves, drinking compared with not drinking is associated with a combined risk of 22 or 23 alcohol-linked diseases and injuries (each weighted by its share of the population's ill health, measured in disability-adjusted life years, DALYs) that is lowest at or near zero for people aged 15 to 39 and, in the newer model, at about half to two thirds of a standard drink (10 g of ethanol) a day worldwide for people aged 40 and older (0.114 to 1.87 across regions): these are model estimates for whole populations, resting on relative-risk curves fitted to observational studies of self-reported drinking; a lowest point is where the model's estimated gains in some conditions and losses in others balance best for a population, not one person's risk (the 2020 authors put individual risk outside their study's scope, while the 2016 authors presented the zero as the amount that minimises an individual's risk and concluded that drinking none at all carries the least risk); and every lowest point above zero comes from lower risks of ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in those studies (editors' reading of how the models are built), which genetic studies mostly do not find. In GBD 2016 (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018), one curve weighted by the world's 2016 disease mix had its lowest point at 0 standard drinks a day (95% uncertainty interval 0 to 0.8 a day; the abstract prints it per week) and rose with intake; of its 23 conditions only ischaemic heart disease had a significant dip (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 in women at 0.92), diabetes and ischaemic stroke dipped non-significantly, and the risks of all the others, every cancer it modelled among them, rose with intake; in women the lower heart disease and diabetes risks were offset by rising cancer risks. In GBD 2020 (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022), with weights from each region's, age group's and sex's own disease mix, the lowest point at ages 15 to 39 was 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions (worldwide 0.136 for men and 0.273 for women), and the combined risk was back at a non-drinker's level (where the model's average of gains and losses equals a non-drinker's combined risk) at 0.249 drinks a day for men and 0.546 for women worldwide (about 2.5 and 5.5 g; editors' arithmetic), injuries, whose risk rose with intake, making up much of the ill health weighed at these ages (66.3% in men, 47.9% in women); at 40 to 64 the lowest point was 0.527 (men) and 0.562 (women) drinks a day and the non-drinker level was reached at 1.69 and 1.82; at 65 and older, 0.636 and 0.656, and 3.19 and 3.51. Differences between women and men were not significant. Worldwide and age-standardised, the 2020 lowest point was 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700) drinks a day, and 0.534 (0 to 1.00) when the 2016 curves were given the 2020 weights, so the move away from zero comes mostly from the weights (editors' reading). Drinking a lot on some days was not modelled in either model; alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and dementia were left out of the 2020 curves, and the authors say that including the last three would possibly lower the amounts. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Two world models by one research team added up the risks of 22 or 23 diseases and injuries linked to alcohol, each counted by how much illness it causes. For people aged 15 to 39, the overall risk was lowest at no alcohol or almost none, and it was back at a non-drinker's level by about a quarter of a 10-gram drink a day for men and half a drink for women. For people aged 40 and over, the newer model put the lowest point at about half to two thirds of a drink a day, because some studies link small amounts to less heart disease, stroke and diabetes; most studies using genes did not find this for heart disease and diabetes. The lowest point is where the model's gains and losses balance for a whole population, not one person's risk, and in the older model the risk of every cancer it looked at rose with drinking. The models did not look at drinking a lot on some days.
population: The world's population aged 15 and older as modelled: 195 locations, 1990 to 2016 (GBD 2016), and GBD regions by 5-year age group and sex, 1990 to 2020 (GBD 2020)
exposure: Average daily alcohol intake, in standard drinks of 10 g of ethanol (curves fitted for 0 to 12.5 drinks a day in 2016, sampled from 0 to 100 g a day in 2020); current drinking means at least one drink in the past 12 months
comparator: Not drinking: the non-drinking groups of the underlying studies, whose make-up varied (in 2016 adjusted for former drinkers only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes; in 2020 through bias covariates chosen by the model)
outcome: A combined, DALY-weighted risk of 23 (2016) or 22 (2020) alcohol-linked conditions, including heart disease, stroke, diabetes, cancers, tuberculosis and injuries: the intake at which it is lowest (theoretical minimum risk exposure level, TMREL) and, in 2020, the intake at which it is back at a non-drinker's level (non-drinker equivalence, NDE)
magnitude: GBD 2016 (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; 23 outcomes, 592 studies, 3,992 relative-risk estimates; one curve weighted by global age-standardised 2016 DALY rates, both sexes; standard drink 10 g): lowest point of the weighted curve 0 standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 a day; printed per week in the abstract), rising monotonically; ischaemic heart disease lowest relative risk 0.86 (0.80 to 0.96) in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72 to 0.95) in women at 0.92; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; every modelled cancer rising. GBD 2020 (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022; 22 curves, five re-fitted with 71 more studies; weights by region, age, sex and year; TMREL the lowest point, NDE the return to a non-drinker's risk; standard drinks a day): all populations, TMREL 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30); ages 15 to 39 across regions TMREL 0 to 0.603 (0.400 to 1.00), NDE 0.002 (0 to 0) to 1.75 (0.698 to 4.30); global males TMREL 0.136 (0 to 0.400), NDE 0.249 (0 to 1.00), females 0.273 (0 to 0.500) and 0.546 (0 to 1.30); ages 40 to 64, males 0.527 (0.400 to 1.00) and 1.69 (0.800 to 3.20), females 0.562 (0.400 to 0.800) and 1.82 (1.00 to 3.10); 65 and older, males 0.636 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.19 (1.50 to 5.20), females 0.656 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.51 (1.70 to 5.50); ages 40 and older across regions, TMREL 0.114 (0 to 0.403) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30), NDE 0.193 (0 to 0.900) to 6.94 (3.40 to 8.30). Global, age-standardised, both sexes: GBD 2016 0 (0 to 0.800); GBD 2016 curves with 2020 weights 0.534 (0 to 1.00), NDE 0.669 (0 to 1.40); GBD 2020 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700), NDE 1.72 (0.80 to 3.30). Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL by 0.058 to 0.146 drinks a day on average. In grams (editors' arithmetic, 10 g a drink): 0.249 drinks is about 2.5 g, 0.546 about 5.5 g, 0.511 about 5.1 g.

risk_of_bias.note: The curves are fitted to observational studies of self-reported intake; GBD 2016 describes no appraisal of its 592 studies and allowed for former drinkers in the reference group only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes; GBD 2020 chose bias covariates by a Lasso, with the sets in an appendix not read; the dips at low intake that produce every non-zero lowest point are where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed (editors' checklist high on cards sc_griswold_2018 and sc_bryazka_2022).

inconsistency.note: The two analyses differ on the worldwide figure (0 against 0.511 drinks a day), a difference explained by the change of weights (0.534 with the 2016 curves and 2020 weights); they agree for ages 15 to 39.

indirectness.note: A population-weighted average of curves stands in for the question a person asks; one curve per condition is applied to every region; drinking patterns, several conditions and people under 15 are left out; the 'non-drinkers' of the 2020 curves are not defined in the main text.

imprecision.note: Intervals are narrow at older ages and wide for young adults (NDE 0 to 1.00 drinks a day for men aged 15 to 39) and do not include the choice of weights or of conditions; these limits are counted under risk of bias and indirectness rather than twice.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these papers.

grade.reasoning: The model outputs are not graded as evidence of an effect; the claim is graded from the evidence behind the curves, observational cohort and case-control studies, which starts low and is rated down for risk of bias and indirectness: very low. Worded as an association in modelled populations: these analyses cannot show that alcohol makes the combined risk rise or fall at any amount, and a lowest-risk amount is a property of a weighted average for a population, not a measure of any one person's risk. Genetic (Mendelian randomization) studies, cited here second-hand through the 2020 discussion, use gene variants linked to drinking, which addresses some confounding, but effects of the variants through other routes (pleiotropy), weak instruments, selection (for example analyses split by drinking status) and the inability of most to show a curve at low intake remain; they concern heart disease and diabetes, are rated in the answers on the heart, and are not used to raise or lower this rating. Overlapping evidence: GBD 2016 and GBD 2020 are one group's analyses sharing 17 of 22 curves, and the comment (Burton & Sheron, 2018) restates GBD 2016 and adds no data, so the agreement for young people is not independent replication. Status contested: the 2016 zero, read in the accompanying comment as showing that no level of drinking improves health, and the 2020 J-shaped curves at 40 and older point different ways, and the genetic evidence the 2020 authors cite is a credible critique of the dips that produce every non-zero lowest point.

debate.question: Is there an amount of alcohol that adds no risk to health, or does any amount add some risk?
debate.evidence_yes: The 2020 model (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022; sc_bryazka_2022; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation), which weighted the curves by each population's own mix of diseases, found the combined risk lowest above zero at ages 40 and older: about half to two thirds of a standard drink a day worldwide (0.527 to 0.656), with the model's average of gains and losses not back at a non-drinker's level until 1.69 to 3.51 drinks a day; across regions the lowest point at these ages ran from 0.114 (0 to 0.403) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30) drinks a day, and the abstract calls the curve J-shaped in every region. Worldwide and age-standardised, the lowest point was 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700) drinks a day, and the 2016 curves gave 0.534 with the 2020 weights, so the 2016 zero did not survive a change of weights; the 2016 model's own interval already reached 0.8 drinks a day (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; sc_griswold_2018; funded by the same foundation). The dip comes from observational findings: in the 2016 review ischaemic heart disease had a significant dip at low intake (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men and 0.82 in women at about 0.8 to 0.9 drinks a day), with non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke. The cohort evidence on deaths from any cause is in the answer on living longer.
debate.evidence_no: In the 2016 model the combined risk for the world's population rose steadily from zero: the lower heart disease and diabetes risks seen in women were outweighed by rising cancer risks, and the risk of every cancer it modelled rose with intake; the authors presented the zero as the amount that minimises an individual's risk and concluded that drinking none at all carries the least risk (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018). A comment published with it said in its title that no level of drinking improves health and took the result as strong support for the UK Chief Medical Officers' guideline that there is no safe level (Burton & Sheron, 2018; sc_burton_2018; both authors then employed by Public Health England; its figures are second-hand). The 2020 model agrees for younger people: at 15 to 39 the lowest point ran from 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions, and worldwide the combined risk was back at a non-drinker's level by 0.249 drinks a day for men and 0.546 for women (about 2.5 and 5.5 g; editors' arithmetic), injuries making up 66.3% of the ill health from the 22 conditions in young men. Every lowest point above zero comes from the dips for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes (editors' reading of how the models are built), and the 2020 authors report that most genetic studies found no association of alcohol with heart and blood-vessel disease (67%) or diabetes (75%) (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022). The 2020 curves leave out alcohol use disorder, alcohol-related heart muscle disease, depression, anxiety and dementia; hypothetical curves for the first two lowered the lowest point by 0.058 to 0.146 drinks a day on average, and the authors say the last three would possibly lower it too.
debate.neither_can_show: Any one person's risk: the curves average many conditions weighted by a whole population's disease mix, with one curve per condition applied to every region, and the 2020 authors put individual risk outside their study's scope and call their results for older adults more uncertain. Whether alcohol causes the differences: the curves are fitted to observational studies of self-reported drinking, whose non-drinking groups vary and were adjusted for former drinkers only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in 2016, and in which the 2020 authors name residual confounding, selection bias and reverse causation as possible. Drinking patterns: drinking a lot on some days was modelled in neither analysis. How uncertain the amounts are: the intervals carry sampling and model-parameter uncertainty but are not said to include the choice of weights or of conditions (editors' observation), and the worldwide figure moved from 0 to 0.534 with the same curves when only the weights changed. Independence: both analyses come from one research group and share 17 of the 22 curves, so their agreement for young people is not independent replication.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In both models, for people aged 15 to 39 the combined risk is lowest at or near zero (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022) and is back at a non-drinker's level within about a quarter (men) to half (women) of a 10-g drink a day worldwide (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022), so these models find at most a very small dip for young adults. For people aged 40 and older, the 2020 model puts the lowest combined risk at about half to two thirds of a drink a day worldwide (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022), but, by the editors' reading of how the models are built, only because of lower heart disease, stroke and diabetes risks in observational studies (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018), which genetic studies mostly do not find, as the 2020 authors report (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022); if those dips come from bias, the lowest point would be zero at every age. A lowest-risk amount is where the model's gains and losses across conditions balance best for a whole population; it is not one person's risk (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022), and in the 2016 curves the risk of every cancer modelled rose with intake (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018). Neither model looked at drinking a lot on some days (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022), and neither is a guide to one person's risk.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Dose-response curves for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes at low intake from designs less open to confounding and abstainer bias, above all genetic studies able to show a curve, in large cohorts of several ancestries that separate people who never drank from former drinkers; data on drinking patterns; and weights fixed in advance and published with all sensitivity analyses, with the combined curves checked against deaths from all causes in populations with different mixes of disease. None of the sources read reports these.
