statement: In people who drink, in 19 high-income countries, without known heart or blood-vessel disease at the start (83 cohort studies pooled with individual data; 599,912 people who drank, mean age 57; 40,310 deaths over a median 7.5 years), drinking more than about 100 g of alcohol a week (about 14 g a day, or ten 10-g drinks a week; editors' arithmetic) compared with drinking more than 0 and up to 25 g a week is associated with higher death rates that rise with the amount (Wood et al., 2018; adjusted for age, smoking status and diabetes within sex and study): modelled on US death rates, life expectancy at age 40, compared with people drinking up to 100 g a week, was about 6 months shorter at 100 to 200 g a week, 1 to 2 years shorter at 200 to 350 g and 4 to 5 years shorter above 350 g (men above 196 g, 2.7 years, 2.4 to 3.1); death rates were lowest in the groups below about 100 g a week, in men and women alike, and rose less steeply at older ages. About half of the people who drank reported more than 100 g a week (median 96 g). More drinking went with more strokes, heart failure and deaths from high blood pressure and aortic aneurysm, but slightly fewer heart attacks (hazard ratios per 100 g a week 1.14, 1.09, 1.24, 1.15 and 0.94). Compared with non-drinkers, the main pooled analyses find higher death rates in their categories of 45 g a day or more (315 g a week; editors' arithmetic): relative risk 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32) at 45 to 64 g and 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47) at 65 g or more after adjustment for study characteristics in 107 cohorts (Zhao et al., 2023), and 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82) at 45 g or more in the 7 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger, followed beyond 55 and compared with people who had never drunk (Stockwell et al., 2024). At 25 to 44 g a day the pooled estimates were not statistically clear (1.05, 0.96 to 1.14; in the younger cohorts 1.17, 0.98 to 1.40, which was 1.30, 1.05 to 1.60 without allowing for differences between studies), and were higher in women (1.21, 1.08 to 1.36) than in men (1.01, 0.93 to 1.10). Where the rise begins is not well defined: in the 13 studies of the 2016 analysis that compared with people who had never drunk, 45 to 64 g a day was not clearly raised (1.11, 0.93 to 1.32) but 65 g or more was (1.42, 1.15 to 1.75); in 18 studies of older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers, the 2024 curve did not rise clearly above 1 even at 45 g or more; and the 2024 authors say their categories are too broad to show at what amount the risk of death becomes significantly higher. In a 2006 pooled curve, against each study's lowest-intake category, the lower death rate was no longer significant above 42 g a day across all 56 curves, some of them unadjusted, and above 18 g in women's and 38 g in men's curves adjusted at least for age. The amounts are what people reported, mostly measured once (the 2018 hazard ratios refer to long-term average intake estimated from repeat measures in some participants, its life-expectancy groups to intake reported at the start), and the 2023 authors say intake is mostly under-reported; the 100 g threshold is read from a figure without an interval; people who drank more also smoked more and more often had lower socio-economic status, which the main models allowed for only through smoking status; and some people who had cut down because of illness were probably among the lighter drinkers, so the 2018 authors cannot exclude reverse causation. These designs cannot show that the extra drinking itself shortened life. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 83 studies of people who drink, death rates were lowest in people drinking up to about 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day) and rose above that. Using the researchers' model, 40-year-olds drinking 100 to 200 grams a week could expect about 6 months less life than those drinking up to 100 grams, 200 to 350 grams about 1 to 2 years less, and more than 350 grams about 4 to 5 years less. About half of the people who drank reported more than 100 grams a week. Compared with people who did not drink, the main studies found higher death rates in their groups drinking 45 grams a day or more; at 25 to 44 grams the results were not clear, except in women in one analysis, and the groups were too broad to show where the rise begins. People reported their own drinking, mostly once and often less than they drank; people who drank more also smoked more; and some who cut down because of illness were probably among the lighter drinkers, so the studies cannot show that the extra alcohol itself shortened life.
population: People who drink, in high-income countries: 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease in 83 cohorts pooled with individual data (mean age 57, 44% women); and, for comparisons with non-drinkers, adults in the cohort studies pooled in three meta-analyses (34, 87 and 107 cohorts)
exposure: Self-reported alcohol intake: in grams a week in categories from more than 0 to more than 350 g, corrected to long-term average intake (individual data); in grams a day in the meta-analyses (25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 g or more; 45 g or more in the younger cohorts)
comparator: People drinking more than 0 and up to 25 g a week for death rates, and more than 0 and up to 100 g a week for life expectancy (individual data, current drinkers only); in the meta-analyses, non-drinkers as each study defined them, lifetime abstainers as modelled, or each study's lowest-intake category
outcome: Death from any cause; modelled life expectancy at age 40; first stroke, heart failure, heart attack and other cardiovascular events
magnitude: Wood et al. 2018 (83 cohorts; 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease; 40,310 deaths; median follow-up 7.5 years; reference more than 0 and up to 25 g a week; adjusted for age, smoking status and diabetes, stratified by sex and study): all-cause mortality lowest below about 100 g a week (category values only in a figure; no interval for the threshold); modelled life expectancy at 40 against more than 0 and up to 100 g a week: about 6 months shorter at more than 100 to 200 g, 1 to 2 years at more than 200 to 350 g, 4 to 5 years above 350 g; men above 112 g a week 1.6 years (1.3 to 1.8), above 196 g 2.7 years (2.4 to 3.1); women above 112 or 98 g about 1.3 years (1.1 to 1.5); per 100 g a week, stroke HR 1.14 (1.10 to 1.17), heart failure 1.09 (1.03 to 1.15), fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15 to 1.33), fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), coronary disease other than heart attack 1.06 (1.00 to 1.11), heart attack 0.94 (0.91 to 0.97); about 50% of current drinkers above 100 g a week (median 96 g). Against non-drinkers (study level): Zhao et al. 2023, fully adjusted, 25 to 44 g a day 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14), 45 to 64 g 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32), 65 g or more 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47); men 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10), 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), 1.34 (1.23 to 1.47); women 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36), 1.34 (1.11 to 1.63), 1.61 (1.44 to 1.80); Stockwell et al. 2016, limited adjustment 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00), 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17), 1.29 (1.22 to 1.36), all study-level covariates 1.07 (0.97 to 1.18), 1.24 (1.12 to 1.37), 1.44 (1.30 to 1.60); against strictly defined lifetime abstainers, 13 bias-free studies 0.95 (0.80 to 1.13), 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32), 1.42 (1.15 to 1.75), seven higher-quality studies 1.08 (0.72 to 1.62), 0.95 (0.62 to 1.46), 1.58 (1.05 to 2.38), and without Friesema et al. 1.29 (1.06 to 1.56), 1.07 (0.83 to 1.36), 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27); Stockwell et al. 2024, studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger and followed beyond 55, against lifetime abstainers, with a random study effect, 25 to under 45 g 1.17 (0.98 to 1.40; 1.30, 1.05 to 1.60, without it), 45 g or more 1.51 (1.25 to 1.82), former drinkers 1.32 (1.13 to 1.54); in 18 studies of older cohorts with both abstainer biases, no clear rise even at 45 g or more (figure only); categories too broad to locate the rise, by the authors' account; Di Castelnuovo et al. 2006, against each study's lowest-intake category, lower mortality no longer significant above 42 g a day in all 56 curves (men 38 g, women 18 g, in curves adjusted at least for age), and the fitted curves cross a relative risk of 1 at about 44 g a day (men 41 g, women 25 g; editors' calculation from the printed parameters). Unit conversions (editors' arithmetic): 100 g a week is about 14 g a day; 45 g a day is 315 g a week; 25 g a day is 175 g a week.

risk_of_bias.note: Wood et al. (ROBINS-E high on card sc_wood_2018): the main models adjust only for age, smoking status (current or not) and diabetes within sex and study; people who cut down because of illness probably stay in the lighter groups (residual reverse causation, which the authors cannot exclude); intake was self-reported once and corrected for regression dilution with repeat measures from about 12% of participants (71,011 people; editors' arithmetic). The meta-analyses compared with non-drinkers that include former drinkers in most cohorts and are critically low on AMSTAR 2.

inconsistency.note: The main analyses all find higher death rates at the heaviest intakes; where the rise begins differs with the comparison (the lightest drinkers or non-drinkers), with sex (25 to 44 g a day: women 1.21, men 1.01) and between the main models and the small subsets compared with people who had never drunk (45 to 64 g a day 1.11, 0.93 to 1.32, in 13 cohorts), which the claim states rather than resolves; the one subset without a clear rise even at 45 g or more, older cohorts whose comparison groups included former and occasional drinkers, fits the abstainer-bias explanation. Not rated down.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: people who drink, mostly middle-aged and older, in high-income countries; the life-expectancy differences are modelled on US death rates for 2007 to 2010, which the claim says.

imprecision.note: Large numbers (40,310 deaths in the individual data); the threshold itself has no interval because it is read from plotted category results, which the claim states as 'about'.

publication_bias.note: Egger tests found none in the 2016 and 2023 meta-analyses; not assessable for the pooled individual data.

large_effect.note: No category ratio above 2 is printed in the texts read.

dose_response.note: Death rates and modelled life-expectancy losses rise step by step with intake above about 100 g a week (about 6 months, 1 to 2 years, 4 to 5 years), and across the meta-analyses' categories (for example 1.05, 1.19 and 1.35 at 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 g a day or more), in individual data from 83 cohorts and in study-level data from 107.

plausible_confounding.note: Reverse causation from people who cut down because of illness would make the lighter groups look worse and hide part of the rise, while smoking and lower socio-economic status, which rise with intake, could add to it; they pull in opposite directions; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low, is rated down once for risk of bias and up once for a dose-response gradient: low. The upgrade is made although the evidence was rated down, because the gradient appears within people who drink (no abstainer comparison is needed for it), in individual data from 83 cohorts, and again in study-level data compared with non-drinkers; a strict reading that withholds the upgrade, because smoking and lower socio-economic status also rise with intake and the main models allow only for smoking status, gives very low. Worded as an association: these designs cannot show that the extra drinking caused the deaths. Status replicated: Wood et al. (a consortium analysis of 83 cohorts), the Stockwell–Zhao group's analyses (counted once) and Di Castelnuovo et al. are different teams whose estimates all rise at heavier intake, though they may share some cohorts; the threshold of about 100 g a week itself rests on one pooled analysis, and against non-drinkers the intake at which the rise begins is not well defined (the strict subsets and the 2024 authors' own caveat). Whether the cohorts of the 2018 analysis overlap with those of the meta-analyses is not reported.

statement: In adults followed in cohort studies, mostly in high-income countries, drinking a little compared with not drinking is associated with less coronary heart disease, but how much less depends on who is counted as not drinking, and no paper read gives absolute risks, so the ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them (in most studies people not drinking at the start, including former drinkers), people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.77) for new coronary heart disease (29 studies) and 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81) for coronary death (31 studies); at 2.5 to 14.9 g of ethanol a day (up to about one drink, counted as 12.5 g where a study gave no grams) the figures were 0.75 (0.65 to 0.88) and 0.79 (0.73 to 0.86), below 2.5 g a day 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06) and 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), and at every higher intake, up to more than 60 g a day, 0.66 to 0.79; 8 of the 84 cohort reports gave only unadjusted estimates (Ronksley et al., 2011). In the 7 to 9 studies that compared with lifetime abstainers the figures were similar (0.73, 0.61 to 0.88; 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85), and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31, 1.02 to 1.68; against non-drinkers in the paper's table, against people who drank in its text). A review that compared with lifetime abstainers, leaving out former drinkers and correcting estimates of deaths (not of new cases) from studies whose comparison group was current non-drinkers, and that kept men, women, deaths and new cases apart (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; 24 of its 44 cohort and case-control studies) found lower point estimates at about one drink of 12 g a day in all four groups, but men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27); with all 44 studies, including those that combined men and women or deaths and new cases, every estimate at about one to three drinks a day was lower (0.62 to 0.81), and occasional drinking (less than weekly, or under 2.5 g a day) was not associated with coronary risk in any group. Of 23 conditions in the GBD 2016 curves fitted to 592 studies, only ischaemic heart disease showed a significant dip, lowest at 0.83 drinks of 10 g a day in men (relative risk 0.86, 95% uncertainty interval 0.80 to 0.96) and 0.92 in women (0.82, 0.72 to 0.95). Self-reported drinking showed the same dip in Chinese men (Millwood et al., 2019) and in UK Biobank, where allowing for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable and red meat intake and self-rated health removed the statistically clear difference at moderate intake (more than 8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g a week) and, read approximately from the paper's figure, reduced but did not remove it at light intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). Whether alcohol causes the lower risk is disputed: in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, former drinkers had more coronary deaths than lifetime abstainers (men 1.25, women 1.54), and in men drinking 60 g a day or more the lower risk seen against current non-drinkers (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) was not seen against lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014); the genetic studies read do not find the lower risk (see the answer on gene studies). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In many long-term studies, people who drank a little (up to about one drink a day) had about a quarter less heart disease than people who did not drink. But the people who did not drink included some who had stopped, perhaps because they were ill. When the comparison was with people who had never drunk, and men, women, deaths and new cases were kept apart, the difference in men's heart deaths was small and could be chance. In a large UK study, allowing for smoking, weight, exercise, diet and health made the difference at moderate drinking no longer clear. The gene studies we read did not find it. So it is not known whether alcohol itself lowers heart risk, and none of these studies says how many people out of 100 the difference would mean.
population: Adults in cohort studies published up to 2010, mostly from high-income countries: 84 prospective cohort reports of adults without cardiovascular disease at the start (Ronksley et al.) and 44 cohort and case-control studies that were not required to exclude heart disease at the start (Roerecke & Rehm 2012); the 592 studies behind the GBD 2016 curves; and the China Kadoorie Biobank (men) and UK Biobank cohorts

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews are rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_ronksley_2011, sc_roerecke_2012) and neither appraised the risk of bias of the cohorts. In most cohorts the comparison group included former drinkers, some of whom stopped because of illness; 8 of 84 reports gave only unadjusted estimates and 11 of 44 studies adjusted for age only; in UK Biobank six lifestyle factors removed the association at moderate intake. These biases can change the estimate materially: against lifetime abstainers, with men, women, deaths and new cases kept apart, men's coronary deaths at about one or two drinks a day were no longer clearly lower.

inconsistency.note: The direction is consistent (by the authors' account, all but one to two study estimates per coronary outcome below 1). Statistical heterogeneity is high (I² 72.2%; up to 84%) and follows partly the reference group, sex and end point, which is the risk-of-bias problem and is not rated twice; women's coronary deaths at about two drinks a day (1.03) are an exception.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: an association in the cohorts studied, mostly in high-income countries, with drinking measured once at baseline.

imprecision.note: The pooled estimates are precise; the stratified lifetime-abstainer estimates are not, which the statement says.

publication_bias.note: Begg's test P 0.089 to 0.75 (Ronksley et al.); one of the Peters' tests positive (Roerecke & Rehm 2012); not rated down.

large_effect.note: Relative risks of 0.71 to 0.79; not large.

dose_response.note: No gradient: coronary risk is similar from 2.5 g to more than 60 g a day against current non-drinkers (an L shape), which does not fit a protective dose–response.

plausible_confounding.note: The remaining confounding (healthier habits of people who drink lightly; illness among former drinkers) would more plausibly exaggerate than hide the lower risk; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (comparison groups that include former drinkers, incomplete adjustment, and confounding shown directly in UK Biobank), so very low. Rated as worded: an association; whether alcohol causes it is the question of the debate box. Overlapping evidence is counted once: the two reviews share many cohorts, the GBD 2016 curves are fitted to largely the same studies and are model estimates used here only for the shape of the ischaemic heart disease curve, and the UK Biobank and China Kadoorie analyses are single cohorts. The many primary cohorts agree in direction, but the status is contested rather than replicated, because published critiques (Roerecke & Rehm 2012 and 2014 on the reference group; Biddinger et al. 2022 on lifestyle) and the genetic studies change how the association is read, and the reviews' own authors read it differently.

debate.question: Does drinking a little lower the risk of heart disease, or do the comparisons in cohort studies only make it look that way?
debate.evidence_yes: The lower risk is one of the most consistent findings of cohort studies. In 84 cohort reports published to 2009, people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 for new coronary heart disease and 0.75 for coronary death against non-drinkers, with nearly every study's estimate below 1 by the authors' account, and the figures were similar in the 7 to 9 studies that used lifetime abstainers (0.73 and 0.75) (Ronksley et al., 2011; sc_ronksley_2011). With former drinkers removed and mortality estimates corrected for them (estimates of new cases were not corrected), all 44 studies in a second review gave lower risks at about one to three drinks of 12 g a day in men and in women, for deaths and for new cases (0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1) (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; sc_roerecke_2012). The GBD 2016 curves, adjusted for former drinkers in the reference group for this condition, show a significant dip for ischaemic heart disease alone among 23 conditions (0.86 in men and 0.82 in women at just under one drink of 10 g a day; sc_griswold_2018), and self-reported drinking shows the dip again in Chinese men and in UK Biobank (sc_millwood_2019; sc_biddinger_2022). In seven studies, people averaging under 30 g a day without heavy drinking days had a relative risk of 0.64 against lifetime abstainers (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014; sc_roerecke_2014). Short-term experiments, cited second-hand, show alcohol raising HDL cholesterol and lowering platelet activation and fibrinogen, and the authors of two of the reviews argue on Hill's criteria that the association, at least for regular light drinking, is causal (Ronksley et al., 2011; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). A published critique argues that the genetic studies pointing the other way have biases of their own (Mukamal et al., 2020; sc_mukamal_2020).
debate.evidence_no: Much of the lower risk depends on the comparison group and on adjustment. Most cohorts counted former drinkers among non-drinkers, and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31 in Ronksley et al.'s table; against lifetime abstainers, men 1.25 and women 1.54 in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand by Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). With lifetime abstainers as the comparison and men, women, deaths and new cases kept apart, men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27), and the authors concluded that a cardioprotective association cannot be assumed for all people who drink, even at low intake (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012). In UK Biobank, people who drank lightly or moderately smoked less, had lower body mass index, were more active and reported better health than people who did not drink, and allowing for six such factors removed the clear difference at moderate intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). The shape of the cohort results also fits bias better than benefit: against current non-drinkers coronary death was as low above 60 g a day as at one drink (0.75), with no gradient, while in men drinking 60 g or more it was not lower against lifetime abstainers (1.00, second-hand). The genetic studies read, which are less exposed to these biases, do not find a lower risk: a variant that makes people drink less went with less, not more, coronary heart disease (0.90; Holmes et al., 2014; sc_holmes_2014), and in Chinese men the dip seen with self-reported drinking was absent when men were grouped by genotype (heart attack 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18, per 280 g a week; Millwood et al., 2019) (see the answer on gene studies). The experiments measure markers, not heart disease, and HDL cholesterol is also raised by heavy drinking and is highest in people with alcohol use disorder (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014).
debate.neither_can_show: No long-term randomized trial of drinking and heart disease exists (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). The cohorts measured drinking once, by self-report, mostly in high-income countries, and cannot fully separate alcohol from the health, habits and social position of people who choose to drink a little; lifetime abstainers, too, may differ from people who drink in ways that were not measured. The genetic studies test lifelong differences in drinking and cannot show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence (see the answer on gene studies). No paper read gives absolute risks, so how many heart attacks any difference would mean cannot be said. The reviews share many cohorts, and the GBD 2016 curve is fitted to largely the same studies, so their agreement is not independent replication.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The sources agree that, in cohort studies, people who drink a little have less coronary heart disease than people who do not drink (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; Ronksley et al., 2011); they disagree on why. The strongest argument for a real protective effect is how consistent the association is across cohorts, sexes and end points (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; Ronksley et al., 2011), and that in the pooled data it survives leaving out former drinkers and correcting the death estimates (not those of new cases) for them (0.62 to 0.81; Roerecke & Rehm, 2012). The strongest arguments against are that it shrinks or becomes uncertain when men, women, deaths and new cases are kept apart (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012), that it weakened with fuller allowance for lifestyle in a large recent cohort (Biddinger et al., 2022), that against current non-drinkers it is as large at heavy intake as at light intake (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014; Ronksley et al., 2011), and that genetic studies, with different weaknesses (Mukamal et al., 2020), do not reproduce it (Holmes et al., 2014; Millwood et al., 2019). On the evidence read, a lower coronary risk with light drinking is observed but has not been shown to be caused by alcohol; if there is an effect, these studies cannot say how large it is, and none gives an absolute risk. The editors do not read this evidence as showing harm to the heart from light drinking either; that question rests on the genetic studies and their critique (see the answer on gene studies).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A long-term randomized trial of light drinking against not drinking with heart disease as the outcome. Short of that: individual-level reanalyses of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories that separate lifetime abstainers, former and occasional drinkers, measure drinking and drinking pattern repeatedly and take account of health before the start, reported with absolute risks; set beside genetic analyses in several ancestries that can estimate the curve at low intake without dividing people by how much they say they drink. None of the sources read reports these.

statement: In people of European descent and in Chinese men, genetic variants that predict more drinking, compared with variants that predict less, are associated with more coronary heart disease in the European studies but not with heart attacks in the Chinese study; in its main analysis none of the four genetic studies read found lower coronary risk with genetically higher intake, none can show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence, and a published critique argues that such studies remain observational and have biases of their own. No study gives absolute risks. In a collaboration of 56 European-descent studies (261,991 people), carriers of a variant of the alcohol-metabolising gene ADH1B reported 17.2% less drinking (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%) and had lower odds of coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96; 46 studies, 20,259 events in 168,731 people); the authors stated in their Methods that a protective effect of light to moderate drinking would show as higher odds in carriers who drank lightly to moderately, but the odds were similar at every level of drinking and each of those estimates was compatible with no difference (more than 0 to under 7 UK units of 7.9 g a week, 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02), and the variant went with lower blood pressure even in people who said they did not drink (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank (371,463 people; the disease analyses were in people who drank, whose number is not printed), a genetic score built from variants for alcohol use disorder was associated with coronary artery disease, odds ratio 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (a unit the paper does not define), and curves fitted with a method whose key assumption is not reported as tested in the main text rose from the first drink, though a second score suggested no rise below roughly 7 to 14 drinks of 14 g a week, with slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some analyses in women, which the authors attribute to pleiotropy in that score and low power (Biddinger et al., 2022). In European summary data with up to 94 variants, the odds ratio was 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36) per standard deviation of log drinks a week and 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, which the variants also predicted; the ADH1B variant alone was associated with coronary artery disease (Larsson et al., 2020). In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults, men's genotype-predicted mean intakes (4 to 256 g a week by group) were not associated with heart attack (relative risk 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18, per 280 g a week, which is 40 g a day; 1,696 cases, an interval that allows about a fifth lower or a fifth higher risk) or with coronary heart disease (1.05, 0.94 to 1.17), although self-reported drinking in the same men showed lower heart-attack rates at moderate intake than in non-drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). Three authors (Mukamal et al., 2020; no funding or interests statement printed) argue that such analyses can be biased by ancestry, by parents' genes and drinking, by weak links between genes and reported intake, by genes that act through acetaldehyde rather than amount, by lowering heavy drinking days together with average intake, and by testing lifelong rather than adult drinking; they quantify none of these and report no figures from the studies they criticize, and they also cite three East Asian genetic association reports (by their titles not analyses of alcohol) that found more coronary heart disease with the ALDH2 variant that lowers drinking; Roerecke and Rehm (2014) judged the ADH1B result hard to compare with cohort studies because the variant also lowers binge drinking, while calling such genetic studies a possibly very useful tool. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Some people carry genes that make them drink less, or more. Comparing them avoids some of the problems of asking people how much they drink. In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking less went with slightly less heart disease, and genes for drinking more with more. In a large study of Chinese men, genes for drinking more made no clear difference to heart attacks either way. None of the studies we read found that genes for drinking more lowered heart risk. One UK study suggested that risk rises from the first drink, but a different set of genes gave a different answer. Three researchers argue that gene studies can be misled, for example by family background, by heavy drinking days, or by genes that act in other ways; they did not measure how much this matters, and they note that some other Asian gene studies pointed the other way. None of the studies says how many people out of 100 are affected.
population: People of European descent in 56 pooled studies (Holmes et al.), in UK Biobank (Biddinger et al.) and in genome-wide consortia with UK Biobank (Larsson et al.); adults in ten areas of China (China Kadoorie Biobank; genetic coronary results for men, women as a check); and a published methodological critique
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake: carriage of the ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele (lower intake); a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder scaled to genetically predicted intake; up to 94 variants for log drinks a week; ALDH2 rs671 and ADH1B rs1229984 genotypes combined with area into six groups of mean male intake (4 to 256 g/week)
comparator: Non-carriers, or lower genetically predicted intake (per standard deviation; per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean male intake against the lowest group)
outcome: Coronary heart disease or coronary artery disease (incident and prevalent events in the ADH1B study), heart attack (myocardial infarction), and the shape of the association at low intake
magnitude: Holmes et al. 2014 (56 studies, 261,991 European-descent people; ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele carriers against non-carriers): weekly intake 17.2% lower (15.6% to 18.9%), binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84), abstention 1.27 (1.21–1.34); coronary heart disease OR 0.90 (0.84–0.96; 20,259 events; I² 17%), 0.81 (0.72–0.91) in four studies with at least 1,000 events; self-reported non-drinkers 0.98 (0.88–1.10), drinkers 0.86 (0.78–0.94), difference P = 0.095; light (more than 0 to under 7 UK units/week of 7.9 g) 0.90 (0.79–1.02), moderate (7 to under 21) 0.89 (0.75–1.06), heavy (21 or more) 0.97 (0.76–1.24), trend P = 0.83; systolic blood pressure in self-reported non-drinkers −0.80 mm Hg (−1.41 to −0.19); no instrumental-variable estimate. Biddinger et al. 2022 (UK Biobank, 371,463; 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder, F 780; OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10–1.74; P = .006), myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05–1.78; P = .02, above the paper's threshold of P < .008); nonlinear: quadratic fit best (P < .001), risk rising from zero intake with the primary score; secondary score: no rise until roughly 7 to 14 drinks (14 g) a week. Larsson et al. 2020 (up to 94 variants; per SD of log drinks/week): coronary artery disease 1.16 (1.00–1.36; P = 0.052), 1.08 (0.91–1.27) adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation; never-smokers 1.39 (0.98–1.96); instrument and smoking initiation OR 1.24 (1.15–1.33); ADH1B variant alone, positive (P < 0.05). Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; six genotype–area groups, mean intake 4 to 256 g/week; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): myocardial infarction RR 0.96 (0.78–1.18; 1,696 cases), coronary heart disease 1.05 (0.94–1.17; 6,145 cases); single variants (GG against AG) myocardial infarction rs671 1.02 (0.92–1.13), rs1229984 1.11 (0.95–1.31); women 0.94 (0.74–1.20). Mukamal et al. 2020: no estimates. No absolute risks in any study.

evidence.extracted: An essay, with no methods, data or effect estimates of its own, arguing that Mendelian randomization is an instrumental-variable method subject to confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation and failure of replication; that the example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease shows it must be treated with the caution due to all observational epidemiology; and that it should be renamed genetic instrumental variable analysis, without the words randomization or causality.

evidence.extracted: Population structure: the ADH1B variant used as an instrument in alcohol analyses (its refs 1 and 2, Holmes et al. and Millwood et al.) is said to be most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern descent, including Jews; in the ADH1B analysis it went with lower reported drinking but also with more education, which the authors read as likely to reflect ancestry and a healthier lifestyle (no figures given). Adjustment with a few principal components succeeds only if the subpopulation is large enough to appear among them, and Ashkenazi Jews are about 0.2% of Europe's population. Parental genotype: carriers of variants that lower drinking carry them from at least one parent and so are less likely to have been raised by a parent with alcohol dependence, which the essay cites as a risk factor for later cardiovascular disease.

evidence.extracted: Drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects; genetic variants lower all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and those linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Genotype tests lifelong (and parental) rather than adult exposure; given common unhealthy drinking patterns in adolescence and early adulthood, their lower prevalence in young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking starts atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), such analyses may be testing adult binge drinking and possibly also teenage and young-adult binge drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.

risk_of_bias.note: The genetic design protects against confounding by lifestyle and against illness changing drinking, because genotype is fixed at conception (the cards rate confounding some concerns, not high), so the editors do not rate down for classical confounding. It does not protect against pleiotropy (the European instrument predicted smoking initiation, and its coronary estimate fell from 1.16 to 1.08 after allowing for it; the ADH1B variant went with lower blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index in people reporting no drinking; scores for alcohol use disorder may act on other behaviours), selection (studies joined by collaboration and prevalent cases in the ADH1B study; UK Biobank volunteers; estimates within strata of reported drinking, which genotype itself changes) or sample overlap (UK Biobank in both exposure and outcome data). Weak instruments are not the problem here (F 780 in UK Biobank; more than 50-fold differences in mean intake in China). Because the pleiotropy checks moved one estimate to no difference, rated down one level.

inconsistency.note: The European studies point to more coronary disease with genetically higher intake (0.90 for the intake-lowering variant; 1.16 to 1.38 per SD); the Chinese study, with the largest genetic differences in intake, finds no association with heart attack (0.96) or coronary heart disease (1.05). Not explained by the sources (ancestry, mainly spirits in China, different genes, different outcome definitions).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: what the genetic studies find. As evidence about light drinking in adult life it would be indirect (genotypes mark lifelong differences; the European estimates are per SD of genetically predicted intake and cannot be put into grams; only one analysis addresses low intake, with an untested assumption); stated rather than rated, as certainty is already at the floor.

imprecision.note: The Chinese heart-attack estimate (0.78 to 1.18; 1,696 cases) includes both a fifth lower and a fifth higher risk; the European summary-data estimate is borderline (1.00 to 1.36); the ADH1B drinking-category estimates each include no difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with four studies; the ADH1B study used mainly unpublished genetic data.

grade.reasoning: Mendelian randomization is observational and starts low (round brief). The genetic design addresses confounding by lifestyle and reverse causation, which is why risk of bias is rated down for pleiotropy, selection and sample overlap rather than for classical confounding; those threats, and the inability to show a curve at low intake (the one nonlinear analysis changed with the score used), remain. Rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded: genetic associations; whether they show that alcohol raises, or does not lower, coronary risk is the question of the debate box. Not fully independent: Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. share two authors, and Larsson et al. and Biddinger et al. both use UK Biobank outcome data. The critique (Mukamal et al.) concerns Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. only and was published before the other two. Status contested: credible results point in different directions and a published critique changes how they are read.

debate.question: Do the gene studies show that drinking more raises the risk of heart disease, and that a little drinking does not protect the heart?
debate.evidence_yes: The genetic design avoids the two biases that critics of cohort studies stress most: genotype is fixed at conception, so it is not chosen together with a lifestyle, and it is not changed by illness, as drinking can be. With strong instruments, three European-descent analyses point the same way: carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of coronary heart disease (0.90, 0.84 to 0.96; 0.81 in the four largest studies), and the pattern the authors' Methods said a protective effect would produce, higher odds in carriers who drank lightly or moderately, did not appear (Holmes et al., 2014; sc_holmes_2014); a score for alcohol use disorder (F statistic 780) gave 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per SD in UK Biobank, with three methods robust to some pleiotropy pointing the same way and no association with the continuous traits reported in 34,423 lifelong abstainers apart from HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A (no disease results for abstainers are printed) (Biddinger et al., 2022; sc_biddinger_2022); and up to 94 variants gave 1.16 (1.00 to 1.36), larger in never-smokers (1.39, 0.98 to 1.96), with the ADH1B variant alone also positive (Larsson et al., 2020; sc_larsson_2020). In Chinese men the dip in heart attacks seen with self-reported drinking did not appear when men were grouped by genotype (Millwood et al., 2019; sc_millwood_2019): in its main analysis, no genetic study read found lower coronary risk with genetically higher intake.
debate.evidence_no: The genetic results are not consistent and rest on assumptions that cannot all be checked. With the strongest instrument, in Chinese men, genetically higher intake showed no association with heart attack (0.96, 0.78 to 1.18) or coronary heart disease (1.05, 0.94 to 1.17), neither harm nor benefit (Millwood et al., 2019). In European summary data the coronary association was borderline and fell to 1.08 (0.91 to 1.27) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, which the alcohol variants also predicted (odds ratio 1.24 for starting to smoke) (Larsson et al., 2020). The ADH1B variant went with lower blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index in people who reported not drinking, about as much as in people who drank lightly, which points either to misreported drinking or to a path other than alcohol; its light-drinking estimate (0.90, 0.79 to 1.02) is compatible with no difference; and carriers had slightly more education (Holmes et al., 2014). The UK Biobank curves that rise from the first drink come from a method that is valid only if the score shifts intake by the same amount at every level, which is not reported as tested in the main text, and a second score gave no rise below roughly 7 to 14 drinks a week, with slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some analyses in women, which the authors attribute to pleiotropy in that score (Biddinger et al., 2022). A published critique (Mukamal et al., 2020; sc_mukamal_2020) argues that the ADH1B variant is most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern descent, so ancestry could confound it in European data (Ashkenazi Jews are about 0.2% of Europe's population, too few for standard ancestry adjustment to capture); that parents' genes shape exposure to a parent's alcohol dependence in childhood; that the variant's null association with HDL cholesterol, which alcohol raises in trials, suggests a weak instrument; that ALDH2 variants raise acetaldehyde in people who drink, so stronger associations in people who drink may reflect toxicity rather than amount; that genes lower heavy drinking days together with average intake, so the studies may be showing the harm of heavy drinking days; and that genotype tests lifelong, including youthful, drinking rather than limited drinking in mid-life; it also cites three East Asian genetic association reports (by their titles not analyses of alcohol) that found more coronary heart disease with the ALDH2 variant that lowers drinking. Roerecke and Rehm (2014; sc_roerecke_2014) also judged the ADH1B result hard to compare with cohort studies because the variant lowers binge drinking too.
debate.neither_can_show: Neither side can show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence: one variant or score shifts intake across the whole range, the European estimates are per SD of genetically predicted intake and cannot be put into grams, and the only nonlinear analysis depended on an assumption not reported as tested in the main text and on the score used. Genotypes mark lifelong differences in drinking, so the studies cannot separate adult from youthful drinking, or average amount from heavy drinking days. Whether the variants act only through the amount drunk cannot be proved: the critique shows that biases are possible but quantifies none, and the studies' checks (ancestry adjustment, people who do not drink as a negative control, pleiotropy-robust methods, allowance for smoking liability) reduce but cannot rule them out. The results come from people of European descent and from Chinese men; women in China served only as a check, because few drink. None of the studies reports absolute risks.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The four genetic studies agree on one point: in its main analysis, none finds that genetically higher intake goes with lower coronary risk (Biddinger et al., 2022; Holmes et al., 2014; Larsson et al., 2020; Millwood et al., 2019), which a real protective effect of drinking would predict. Beyond that they differ: two European studies find more coronary disease with genetically higher intake (Biddinger et al., 2022; Holmes et al., 2014), and the third a borderline association that shrinks to no difference once genetic liability to smoking is allowed for (Larsson et al., 2020), and the Chinese study, with the largest genetic differences in intake, finds neither more nor fewer heart attacks (Millwood et al., 2019). The critique (Mukamal et al., 2020) is right that these are observational analyses whose assumptions must be defended, and some of its concerns have support in the studies' own data (associations in people who say they do not drink; heavy drinking days moving with average intake; Holmes et al., 2014); but it quantifies none of them, and the biases it names for genetic studies (confounding, misreported drinking, selective publication) apply equally to the cohort studies that show the protective association. Read together, the genetic evidence weakens the case that light drinking protects the heart, without showing that light drinking harms it or how large any effect at low intake might be.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Genetic analyses of new coronary events in several ancestries, including east Asian cohorts with many more heart attacks, using several independent alcohol variants, within-family designs to remove effects of ancestry and of parents, nonlinear methods that do not divide people by how much they say they drink, and people confirmed by biomarkers not to drink as a test of paths outside alcohol; reported with the strength of each instrument and with absolute risks. A long-term randomized trial of light drinking against not drinking would answer the light-drinking question directly. None of the sources read reports these.

statement: In people averaging less than 30 g of ethanol a day, in seven observational studies pooled by one team, drinking heavily on some occasions compared with drinking the same average amount without such occasions is associated with a higher risk of ischaemic heart disease (reported as incidence, a term the paper elsewhere uses for deaths and new cases combined); no absolute risks are given. Against lifetime abstainers, people without heavy drinking occasions had a pooled relative risk of 0.64 (95% CI as printed 0.53 to 0.71, an interval that does not fit its point estimate on the log scale, so one figure is probably misprinted; editors' calculation) and people with them 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37), that is, no lower risk than lifetime abstainers; the ratio between the two groups was 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). The same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, gave 1.45 (1.24 to 1.70) for people with irregular heavy drinking occasions against people who drank without them. The article does not say what counted as a heavy drinking occasion, which seven studies were pooled or how many people and events they included (all only in a supplement not read); all seven adjusted for age and smoking, one author searched for and extracted the studies, and their risk of bias was not assessed. The review of average intake against lifetime abstainers and the GBD 2016 model did not take drinking pattern into account, and genetic variants that lower average intake also lower heavy drinking (odds of binge drinking 0.78, 0.73 to 0.84, in carriers of the ADH1B variant; Holmes et al., 2014), so Roerecke and Rehm (2014) judged the genetic ADH1B result hard to compare with cohort studies, and Mukamal et al. (2020) argue that genetic studies linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: One team pooled seven studies of people who drank under 30 grams of alcohol a day on average. People who never had heavy drinking days had about a third lower heart disease risk than people who had never drunk. People with heavy drinking days had no lower risk. The team's earlier review pointed the same way. The paper does not say what counted as a heavy day or which studies were used, and the review did not rate the studies' quality. Gene studies lower heavy drinking along with the average amount, so critics say they may partly show the effect of heavy days. None of the studies says how many people out of 100 are affected.
population: People who drink, averaging under 30 g of ethanol a day, in seven observational studies of adult population samples (identities, designs and countries only in the supplement), with lifetime abstainers as the reference; and, second-hand, the studies of the same team's 2010 review
exposure: Heavy drinking occasions (episodic heavy drinking) as defined by each study, at an average intake under 30 g/day; the definition is not given in the article
comparator: Drinking the same average amount without heavy drinking occasions; both groups also compared with lifetime abstainers
outcome: Ischaemic heart disease (ICD-9 410–414, ICD-10 I20–I25), reported as incidence, a term the paper elsewhere uses for deaths and new cases combined
magnitude: Roerecke & Rehm 2014 (seven studies; against lifetime abstainers; ischaemic heart disease reported as incidence (mortality and morbidity combined, by the paper's use of the term elsewhere); most-adjusted estimates, all adjusted for age and smoking): average under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions RR 0.64 (0.53–0.71 as printed; geometric midpoint of that interval 0.61, editors' calculation), I² 10%, Egger P = 0.35; with heavy drinking occasions 1.12 (0.91–1.37), I² 0%, Egger P = 0.58; ratio with against without 1.75 (1.36–2.25), equal to 1.12/0.64 (editors' arithmetic), method of its interval not described. Roerecke & Rehm 2010, as cited by Roerecke & Rehm 2012: RR 1.45 (1.24–1.70), drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them. Holmes et al. 2014: ADH1B intake-lowering variant, binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84) and 17.2% fewer UK units a week. No absolute risks, numbers of participants or events, or definition of a heavy drinking occasion in the article.

statement: In Chinese men and in people mostly of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more stroke, most clearly with bleeding into the brain (intracerebral haemorrhage), and the Chinese study found no sign of a lower risk at low intake; cohort studies comparing people who drink with people who do not found no overall difference in stroke but more strokes at higher intakes. No paper read gives absolute risks of stroke by amount. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults from ten areas, followed about 10 years, men's stroke risk rose steadily across six groups whose genotypes and area predicted mean intakes of 4 to 256 g of ethanol a week: per 100 g a week (about 14 g a day, editors' arithmetic) ischaemic stroke 1.09 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.14; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24; 2,790 cases) and all stroke 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); the lowest group, in which two thirds did not drink, showed no sign of a raised risk, and the next two groups (about 100 g a week) had higher, not lower, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage than the three lowest groups pooled (about 25 g a week); the same genotypes showed no association in women, few of whom drink (ischaemic stroke 0.98, 0.88 to 1.09; intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96, 0.82 to 1.12); and self-reported drinking in the same men showed a U shape, with lower stroke risk at about 100 g a week than in non-drinkers and former drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). Only on the condition that there is no material protective effect and that the relation is roughly log-linear, those authors estimate that alcohol caused about 8 in 100 ischaemic strokes and 16 in 100 intracerebral haemorrhages among all the men (a model estimate). In summary data, mostly of European descent, the odds of stroke were 1.27 (1.12 to 1.45) per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week, 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46) and intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32) (Larsson et al., 2020); in UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder gave 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54), not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of ischaemic stroke in the studies with subtype data (0.83, 0.72 to 0.95) but no difference in all stroke (0.98, 0.90 to 1.07; 10,164 strokes); the authors call the number of strokes an important limitation and say the ischaemic-stroke result needs replication (Holmes et al., 2014). In cohort studies, people who drank had, against non-drinkers (most groups including former drinkers), no different risk of new stroke (0.98, 0.91 to 1.06; 17 studies) or of stroke death (1.06, 0.91 to 1.23; 10 studies), and against lifetime abstainers a higher risk of stroke death (1.29, 1.09 to 1.53; 3 studies); by intake, new strokes were less common at up to 14.9 g a day (0.81 and 0.80; 3 studies each) and more common above 60 g a day (1.62, 1.32 to 1.98; 4 studies) (Ronksley et al., 2011); in the GBD 2016 curves ischaemic stroke dipped at low intake without statistical significance. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a study of more than 160,000 Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and the risk rose steadily with the amount, with no dip at low amounts. Strokes caused by bleeding in the brain rose the most. Women, few of whom drink, showed no link with the same genes. Most gene studies of people of European descent found the same direction. Older studies that compared people who drink with people who don't found no overall difference in stroke, slightly fewer strokes at low amounts in a few studies, and more at high amounts. None of these studies says how many extra strokes this means out of 100.

risk_of_bias.note: Rated for the genetic association. The genetic design protects against confounding by lifestyle and against illness changing drinking, and here the remaining threats were tested without removing the association: in China, women, in whom the same genotypes barely change drinking, showed no stroke association (a check for paths outside alcohol), the instrument was very strong and comparisons were within area; in European data the estimate fell only from 1.27 to 1.21 after allowing for genetic liability to smoking, never-smokers gave similar results, and the ADH1B variant alone, which did not predict smoking, gave 1.31 for ischaemic stroke. Paths that remain possible (acetaldehyde exposure per drink with ALDH2, education with ADH1B, UK Biobank in both exposure and outcome data, prevalent cases in the ADH1B study) are judged unlikely to change the direction, so the editors do not rate down. The cohort figures (comparison groups with former drinkers) are given as context: they are not rated here (the answer on heart disease covers coronary disease only) and are not counted as replication of the genetic finding.

inconsistency.note: The genetic studies agree in direction for ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage; the ADH1B study's null result for all stroke (0.98) rests on fewer strokes and a smaller difference in intake, which its authors call a limitation, and its ischaemic-stroke subset agrees. The cohort dip at low intake, against its absence in the Chinese genetic analysis, is the reference-group question of the cohort studies and is stated rather than rated.

indirectness.note: Chinese men drinking mainly spirits and European-descent populations; the European estimates are per SD of genetically predicted log drinks a week and cannot be put into grams; women only as a check in China. Stated, not rated.

imprecision.note: The main genetic intervals exclude no difference; the European intracerebral haemorrhage interval is wide (1.70 to 7.32).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable with four genetic studies.

large_effect.note: Per 100 g a week the relative risks are 1.09 to 1.18; not large.

dose_response.note: Risk rose steadily across the six genetic groups in China and, in cohorts, from about 15 g to more than 60 g a day. Not upgraded: the Chinese gradient is the slope estimate itself, fitted through six group means of self-reported intake, and pleiotropy cannot be wholly excluded; with this upgrade the rating would be moderate.

grade.reasoning: Mendelian randomization is observational and starts low (round brief). The design addresses confounding by lifestyle and reverse causation, and its main remaining weaknesses were tested here (a check in women, allowance for genetic liability to smoking, never-smokers, a single-variant analysis), so the editors do not rate down for confounding or risk of bias; this is logged for the senior author under the round's rule. What the design cannot show is the size of the effect in grams in European data and the curve at the lowest intakes outside the Chinese study. No downgrade and no upgrade: low. Status replicated: two independent genetic studies in different ancestries (Millwood et al.; Larsson et al.) agree, Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank, overlapping Larsson et al.'s outcome data) points the same way, and the ADH1B study agrees for ischaemic stroke; Holmes et al. and Millwood et al. share two authors. The cohort results (Ronksley et al.) and the GBD 2016 curves describe the conventional association and are not counted as replication of the genetic finding.

statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with higher blood pressure, and in the European studies with more high blood pressure (hypertension; the Chinese study reports blood pressure only); in the Chinese study the rise for each gram was about the same as with self-reported drinking; no paper read gives the absolute risk of hypertension by amount drunk. In the China Kadoorie Biobank (55,879 men in this analysis), men's systolic blood pressure was 4.3 mm Hg higher (95% CI 3.7 to 4.9) per 280 g of ethanol a week (40 g a day) of genotype-predicted mean intake, which, if the rise is even, is about 1.5 mm Hg per 100 g a week (editors' calculation), against 4.8 mm Hg (4.5 to 5.1) per 280 g a week of self-reported usual intake among men who drank; in women, few of whom drink, the same genotypes went with 0.6 mm Hg lower pressure (−1.0 to −0.1) (Millwood et al., 2019). In 48 European-descent studies (227,559 people), carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had systolic pressure 0.88 mm Hg lower (0.56 to 1.19 lower), and their odds of hypertension were 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 104,570 people with hypertension), though by reported drinking the lower odds were clear only in people drinking 21 UK units (of 7.9 g) a week or more (0.89, 0.81 to 0.99; 0.98, 0.93 to 1.03, in lighter drinkers); the lower pressure was as large in people who said they did not drink (0.80 mm Hg lower) as in people who drank lightly to moderately (0.68 lower), which, in the editors' reading, points either to misreported drinking or to a path other than current drinking (Holmes et al., 2014). In UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder was associated with hypertension, odds ratio 1.28 (1.18 to 1.39) per standard deviation of genetically predicted intake (Biddinger et al., 2022), and in European summary data genetically predicted drinking went with higher systolic and diastolic pressure, in units the paper's figure does not make clear (Larsson et al., 2020). In UK Biobank's self-reported data, the lower hypertension risk of people who drank moderately, against people who reported no drinking at the start, was no longer statistically clear once six lifestyle factors were allowed for, and at light intake, read approximately from the paper's figure, it was reduced but not removed. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In a Chinese study, men's top blood-pressure number rose by about 4 points (mm Hg) for each extra 40 grams of alcohol a day that their genes predicted, about the same as when men were asked how much they drank. In European studies, people with a gene that makes them drink a little less had slightly lower blood pressure and slightly less high blood pressure, most clearly among heavier drinkers, and a gene score for alcohol problems went with more high blood pressure. The European gene also went with lower blood pressure in people who said they did not drink, so it may act in other ways too. The studies do not say how many more people out of 100 get high blood pressure at each amount.
population: Men in the China Kadoorie Biobank (161,498 genotyped adults; women as a check); people of European descent in 56 pooled studies (Holmes et al.), UK Biobank (Biddinger et al.; Mass General Brigham Biobank for replication) and UK Biobank-based summary data (Larsson et al.)
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake (ALDH2 and ADH1B genotypes with area; the ADH1B rs1229984 variant; a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder; up to 94 variants for log drinks a week), and self-reported usual intake among men who drank (China)
comparator: Lower genetically predicted intake (per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean male intake; non-carriers; per standard deviation); people who did not drink, for the conventional UK Biobank comparison
outcome: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mm Hg) and hypertension
magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (men; per 280 g/week, which is 40 g/day): systolic blood pressure +4.3 mm Hg (3.7–4.9) genetic, +4.8 (4.5–5.1) conventional among current drinkers; about +1.5 mm Hg per 100 g/week if linear (editors' calculation); women −0.6 (−1.0 to −0.1). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering ADH1B variant; 17.2% fewer units a week): systolic −0.88 mm Hg (−1.19 to −0.56), hypertension OR 0.94 (0.91–0.98); by self-reported drinking −0.80 (none), −0.68 (more than 0 to under 21 units/week), −1.70 (21 or more); hypertension by self-reported drinking 0.95 (0.89–1.02), 0.98 (0.93–1.03), 0.89 (0.81–0.99), trend P = 0.197. Biddinger et al. 2022 (OR per SD of genetically predicted intake): hypertension 1.28 (1.18–1.39); within categories per 1 drink/day of allele score 1.3 (light), 1.7 (moderate), 2.6 (highest); conventional moderate-intake difference not significant after six lifestyle factors. Larsson et al. 2020: systolic 0.12 (0.05–0.20) and diastolic 0.15 (0.05–0.25) per SD of log drinks/week, units unclear. No absolute risks of hypertension by intake.

statement: In people of European descent, mostly in UK Biobank, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more peripheral artery disease and possibly with abdominal aortic aneurysm and atrial fibrillation, while results for heart failure differ between the two genetic studies read, and for blood clots in the veins the one estimate was close to no difference but too imprecise to rule out a moderate rise or fall; the findings come from two studies whose outcome data overlap, some rest on few cases, and no absolute risks are given. Per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week (a unit the paper does not convert into drinks), the odds ratios were 3.05 (95% CI 1.92 to 4.85) for peripheral artery disease (3,415 cases), 2.55 (1.49 to 4.35) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; 2.60 (1.15 to 5.89) for abdominal aortic aneurysm (1,094 cases), 2.29 (0.89 to 5.93) after that allowance; 1.17 (1.00 to 1.37) for atrial fibrillation, 1.11 (0.93 to 1.32) after it; 1.00 (0.68 to 1.47) for heart failure; 1.04 (0.77 to 1.39) for venous thromboembolism; and 1.03 (0.56 to 1.90) for narrowing of the aortic valve, for which two other methods (weighted median and MR-Egger) suggested a positive association and directional pleiotropy was indicated, the main text not naming the test (Larsson et al., 2020). With the ADH1B variant alone, genetically higher intake was associated with peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm. In UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder was associated with atrial fibrillation (1.24, 1.08 to 1.44; 14,367 cases in the whole sample) and heart failure (1.39, 1.08 to 1.78; 5,812 cases in the whole sample), the heart-failure result not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes; the analyses were in people who drank, whose case numbers are not printed (Biddinger et al., 2022). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Two gene studies, both using a large UK study of volunteers, looked at other heart and blood-vessel problems. Genes for drinking more went with more narrowed arteries, mostly in the legs (peripheral artery disease), even after allowing for genes linked to smoking. In one study, links with a swollen main artery in the belly (aortic aneurysm) and with an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) became unclear once genes linked to smoking were allowed for; the other study found a link with an irregular heartbeat. For heart failure, the two studies disagreed. For blood clots in the veins, no clear link was found, but the study could not rule one out. Some of these results rest on few cases, and neither study gave numbers out of 100.
population: People of European descent in genome-wide consortia (atrial fibrillation) and UK Biobank (the other outcomes) (Larsson et al.), and in UK Biobank (Biddinger et al.)
exposure: Genetically predicted alcohol intake: up to 94 variants for log drinks a week, or the ADH1B rs1229984 variant alone (Larsson et al.); a 5-variant score for alcohol use disorder (Biddinger et al.)
comparator: Lower genetically predicted intake (per standard deviation)
outcome: Peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, venous thromboembolism and aortic valve stenosis
magnitude: Larsson et al. 2020 (OR per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week; inverse-variance weighted, then adjusted for genetic liability to smoking initiation): peripheral artery disease 3.05 (1.92–4.85), 2.55 (1.49–4.35); abdominal aortic aneurysm 2.60 (1.15–5.89), 2.29 (0.89–5.93); atrial fibrillation 1.17 (1.00–1.37), 1.11 (0.93–1.32); heart failure 1.00 (0.68–1.47), 0.88 (0.57–1.37); venous thromboembolism 1.04 (0.77–1.39), 1.05 (0.75–1.47); aortic valve stenosis 1.03 (0.56–1.90), 0.94 (0.46–1.91), with directional pleiotropy indicated (test not named in the main text); ADH1B variant alone positive (P < 0.05) for peripheral artery disease, aortic valve stenosis and abdominal aortic aneurysm. Biddinger et al. 2022 (OR per SD of genetically predicted consumption): atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08–1.44; P = .003), heart failure 1.39 (1.08–1.78; P = .009, threshold P < .008). No absolute risks.

statement: In people taking part in 572 case–control and cohort studies published from 1956 to 2012 (486,538 people with cancer; 41% of the studies from North America, 32% from Europe and 18% from Asia), drinking more than 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average (more than one drink as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers were not separated) is associated with more cancers of the mouth and pharynx, the oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only), the larynx, the colon and rectum and the female breast, and, at heavy drinking, of the liver, with the relative risk rising with the amount (Bagnardi et al., 2015; funded by Italian cancer-research charities, no conflicts declared). The review reports no absolute risks, so its ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. For heavy drinking (above 50 g a day, more than four drinks) the pooled relative risks were 5.13 (95% CI 4.31–6.10) for the mouth and pharynx, 4.95 (3.86–6.34) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 2.65 (2.19–3.19) for the larynx, 2.07 (1.66–2.58) for the liver, 1.61 (1.33–1.94) for the breast (from 11 of the 118 breast studies, editors' count) and 1.44 (1.25–1.65) for the colon and rectum; for moderate drinking (above 12.5 and up to 50 g a day) they were 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 1.08 (0.97–1.20, no clear difference), 1.23 (1.19–1.28) and 1.17 (1.11–1.24). The colorectal association differed by sex (P = 0.010): it was clear in men (heavy drinking 1.53, 1.30–1.80) but not in women (moderate 1.07, 0.99–1.16; heavy 1.24, 0.68–2.25, from 4 studies). Heavy drinking was also associated with cancers of the stomach (1.21, 1.07–1.36), pancreas (1.19, 1.11–1.28), lung (1.15, 1.02–1.30) and gallbladder (2.64, 1.62–4.30; 8 studies of this cancer in all), and the authors say that smoking not fully taken into account may explain part of the lung and stomach results (their earlier review found no link with lung cancer in people who never smoked); moderate drinking went with small increases in prostate cancer (1.06, 1.01–1.11) and melanoma (1.20, 1.03–1.41), clear only in North American studies (and, for melanoma, in the two cohort studies), although the differences between regions were not statistically significant; there was no clear association with adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus and gastric cardia or with cancers of the small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain; and cancers of the kidney and thyroid and both kinds of lymphoma were less common in people who drank (for example non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.75, 0.64–0.88, at heavy drinking): for the lymphomas the authors suggest that people stop or cut down when early symptoms start, while they read the kidney result both as protection and, in their conclusion, as no association (the World Cancer Research Fund rates a lower kidney cancer risk at up to 30 g a day as probable, as relayed by Rumgay et al., 2021). The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, whose review of studies probably overlaps with this one (its study list was not read), fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer it included (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018). Results varied widely between studies (I² up to 91%); only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates, so differences in smoking and other habits were often not taken into account, although the authors report that keeping only adjusted estimates did not materially change the results (figures in a supplement not read); case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohort studies at some sites (heavy drinking and liver cancer 2.79 against 1.12; larynx 2.81 against 1.12), a difference statistically clear for the mouth and pharynx (P = 0.007) but not for the liver or larynx (P = 0.226 and 0.216); and the review neither appraised the studies nor tested for publication bias. That alcohol causes cancer at these sites is the judgment of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, whose list a 2021 cancer-burden model used (Rumgay et al., 2021); this pooling of observational studies cannot show it by itself. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Across 572 studies, people who drank more than about one drink a day (12.5 g of alcohol) had more cancer of the mouth and throat, of one type of gullet cancer, of the voice box, of the bowel and of the breast than people who did not drink, and people who drank more than four drinks a day also had more liver cancer. At more than four drinks a day, mouth and throat cancer and that gullet cancer were about 5 times as common, voice-box cancer about 2.7 times, liver cancer about 2 times, breast cancer about 1.6 times and bowel cancer about 1.4 times. The bowel cancer link was clear in men but not in women. The review gives no numbers out of 100. Kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were less common in people who drank; for the lymph glands, the authors think this partly reflects people cutting down when they first feel ill. Results varied a lot between studies, about half the studies did not take smoking or other differences into account (though the authors say that leaving those studies out changed little), and the review did not check the studies' quality. An international cancer agency judges that alcohol causes these cancers; this review alone cannot show it.
population: People in 572 case–control (409) and cohort (163) studies published 1956 to 2012 in English, 41% from North America, 32% from Europe and 18% from Asia; 486,538 people with cancer at 23 sites; ages not reported
exposure: Average alcohol intake as self-reported in each study, converted to grams of ethanol a day (one drink = 12.5 g): moderate, above 12.5 and up to 50 g a day; heavy, above 50 g a day (light drinking, up to 12.5 g, is the subject of a separate answer)
comparator: Each study's nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 138 of the 572 studies (24%); whether nondrinkers included former drinkers was not recorded
outcome: Incidence (541 studies) or death (31 studies) from cancer at 23 sites, as defined in each study
magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, pooled relative risks (random effects; 95% CI) against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers, moderate then heavy drinking: mouth and pharynx 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 5.13 (4.31–6.10; I² 72%, 77%); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 4.95 (3.86–6.34; I² 85%, 91%); larynx 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 2.65 (2.19–3.19); colon and rectum 1.17 (1.11–1.24), 1.44 (1.25–1.65), by sex men 1.21 (1.11–1.32), 1.53 (1.30–1.80), women 1.07 (0.99–1.16), 1.24 (0.68–2.25; 4 studies), heterogeneity P = 0.010; liver 1.08 (0.97–1.20), 2.07 (1.66–2.58); female breast 1.23 (1.19–1.28), 1.61 (1.33–1.94; I² 54%, 10%; heavy from 11 studies, editors' count); heavy only: stomach 1.21 (1.07–1.36), pancreas 1.19 (1.11–1.28), lung 1.15 (1.02–1.30), gallbladder 2.64 (1.62–4.30; 8 studies of this cancer in all); moderate: prostate 1.06 (1.01–1.11), melanoma 1.20 (1.03–1.41; in the 2 cohort studies 1.27, 1.13–1.42); between-area heterogeneity P = 0.214 (prostate) and 0.110 (melanoma); inverse: kidney moderate 0.79 (0.72–0.86), thyroid moderate 0.81 (0.71–0.94), Hodgkin's lymphoma heavy 0.63 (0.41–0.97), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma heavy 0.75 (0.64–0.88). By design, heavy drinking: mouth and pharynx 5.34 (4.46–6.39; 35 case–control studies) against 3.13 (1.59–6.19; 3 cohort studies), heterogeneity P = 0.007; liver 2.79 (2.00–3.87; 24 case–control) against 1.12 (1.02–1.23; 7 cohort), P = 0.226; larynx 2.81 (2.33–3.39) against 1.12 (0.75–1.67; 3 cohort), P = 0.216. No absolute risks reported.

risk_of_bias.note: Bagnardi et al. (card sc_bagnardi_2015: AMSTAR 2 critically low): no protocol, no appraisal of the primary studies, and adjusted estimates pooled with crude ones (297 of 572 studies adjusted); case–control studies, open to recall and control-selection bias, are 409 of the 572 and gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites; residual confounding by smoking is possible for the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, larynx, lung and stomach. Counted once. The authors report that keeping only adjusted estimates did not materially change the results, but those figures are in a supplement that was not read.

inconsistency.note: I² reaches 91% at heavy drinking, so the size differs widely between studies, but for the main sites the direction is the same across designs, sexes and world regions (Tables 2 to 4), and the claim gives design-specific figures rather than one number; not rated down. The colorectal association was clear in men but not in women (heterogeneity P = 0.010; women, heavy drinking 1.24, 0.68–2.25, from 4 studies), which the statement reports; the direction is positive in both sexes.

indirectness.note: Self-reported average intake and cancer incidence (541 studies) or death (31) in the populations studied, as the claim says; drinking pattern and beverage type were not analysed and the claim does not speak to them.

imprecision.note: Narrow intervals for the moderate and heavy estimates at the main sites; the liver estimate at moderate intake includes 1 and is reported as no clear difference; the gallbladder estimate rests on 8 studies.

publication_bias.note: Not examined in this review (the authors refer to their earlier site-specific reviews); small-study effects could inflate the moderate-intake estimates but are unlikely to produce relative risks of 2 to 5; stated, not rated down.

large_effect.note: Relative risks near 5 for the mouth, pharynx and oesophagus at heavy drinking, but confounding by smoking, a bias away from the null, remains in many estimates, and the cohort estimate for the mouth and pharynx is 3.13 (1.59–6.19; 3 cohorts); not applied.

dose_response.note: At each main site the relative risk rises from light to moderate to heavy drinking, and the dose–response meta-regression, which allows for correlation within studies, shows steep rises for the mouth, pharynx and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (Figure 3); part of the category gradient compares different sets of studies.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down one level for risk of bias and up one level for the dose–response gradient, which gives low; a strict reading without the upgrade would give very low. Rated as worded: an association that grows with the amount; that alcohol causes these cancers is the classification of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, cited by the papers, and is not tested by this pooling. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 review probably shares many primary studies with this one (its study list was not read), and the 2021 model only uses IARC's list, so neither is counted as independent replication. Status replicated: independent subsets of the 572 studies, by design, sex and world region, agree in direction for the main sites.
