statement: In people taking part in the same 572 case–control and cohort studies (Bagnardi et al., 2015), light drinking (up to 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average, one drink or less as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers not separated) is associated with slightly more of some cancers and slightly fewer of others, with no absolute risks reported: pooled relative risks of 1.13 (95% CI 1.00–1.26) for cancers of the mouth and pharynx, 1.26 (1.06–1.50) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 1.04 (1.01–1.07) for female breast cancer and 1.04 (1.01–1.08) for prostate cancer (from 26, 34, 115 and 36 studies; editors' counts from the review's Table 2); no clear difference for cancers of the colon and rectum (0.99, 0.95–1.04), liver (1.00, 0.85–1.18) or larynx (0.87, 0.68–1.11); and lower figures for lung cancer (0.84, 0.79–0.88), adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus and gastric cardia (0.86, 0.76–0.98), cancers of the kidney (0.92, 0.86–0.99) and thyroid (0.81, 0.74–0.88), and both kinds of lymphoma (Hodgkin's 0.73, 0.59–0.89; non-Hodgkin's 0.88, 0.80–0.97). Differences this small can be produced or hidden by people who drink more reporting less, which the authors say may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations, by smoking and other differences (only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates), and by former or occasional drinkers among the comparison group; the authors report that keeping only adjusted estimates, or dropping studies with occasional drinkers in the comparison group, did not materially change the results (figures in a supplement not read). The raised figures also depend on how the studies are split: for the mouth and pharynx the light-drinking figure was 1.22 (1.10–1.35) in case–control studies, which ask about drinking after the cancer is found, but 0.86 (0.60–1.23) in cohort studies, while for the breast it was 1.06 (1.03–1.10) in cohort studies and 1.04 (0.99–1.09) in case–control studies; the mouth, pharynx and oesophagus figures were statistically clear in men (1.20 and 1.39) but not in women and, by world region, only in Asian studies (1.33 and 1.54), where the authors point to a common variant of a gene for breaking down alcohol, although the regions did not differ significantly (P = 0.375 and 0.503). The lower lung and oesophageal adenocarcinoma figures appear in the review's figure but not in its text, and its continuous dose–response model found a slight rise in lung cancer risk with intake and no trend for oesophageal adenocarcinoma. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study fitted risk curves that rise with intake for each of the eight cancers it modelled, which did not include kidney, thyroid or lymphoma (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; list as given by GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022), and a model of cancers in 2020 attributes 41,300 new cases worldwide (95% uncertainty interval 35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, against lifetime abstention, counting only cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer lists as caused by alcohol, leaving out a probable protective association with kidney cancer and counting former drinkers as unexposed (Rumgay et al., 2021); both depend on the shape of the risk curves at low intake, which is what these studies leave uncertain. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In the same studies, people who had up to about one drink a day (12.5 g of alcohol) had slightly more mouth and throat cancer (1.13 times, a borderline result), one type of gullet cancer (1.26 times), breast cancer (1.04 times) and prostate cancer (1.04 times) than people who did not drink, and slightly less lung, kidney and thyroid cancer and cancer of the lymph glands. The review gives no numbers out of 100. The mouth and throat result came from studies that asked people about their drinking after their cancer was found, not from studies that followed people over time; the breast result was clearer in studies that followed people over time. Differences this small could come from people who drink more saying they drink less, from smoking and other differences, or from people who had stopped drinking being counted with people who did not drink. A model estimated that drinking up to 10 g a day caused about 41,000 new cancers worldwide in 2020, compared with no one ever drinking; that figure depends on the shape of the risk curves at low amounts, which is what these studies leave uncertain.
population: People in 572 case–control and cohort studies published 1956 to 2012 (486,538 people with cancer), mostly from North America, Europe and Asia
exposure: Light drinking: average intake up to 12.5 g of ethanol a day (up to one drink as the review defines it), self-reported
comparator: Nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers not separated
outcome: Incidence of, or death from, cancer at 23 sites
magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, light drinking against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers (pooled RR, 95% CI; I²; studies, editors' count from Table 2): mouth and pharynx 1.13 (1.00–1.26; 26%; 26 studies); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.26 (1.06–1.50; 68%; 34); female breast 1.04 (1.01–1.07; 63%; 115); prostate 1.04 (1.01–1.08; 36); colon and rectum 0.99 (0.95–1.04); liver 1.00 (0.85–1.18); larynx 0.87 (0.68–1.11); lung 0.84 (0.79–0.88); oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76–0.98); kidney 0.92 (0.86–0.99); thyroid 0.81 (0.74–0.88); Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.73 (0.59–0.89); non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.88 (0.80–0.97). By design, cohort against case–control studies: mouth and pharynx 0.86 (0.60–1.23) against 1.22 (1.10–1.35); breast 1.06 (1.03–1.10) against 1.04 (0.99–1.09). By sex: mouth and pharynx men 1.20 (1.06–1.35), women 1.00 (0.78–1.27); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma men 1.39 (1.11–1.74), women 1.14 (0.87–1.49). Rumgay et al. 2021 (model): 41,300 (35,400–145,800) new cancers in 2020 attributed to intake up to 10 g a day against lifetime abstention.

risk_of_bias.note: As for the moderate and heavy estimates (card sc_bagnardi_2015: AMSTAR 2 critically low), and at light intake the biases are as large as the associations: under-reporting moves people who drink more into the light category, former and occasional drinkers in the reference group can move the estimates either way, and about half the estimates are crude; the authors concede that under-reporting may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations. In the review's own splits, the mouth and pharynx excess comes from case–control studies, which are open to recall bias (1.22 against 0.86 in cohort studies), while the breast excess is clearer in cohort studies (1.06).

inconsistency.note: Positive associations at some sites and inverse ones at others (lung, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, kidney, thyroid, lymphomas); within sites, the mouth and pharynx excess appears in case–control but not cohort studies (heterogeneity P = 0.007), the oral and oesophageal excesses were clear in men and in Asian studies only, although the regional differences were not significant (P = 0.375 and 0.503), and the review's continuous model shows a slight rise in lung cancer risk where its light-drinking category shows 0.84; I² 26% to 68% for the positive estimates; no adequate explanation.

indirectness.note: Light drinking as the studies classed it (midpoint up to 12.5 g a day), in the populations studied.

imprecision.note: The breast estimate is precise (1.01–1.07); the interval for the mouth and pharynx reaches 1.00; not rated down separately, the certainty being already at the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not examined in the review; small light-drinking effects are the kind most open to selective publication; stated rather than rated, the certainty being already at the floor.

dose_response.note: Not applied: whether the gradient seen at higher intake continues to the lowest intakes is the question this claim addresses, and the biases are largest there.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias and inconsistency, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: small associations in both directions at light intake, site by site; with these data none can be told apart from bias, and the review's own splits by design, sex and region do not agree on where the excess lies. The Global Burden of Disease curves probably draw on many of the same studies and cover only eight cancers, and the 2020 model's low-intake figure rests on the shape of its curves at low intake, so neither is independent support. Status mixed: findings differ by site, by design and by region without an adequate explanation.

statement: In the world's population in 2020, alcohol drinking compared with a counterfactual in which no one had ever drunk (lifetime abstention) is estimated by one modelling study to account for 741,300 new cancer cases (95% uncertainty interval 558,500–951,200), about 4 in every 100 new cancers (4.1%, 3.1%–5.3%; non-melanoma skin cancer excluded): about 6 in 100 new cancers in men (568,700 cases; 6.1%) and 2 in 100 in women (172,600; 2.0%) (Rumgay et al., 2021; no funding, no competing interests declared). The model includes only the cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer judges to be caused by alcohol: oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only) 189,700 cases, 31.6% of all oesophageal cancers; liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only) 154,700, 17.3% of all liver cancers; female breast 98,300, 4.4%; colon 91,500, 8.1%; lip and oral cavity 74,900, 20.2%; rectum 65,100, 9.0%; pharynx 39,400, 22.0%; and larynx 27,600, 15.0%. It attributes 346,400 cases (46.7%) to drinking more than 60 g of ethanol a day, 291,800 (39.4%) to 20–60 g and 103,100 (13.9%; interval 82,600–207,200) to less than 20 g a day (up to about two drinks), including 41,300 (35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, of which 24,600 were in women, 14.3% of women's alcohol-attributed cancers. These are model estimates, not counts of people whose cancer was traced to drinking: they combine drinking estimated from 2010 per-capita consumption (recorded, unrecorded and tourist) and surveys, assumed to act 10 years later, with relative-risk curves for current drinking from World Cancer Research Fund reviews of observational studies, whose reference group the paper does not state, applied in the same way to every country; former drinkers carry no extra risk in the main analysis; the uncertainty intervals carry only the uncertainty in drinking and in the relative risks, leave out that in cancer incidence, the 10-year delay and the model's structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures; the hepatocellular share behind the liver figure comes from unpublished estimates; and the totals count harms only, a probable protective association with kidney cancer at intakes up to 30 g a day having been deliberately left out. Adding stomach and pancreatic cancer raised the total to 808,700, and counting former drinking raised it to 925,900, though the increment the paper gives for this (135,000) does not match its own totals. Earlier global estimates cited by the paper, for other years and with other choices, were 5.5% of new cancers in 2012 and 4.8% to 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019; an earlier model by an overlapping team, counting deaths from cancers of the mouth and oropharynx, oesophagus, colon and rectum, liver and breast and from other neoplasms, without the 2020 model's restriction to squamous cell and hepatocellular cancers, estimated 487 thousand cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004 (377 thousand in men, 111 thousand in women; no uncertainty intervals; Rehm et al., 2009); and in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, cancers made up 27.1% of the deaths attributed to alcohol in women aged 50 and older and 18.9% in men (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: A model estimated that about 741,000 new cancers worldwide in 2020, about 4 in every 100 new cancers, were caused by drinking, compared with a world where no one had ever drunk: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast, bowel and mouth cancers made up most of them. Most were linked to drinking more than 20 g of alcohol a day (about two drinks); about 103,000 were linked to less than that, and about 41,000 to up to 10 g a day, more than half of these in women. These are computer estimates, not counted cases: they take cancer risks from studies of groups of people and apply them to every country, and some of the model's choices are uncertain. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004.
population: The world's population in 2020 (exposure modelled for ages 15 and over), all countries in GLOBOCAN 2020; for comparison, the world's population in 2004 and in 2016
exposure: Current drinking, estimated from 2010 adult per-capita consumption (recorded, unrecorded and tourist) and surveys, with intake among current drinkers modelled from 0.1 to 150 g of ethanol a day; categories below 20 g, 20–60 g and above 60 g a day
comparator: A counterfactual of lifetime abstention for everyone (theoretical minimum-risk exposure); no alcohol consumption in the 2004 model
outcome: New cancer cases in 2020 (GLOBOCAN 2020) at the sites with sufficient evidence of causation by alcohol in IARC monograph 100E: lip and oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma), colon, rectum, liver (hepatocellular carcinoma), larynx and female breast; for comparison, cancer deaths in 2004 (WHO comparative risk assessment) and the cancer share of alcohol-attributable deaths in 2016 (Global Burden of Disease)
magnitude: Rumgay et al. 2021 (model; 95% uncertainty intervals): 741,300 (558,500–951,200) new cases in 2020, attributable fraction 4.1% (3.1–5.3); men 568,700 (422,500–731,100), 6.1% (4.6–7.9); women 172,600 (135,900–220,100), 2.0% (1.6–2.5). By site (cases; fraction): oesophagus 189,700 (110,900–274,600; 31.6%); liver 154,700 (43,700–281,500; 17.3% of all liver cancers); female breast 98,300 (68,200–130,500; 4.4%); colon 91,500 (68,300–114,500; 8.1%); lip and oral cavity 74,900 (44,600–119,600; 20.2%); rectum 65,100 (48,500–82,000; 9.0%); pharynx 39,400 (16,100–67,800; 22.0%); larynx 27,600 (15,700–43,300; 15.0%). By intake: above 60 g a day 346,400 (227,900–489,400; 46.7%); 20–60 g 291,800 (227,700–333,100; 39.4%); below 20 g 103,100 (82,600–207,200; 13.9%); up to 10 g 41,300 (35,400–145,800), of which men 16,700 (14,300–75,400) and women 24,600 (21,100–70,400). Sensitivity: with stomach and pancreas 808,700 (616,300–1,034,800; 4.5%); with former drinking 925,900 (705,900–1,187,500; 5.2%), stated increment 135,000 against 184,600 from the totals (editors' arithmetic). Rehm et al. 2009 (model, 2004, no intervals): 487 thousand cancer deaths caused by alcohol (men 377, women 111 thousand). GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018 (model, 2016): cancers 27.1% (21.2–33.3) of alcohol-attributable deaths in women aged 50 and older, 18.9% (15.3–22.6) in men.

risk_of_bias.note: The estimate takes the relative-risk curves as causal and unbiased; they come from observational studies with the confounding, under-reporting and reference-group problems set out in the answer on which cancers (low certainty there, very low for light drinking); the World Cancer Research Fund curves used are in an appendix that was not read, and their reference group is not stated in the main text (card sc_rumgay_2021).

inconsistency.note: Earlier global estimates cited by the paper (5.5% of new cancers in 2012; 4.8% and 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019) are of similar size, though they share inputs; the 2004 death estimate measures a different outcome.

indirectness.note: One set of relative risks, mainly from cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every population; exposure from 2010 per-capita consumption and surveys, with under-reporting corrected in one way for all ages and both sexes and a fixed 10-year delay; current drinking only; ten countries imputed from their region; GLOBOCAN incidence itself modelled for many countries.

imprecision.note: The intervals leave out uncertainty in incidence, histological splits, latency and model structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures (103,100, 82,600–207,200; 41,300, 35,400–145,800); the 2004 estimate has no intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a model; publication bias in the studies behind the curves is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Model estimates are not graded as evidence of an effect: the claim describes what the models estimate (relation describes), and its certainty comes from the evidence behind the relative-risk curves (observational, low at best), rated down for the model's indirectness and for its incomplete uncertainty intervals, which gives very low. No upgrade applies to a modelled count. Status replicated by the same team: the 2020 case estimate and the 2004 death estimate come from overlapping authors, the same comparative-risk-assessment method and WHO exposure data; the Global Burden of Disease figure is a share of deaths from a different group drawing on overlapping studies, and is not counted as independent.

statement: In adults in cohort studies and Italian case–control studies, mostly from the USA and Europe, drinking more alcohol on average is associated with a higher risk of liver cirrhosis that grows with the amount, compared with not drinking (lifetime or long-term abstainers) in two meta-analyses by one team, and compared with drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week in a Danish cohort whose women are also among the newer review's studies. None reports absolute risks by amount; in the Danish cohort (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, followed for a median of 14.9 years), 257 of 26,696 men (about 1 in 100) and 85 of 29,221 women (about 3 in 1,000) were diagnosed with alcoholic cirrhosis, 66 and 19 per 100,000 person-years, across all levels of drinking (Askgaard et al., 2015; editors' conversion). In the newer meta-analysis (Roerecke et al., 2019: seven cohorts, whose outcome was mostly death from cirrhosis, and two case–control studies; 2,629,272 people, 5,505 cases; one drink = 12 g of ethanol a day; funded by a US government institute), relative risks against long-term abstainers were 1.11 (95% CI 0.77–1.59) for occasional drinking, 1.40 (1.00–1.97) for one drink a day, 3.02 (1.95–4.70) for two, 3.27 (0.90–11.87) for three to four, 6.26 (2.38–16.50) for five to six and 10.70 (2.95–38.78) for seven or more, with I² from 70.6% to 98.6%, each category pooling four to six cohort entries with 203 to 1,111 cases (editors' count from the forest plot, in which one American cohort is entered twice, for women and for men; four entries and 276 cases at seven or more drinks); at seven or more drinks a day the three cohorts of men gave 1.80 (Chinese men) and 8.30 and 22.39 (two American cohorts), and in the two case–control studies 1 to 4 drinks a day gave 1.19 (0.58–2.43) and 9 to 13 drinks 7.36 (1.91–28.34). In the earlier meta-analysis (Rehm et al., 2010: 17 studies published 1980 to 2003, 3384 cases; against lifetime abstainers of the same sex), drinking more than 60 g a day (more than five drinks) went with relative risks of 22.7 (17.2–30.1) in women and 14 (11.7–16.7) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 6.1 (4.6–8.0) and 5.0 (3.9–6.4) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis, of which there were at most six, four of them Italian (editors' count); in the Danish cohort, 28 to 42 drinks a week against fewer than 14 went with hazard ratios of 6.98 (4.65–10.5) in men and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) in women, adjusted for smoking, education and waist size. At up to about two drinks a day the sources disagree: in the earlier meta-analysis risk was raised in women's studies of cirrhosis death (1.9, 1.1–3.1, at up to 12 g a day; 5.6, 4.5–6.9, at 12 to 24 g), not raised in men's studies of cirrhosis death at up to 12 g a day (1.0, 0.6–1.6) but raised at 12 to 24 g (1.6, 1.4–2.0), not raised in women's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (1.0, 0.5–1.9, at 12 to 24 g) and lower than in abstainers in men's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (0.3, 0.2–0.4, at 12 to 24 g), which the authors could not explain biologically; the newer review's results found no clear sign of a threshold, with few studies to test one, though its discussion reports some evidence of one in men. The two meta-analyses share six studies (editors' comparison), intake was measured once, at the start, reference groups that included former drinkers were corrected upward (by an amount the earlier review does not report, and by about 1.24 in four cohorts of the newer review, editors' calculation), and the Danish cohort paper counted only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic, whereas the newer review took that cohort's women with unspecified cirrhosis added (it lists 393 men and 229 women with either diagnosis, against 257 and 85 with alcoholic cirrhosis in the cohort paper). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: The more people drank, the higher their risk of liver cirrhosis in these studies, compared with people who did not drink. In a Danish study of people aged 50 to 64, about 1 in 100 men and 3 in 1,000 women were diagnosed with alcohol-related cirrhosis over about 15 years. In a review of 9 studies, mostly counting deaths from cirrhosis, the risk was about 1.4 times as high at one drink a day (a drink being 12 g of alcohol; a borderline result), 3 times at two drinks and 11 times at seven or more drinks (a figure from 4 studies). How big the risk was differed a lot between studies: at seven or more drinks a day, from about 2 times to 22 times among men. At up to about two drinks a day, the studies disagree. Drinking was asked about only once, at the start.
population: Adults in cohort studies (among them American Cancer Society volunteers, health-plan members, nurses and physicians; baseline 1959 to 2005; outcome mostly cirrhosis death) and Italian hospital case–control studies, from the USA, Europe and Asia, in two meta-analyses of 17 and 9 studies by one team; and Danish-born adults aged 50 to 64 at the start (1993 to 1997) in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort, whose women are also in the newer review
exposure: Average alcohol intake, self-reported once, in standard drinks of 12 g of ethanol (grams or drinks a day in the meta-analyses; drinks a week in the Danish cohort)
comparator: Lifetime abstainers of the same sex (Rehm et al., 2010; current-abstainer references adjusted to lifetime abstention), long-term abstainers (Roerecke et al., 2019; current non-drinkers corrected upward for former drinking in four cohorts), and people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week (Danish cohort)

risk_of_bias.note: Both meta-analyses are critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_rehm_2010, sc_roerecke_2019): no protocol; Rehm et al. did not appraise their studies; Roerecke et al. rated all but one cohort at moderate risk of bias (single baseline measure, observational design) and one, which dominates the women's high-intake estimates, at serious risk (adjusted for age only); viral hepatitis was taken into account in only one study of the newer review; part of each reference group is modelled by an upward correction for former drinkers; the Danish cohort (card sc_askgaard_2015, ROBINS-E high overall, its amount gradient being the most robust result) counts only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic, which depends on known drinking (the newer review used the same cohort's wider outcome of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis, women only). Counted once.

inconsistency.note: The direction is the same at higher intake in every source, but the size differs more than tenfold between cohorts (1.80 to 22.39 at seven or more drinks a day in men), I² is 70.6% to 98.6% in the newer review and 72% to 78% in the earlier one, studies of cirrhosis death and of diagnosed cirrhosis differ systematically, and at low intake the estimates point both ways; only partly explained by the end-point.

indirectness.note: Cohort outcomes are mostly cirrhosis deaths and the Danish outcome is alcoholic cirrhosis; the claim names them.

imprecision.note: At five or more drinks a day the intervals are wide in the newer review (2.95–38.78 at seven or more) but exclude 1 in every source; the low-intake estimates are imprecise, which the claim states rather than relies on.

publication_bias.note: No funnel-plot asymmetry (Begg and Egger tests in Rehm et al.; Egger P = 0.94 at one to two drinks a day in Roerecke et al.), with little power.

large_effect.note: Relative risks of 5 to 23 at five or more drinks a day in all three sources, including the Danish cohort adjusted for smoking, education and waist size (6.98 in men and 16.2 in women at 28 to 42 drinks a week); the remaining biases (an upward correction of about 1.24 for former drinkers in some studies, confounding by viral hepatitis or obesity, the labelling of cirrhosis as alcoholic) could not plausibly produce differences of this size.

dose_response.note: Risk rises step by step with intake in each source (Table 2 in Rehm et al.; Figure 2 in Roerecke et al.; Fig. 1 in Askgaard et al.).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down one level each for risk of bias and inconsistency and up one level each for a large effect and a dose–response gradient, which gives low; a strict reading without the upgrades would give very low. Rated as worded: an association that grows with the amount, large at high intake; the claim does not say at what amount the risk begins, because the low-intake estimates conflict. Overlap: the two meta-analyses are by one team and share six studies, and the Danish cohort is one of the newer review's seven cohorts (its women only, with a wider outcome), so they are not three independent confirmations. Status replicated: the independent cohorts shown one by one in the newer review all point the same way at higher intake.

statement: In adults in the same cohorts and case–control studies, women who drank compared with women who did not had larger relative risks of liver cirrhosis than men who drank the same average amount compared with men who did not, in two meta-analyses by one team and a Danish cohort, but no source tested whether the difference between the sexes is larger than chance. In the earlier meta-analysis (against lifetime abstainers of the same sex; one drink = 12 g of ethanol), at 48 to 60 g a day (about five drinks) the relative risk was 14.7 (95% CI 11.0–19.6) in women and 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 5.9 (3.7–9.3) and 2.3 (1.7–3.2) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (Rehm et al., 2010); in the newer one (against long-term abstainers of the same sex), 1.64 (1.07–2.51) in women and 0.91 (0.31–2.64) in men at one drink a day, 4.33 (2.59–7.25) and 1.97 (0.89–4.37) at two, and 24.58 (14.77–40.90) and 6.93 (1.07–44.99) at seven or more (Roerecke et al., 2019); and in the Danish cohort (against people of the same sex drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week), 3.49 (2.00–6.12) in women and 2.33 (1.52–3.58) in men at 14 to 28 drinks a week, and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) and 6.98 (4.65–10.5) at 28 to 42 (Askgaard et al., 2015). In the earlier meta-analysis the women's and men's intervals did not overlap at 8 of its 12 levels, including every level of cirrhosis death above 12 g a day (editors' comparison), but in the newer review and the Danish cohort they overlapped at every level; at two levels the men's figure was the higher (2.0 against 1.9 at 36 to 48 g a day in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis, and 1.23 against 0.95 for occasional drinking); in the newer review the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one American cohort recruited in 1959–60 and adjusted only for age (52% and 77% of the weight), which is also the earlier review's largest study by number of people (548,185 women, 568 cases), though the newer review reports a similar rising pattern in the four women's cohorts adjusted for smoking and body size (figures in a supplement not read), and the men's estimates rest on two or three cohorts, which at one drink a day point in opposite directions; the earlier review counted three studies without results by sex for both sexes; and each relative risk is set against people of the same sex, so a larger ratio in women does not show that more women than men get cirrhosis at the same amount. No source gives absolute risks for women and men drinking the same amount; in the Danish cohort, alcoholic cirrhosis was diagnosed in 19 women and 66 men per 100,000 person-years, the women having drunk less (median 19 against 26 drinks a week among people who drank daily), and the authors say the 85 cases in women were too few for firm conclusions. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In these studies, the same amount of drinking went with a bigger rise in cirrhosis risk for women than for men, each compared with people of their own sex who did not drink. For example, at about five drinks a day (48 to 60 g), studies of cirrhosis deaths found 14.7 times the risk for women and 7.0 times for men. In that older review the gap between women and men was bigger than the margins of error at most amounts; in a newer review and a Danish study it was not. No study tested whether this difference was more than chance, and much of the evidence on women who drank heavily came from one American study that began in 1959–60. A larger ratio does not mean that more women than men get cirrhosis: in a Danish study, fewer women than men were diagnosed (19 against 66 in 100,000 a year), and the women drank less. No study gave the risk, out of 100, for women and men who drink the same amount.
population: Adults in the cohorts and case–control studies of two meta-analyses (17 and 9 studies, mostly from the USA and Europe) and Danish adults aged 50 to 64 at the start of the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort
exposure: Being a woman who drinks a given average amount (12-g drinks a day or a week)
comparator: Being a man who drinks the same amount; each sex's relative risk is set against non-drinkers (lifetime or long-term abstainers) or people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week of the same sex
outcome: Relative risk of liver cirrhosis (death or diagnosis; alcoholic cirrhosis in the Danish cohort)
magnitude: Rehm et al. 2010, against lifetime abstainers of the same sex, women against men: >48–60 g a day mortality 14.7 (11.0–19.6) against 7.0 (5.8–8.5), morbidity 5.9 (3.7–9.3) against 2.3 (1.7–3.2); >36–48 g morbidity 1.9 (1.4–2.6) against 2.0 (1.5–2.7); continuous model, women only, mortality 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g. Roerecke et al. 2019, against long-term abstainers, women against men: occasional 0.95 (0.77–1.16) against 1.23 (0.46–3.28); 1 drink 1.64 (1.07–2.51) against 0.91 (0.31–2.64); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59–7.25) against 1.97 (0.89–4.37); 3–4 drinks 3.87 (0.80–18.83) against 2.62 (0.42–16.21); 5–6 drinks 12.44 (6.65–23.27) against 3.80 (0.85–17.02); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77–40.90) against 6.93 (1.07–44.99). Askgaard et al. 2015, against fewer than 14 drinks a week of the same sex: 14–28 drinks a week 3.49 (2.00–6.12) against 2.33 (1.52–3.58); 28–42 drinks 16.2 (9.16–28.7) against 6.98 (4.65–10.5); incidence 19 against 66 per 100,000 person-years. Intervals: no overlap at 8 of the 12 levels in Rehm et al. (editors' comparison), overlap at every level in Roerecke et al. and Askgaard et al. No test of a sex difference in any source.

risk_of_bias.note: No source tests whether the dose–response differs by sex; in Rehm et al. the women's and men's estimates come from partly different studies and three studies without results by sex were entered for both (card sc_rehm_2010); in Roerecke et al. the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one 1959–60 cohort adjusted only for age, rated at serious risk of bias (card sc_roerecke_2019), which is also the largest study in Rehm et al.; each relative risk is set against the same sex's reference group, whose make-up and intake may differ between the sexes; women may under-report drinking more than men (a possibility the Danish authors raise, citing other studies).

inconsistency.note: Women's relative risks are higher at most levels in all three sources, though not at every level (2.0 against 1.9 at 36 to 48 g a day in Rehm et al.'s morbidity studies; 1.23 against 0.95 for occasional drinking in Roerecke et al.); not rated down.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded, a comparison of relative risks; whether the absolute risk at the same amount differs is not answered by any source, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: In the newer review and the Danish cohort the women's and men's intervals overlap at every level (men 6.93, 1.07–44.99, at seven or more drinks a day; 85 cases in Danish women); only the earlier review gives intervals that do not overlap (8 of 12 levels, editors' comparison), and there the two sexes' estimates draw on partly different studies; no source tested the difference.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: higher relative risks in women than in men at the same average intake, a difference no source tested; the clearest separation, in the earlier review, comes from estimates that draw on partly different studies for each sex. Overlap: the Danish cohort is inside the newer review, and the two reviews share six studies, among them the 1959–60 American cohort of women that carries most of the newer review's weight at high intake; but the earlier review's studies and the Danish cohort are independent of each other and agree in direction, hence status replicated.

statement: In middle-aged Danish adults followed for about 15 years (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, 1993 to 1997; 35% of those invited took part), drinking every day compared with drinking on two to four days a week, with the weekly amount (in 12-g drinks), smoking, education and waist size taken into account, is associated with a higher risk of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis in men, but not clearly in women, in one cohort study (Askgaard et al., 2015; no funding stated, no conflicts declared). In men, 171 of 7276 who drank daily and 27 of 9165 who drank on two to four days a week were diagnosed (about 2 in 100 against 3 in 1,000; editors' calculation), but those who drank daily also drank more (median 26 against 8.9 drinks a week): the hazard ratio for daily drinking was 8.29 (95% CI 5.52–12.4) adjusted for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) with amount added and 3.65 (2.39–5.55) with smoking, education and waist size as well, while drinking on five or six days a week did not differ clearly from two to four (1.43, 0.84–2.43). In women, 30 of 3931 who drank daily and 15 of 9481 who drank on two to four days a week were diagnosed (about 8 in 1,000 against 2 in 1,000; editors' calculation); with amount and the other factors taken into account, daily drinking gave 1.73 (0.85–3.52) and drinking on five or six days 2.30 (1.14–4.67), with no trend across frequencies (P = 0.14), and the extra risk per weekly drink was largest in women who drank least often (1.09 per drink, against 1.05 in women who drank daily). How often and how much people drank were closely linked (correlation 0.77 in men and 0.85 in women), people who drank daily drank somewhat more even within the same amount category, and the authors say this makes the two hard to separate; in the main analysis amount entered the model as a single continuous term although risk rose steeply with amount, so some confounding by amount may remain (editors' reading); drinking was asked about once, at the start, and binge drinking could not be studied. A 2019 review reports, for this cohort, daily drinking against two to four days a week at the same weekly amount as 2.25 (1.68–3.00) in men and 1.28 (0.82–2.02) in women, figures that are not in the cohort paper's main text; the review lists the cohort with 393 cases in men and 229 in women, the counts of the cohort paper's supplementary analysis of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis, so its figures probably come from that analysis (editors' reading; the supplement is not on file). For a large British cohort of women who drank (the Million Women Study, not read here), the review reports 1.61 (1.40–1.85) for daily against non-daily drinking and 0.69 (0.62–0.77) for drinking with meals against outside meals, associations it calls similar across groups by body size, smoking and beverage without saying what they were adjusted for, and 2.47 (1.96–3.11) for drinking both daily and outside meals, adjusted for amount and beverage type (Roerecke et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In one Danish study of 55,917 people aged 50 to 64, men who drank every day were diagnosed with alcohol-related cirrhosis about 3.7 times as often as men who drank on two to four days a week, after taking into account how much they drank, smoking, schooling and waist size. Women showed no clear pattern. But people who drank every day also drank more, and the study could not fully separate how often from how much. A review reported that, in a large British study of women, daily drinking was linked to 1.6 times the risk of drinking on fewer days, and drinking with meals to a lower risk. The Danish study could not look at drinking a lot on a few days (binge drinking).
population: Danish-born adults aged 50 to 64 at entry (1993 to 1997) in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort, followed to 2011 (26,696 men, 29,221 women); and, second-hand, women in the UK Million Women Study
exposure: Drinking every day (self-reported once, at baseline), with the weekly amount in 12-g drinks taken into account
comparator: Drinking on two to four days a week (Danish cohort); drinking on fewer than seven days a week (Million Women Study, as reported in a review)
outcome: First register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis (hospital or death records); cirrhosis in the Million Women Study as reported in the review
magnitude: Askgaard et al. 2015, daily against two to four days a week (HR, 95% CI): men 8.29 (5.52–12.4) adjusted for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) for age and amount, 3.65 (2.39–5.55) for age, amount, smoking, education and waist; five to six days 1.43 (0.84–2.43); trend P < 0.001. Women 5.01 (2.69–9.31), 1.6 (0.81–3.30) and 1.73 (0.85–3.52); five to six days 2.30 (1.14–4.67); trend P = 0.14. Crude: men 171 of 7276 daily and 27 of 9165 at two to four days; women 30 of 3931 and 15 of 9481. Per weekly drink: men 1.02 (less than one day a week) to 1.05 (daily); women 1.09 to 1.05. Spearman r between frequency and amount 0.77 (men), 0.85 (women). Roerecke et al. 2019 (as reported): Danish cohort 2.25 (1.68–3.00) men, 1.28 (0.82–2.02) women, the cohort listed with 393 and 229 cases of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis; Million Women Study daily against non-daily 1.61 (1.40–1.85) and with meals against outside meals 0.69 (0.62–0.77), adjustment not stated; daily and outside meals 2.47 (1.96–3.11), adjusted for amount and beverage type.

statement: In the world's population, alcohol use compared with no alcohol use is estimated by two global models to account for about 2.3 million (2004, after subtracting deaths the model counted as prevented; editors' rounding) to 2.8 million (2016) deaths a year. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016 (95% uncertainty interval 2.4–3.3 million), 2.2% of age-standardised deaths in women and 6.8% in men, about 2 and 7 in every 100; it ranked alcohol seventh among risk factors overall and first at ages 15 to 49, where 3.8% of women's and 12.2% of men's deaths were attributed to it, the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, with support from the US National Institute on Aging). A comparative risk assessment for 2004, which applied the attributable fractions of WHO's assessments for 2000 and 2002 to WHO's 2004 death estimates, estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, less 227 thousand deaths it modelled as prevented (215 thousand from heart and blood-vessel disease, 12 thousand from diabetes), leaving 2255 thousand, 3.8 in every 100 deaths worldwide (6.3 in 100 deaths of men and 1.1 in 100 of women) and 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60; the deaths caused were mainly from unintentional injuries (666 thousand), heart and blood-vessel disease (545 thousand), cancer (487 thousand), liver cirrhosis (373 thousand) and intentional injuries (272 thousand) (Rehm et al., 2009; supported by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto, the underlying assessments by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; no conflicts declared). These are model estimates, not counted deaths: they combine estimated drinking (sales data, estimates of unrecorded alcohol, which is more than a quarter of the world's drinking, and surveys) with relative-risk curves from observational studies (for the 2004 model, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries), applied to every population. The 2004 estimate has no uncertainty intervals, although its authors describe the uncertainty as fairly low, citing an earlier WHO report, and the 2016 intervals carry sampling error and the uncertainty of the model's parameters but are not said to include uncertainty from the model's structure or from bias in the underlying studies; the same group's next round, cited from unpublished work in a 2022 paper, put deaths in 2020 at 1.78 million (1.39–2.27 million), below the 2016 interval (GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022; not read in its own source); the net figures depend on protective heart and diabetes estimates at low intake, which the 2004 authors call controversial; the 2016 figure is counted against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day, whose interval reached 0.8 drinks (10 g each) a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated its weights (0.534, 0–1.00; GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022); the 2016 authors expect their figures to be underestimates, because unrecorded drinking may still be missed, drinking patterns were not modelled, and harm to others from violence, people under 15 and some outcomes, such as dementia, were left out; and the estimates used different methods and inputs, so the differences between them are not a trend. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: Two global models estimated that alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking. The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women. At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study (about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women), the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm. An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented, mainly from heart disease; that is about 4 in 100 of all deaths. Injuries, heart and blood-vessel disease, cancer and liver cirrhosis made up most of the deaths caused. A later round of the Global Burden of Disease study, quoted second-hand, put the figure at about 1.8 million deaths in 2020. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths. They rely on studies of groups of people (for the older model, mostly in richer countries), and the models used different methods, so the numbers cannot be compared as a trend.
population: The world's population: all ages in the 2004 WHO comparative risk assessment (14 WHO subregions); ages 15 and over in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study (195 locations)
exposure: Alcohol use as modelled from sales data (recorded and unrecorded alcohol) and surveys: average volume, with drinking patterns for injuries and ischaemic heart disease, in the 2004 model; average grams of ethanol a day among current drinkers (10-g standard drinks) in the 2016 model
comparator: A counterfactual of no alcohol use (2004), or the estimated minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day (2016)
outcome: Deaths attributable to alcohol: in 2004, deaths caused, deaths prevented and net deaths (WHO Global Burden of Disease 2004 causes); in 2016, attributable deaths from 23 outcomes
magnitude: GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018 (GBD 2016; 95% uncertainty intervals): 2.8 million (2.4–3.3) deaths in 2016; 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of DALYs; ages 15–49: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; leading attributable causes at 15–49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0–1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7–1.9) and self-harm 1.1% (0.6–1.5) of total deaths; minimum-risk level 0 (0.0–0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day. Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment, 2004; thousands; no intervals): caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443); prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths, 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); under age 60, 5.3% (men 7.9%, women 1.9%); deaths caused by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators, 2022: global minimum-risk level 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the GBD 2016 curves and GBD 2020 weights; citing unpublished GBD 2020 work, 1.78 million (1.39–2.27) deaths in 2020.

inconsistency.note: The two models give figures of similar size (2.3 to 2.8 million a year) for different years and with different methods. indirectness.note: Relative risks transferred to every population; exposure from sales data, expert estimates of unrecorded alcohol (more than a quarter of the total) and surveys; drinking patterns estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion in 2004; harm to others only through US road-injury data in 2016; the 2016 counterfactual from one global weighting of the curves.

imprecision.note: No uncertainty intervals in the 2004 model; the 2016 intervals (2.4 to 3.3 million) are not said to include structural uncertainty or bias in the underlying studies. publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a model; publication bias in the studies behind the curves is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Model estimates are not graded as evidence of an effect: the claim describes what the models estimate (relation describes), and its certainty comes from the observational evidence behind the relative-risk curves (low), rated down for the models' indirectness and their incomplete uncertainty, which gives very low. No upgrade applies to a modelled count. Status replicated by the same team, under the flag's shared analysis model (METHODS §6.4) rather than shared investigators: the 2016 and 2004 estimates come from different groups, but both use the comparative-risk-assessment method, the 2016 exposure model follows the approach of Rehm and colleagues (GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018, Methods › Data sources, 2nd paragraph), and both draw on much the same cohort literature and WHO consumption data, so their agreement is not independent replication (METHODS §6.3); the second-hand 2020 figure comes from the GBD group itself and is not counted.

statement: In adults aged 18 or older living in US households and some group homes, a national face-to-face survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 36,309 people, 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared) found DSM-5 alcohol use disorder, diagnosed with a structured interview (the AUDADIS-5) given by interviewers who were not clinicians, in 13.9 in 100 adults in the past year (SE 0.31) and in 29.1 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild (7.3 in 100 adults mild, 3.2 moderate, 3.4 severe). The disorder was more common in men than in women (17.6 against 10.4 in 100 in the past year) and at ages 18 to 29 (26.7 in 100) than at 65 or older (2.3 in 100). Among adults who had drunk alcohol in the past year, 17.5 in 100 (95% CI 16.7 to 18.3) met the older DSM-IV criteria in the same survey, as did 54.5 in 100 of those who had drunk heavily at least once a week (4 or more US standard drinks of 14 g of alcohol in a day for women, 5 or more for men) (Grant et al., 2017). The figures depend on the survey: another national survey, cited by the same authors, found 7.0 in 100 adults with the disorder in the past year in 2013 and about 7.5 in 100 throughout 2002 to 2013, a little over half of NESARC-III's 12.7 in 100 by the older DSM-IV definition, against which the authors set it; they do not explain the difference. NESARC-III left out homeless people, people in prison and most people in treatment, which the authors say may lower its figures, and 4 in 10 of the people sampled did not take part. By the older DSM-IV definition, the same institute's surveys found 8.5 in 100 adults with the disorder in 2001–2002 and 12.7 in 100 in 2012–2013. The authors read this as a real rise, pointing to near-identical questions, weighting for non-response and other alcohol indicators that rose over the same years (Grant et al., 2017); in the editors' reading these surveys cannot show whether the disorder became more common, because their design and response differed (81.0% against about 60%) and the other national survey, as the authors report it, showed a stable figure over the same years. For the world, a narrative review relays WHO estimates for 2016 of 5.1 in 100 people aged 15 or older (8.6 in 100 men, 1.7 in 100 women), which its authors call rough estimates; these figures are second-hand (Carvalho et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In a large US survey in 2012–2013, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year, about half of them in a mild form, and about 29 in 100 had had it at some time in their lives. It was most common in young adults and in men. Among adults who drank that year, about 18 in 100 met the older (DSM-IV) criteria. Another US survey found a little over half as many people with the disorder, so the number depends on how it is measured, and the survey left out people who were homeless or in prison and most people in treatment. A review passes on world estimates of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older in 2016. The survey's authors think the disorder became more common in the US between 2001 and 2013; in our reading, their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
population: Adults aged 18 or older in US households and selected group quarters (not homeless people, people in prison or most people in treatment), interviewed in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III, 36,309 people) and in 2001–2002 (NESARC, 43,093 people); the world population aged 15 or older in 2016 (WHO estimates, relayed second-hand)

comparator: None for the prevalence; another US national survey (the National Survey on Drug Use and Health) as the authors report it; the 2001–2002 survey for the DSM-IV figures

Response 60.1% (screener 72.0%, person 84.0%). National Survey on Drug Use and Health, as cited: past-year AUD 7.0% in 2013, about 7.5% and stable over 2002–2013, which the authors set against NESARC-III's DSM-IV 12.7%. The other survey was not read; its figures are taken as the authors give them, and the stable 2002–2013 figure is cited in the paper to a 2004 NESARC article that cannot contain it (reporting issue on sc_grant_2015).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in survey populations): it starts low and is never upgraded. Rated down one level for risk of bias (response, frame and diagnosis by interviewers who were not clinicians; JBI moderate on the card) and one for inconsistency (another national survey gives a little over half the past-year figure, unexplained), which reaches very low. statement: In US adults with DSM-5 alcohol use disorder in a national household survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared), 7.7 in 100 of those who had the disorder in the past year and 19.8 in 100 of those who had had it at some time said they had sought treatment or help for it, counting 12-step groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (the abstract calls this being treated). Seeking help rose with severity: 4.4, 8.7 and 34.7 in 100 of people with mild, moderate and severe lifetime disorder. Among people with the disorder in the past year, 4.5 in 100 had used 12-step groups, 3.6 in 100 a health care practitioner, 2.0 in 100 an outpatient service and 1.8 in 100 a rehabilitation programme. For other countries, a narrative review relays, second-hand, that 22.3 in 100 patients identified with alcohol dependence in primary care in six European countries received interventions, and 21.9 in 100 worldwide in an overview published in 2004 (Carvalho et al., 2019; two authors declare fees or grants from companies, including drug companies, outside the work). Help-seeking was self-reported at one interview, the survey did not cover most people who were in treatment, which may make its figures too low (the authors say this of prevalence; for help-seeking it is the editors' inference), and 4 in 10 sampled people did not take part. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a US survey in 2012–2013, about 20 in 100 people who had ever had alcohol use disorder said they had ever looked for treatment or help, and about 8 in 100 of those who had it in the past year. Groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous were the most common kind of help. People who had ever had severe disorder looked for help more often (about 35 in 100) than people with mild disorder (about 4 in 100). A review passes on figures of about 22 in 100 for Europe and the world, though these count people who received treatment, not people who looked for it. People reported this themselves, and the survey did not include most people who were in treatment at the time.

statement: In people in alcohol withdrawal, withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) is defined in DSM-5, as a narrative review sets it out (Schuckit, 2014; no funding statement, no conflicts reported), as alcohol withdrawal after stopping or cutting down heavy, prolonged drinking (at least two of eight signs: an overactive nervous system, hand tremor, sleeplessness, nausea or vomiting, brief hallucinations or illusions, agitation, anxiety, seizures) together with delirium, a disturbance of attention, awareness and thinking that comes on quickly and fluctuates. The review relays, second-hand and without the designs or settings of its sources, that about half of people with alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop and that seizures, delirium or both develop in 3 to 5 in 100 of them; that 3 to 5 in 100 patients in hospital for alcohol withdrawal meet the criteria for withdrawal delirium, a rate it says depends on how clinicians apply the criteria and on the setting; that it usually begins about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear and lasts from 1 to 8 days or more, usually 2 or 3; and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with withdrawal delirium die, usually from overheating, heart rhythm disturbances, complications of seizures or other illnesses, a rate the author says timely diagnosis and treatment could lower. It names, as signs that delirium is more likely, a high withdrawal score (above 15 on the CIWA-Ar scale, especially with a systolic blood pressure above 150 mm Hg or a pulse above 100 a minute), recent withdrawal seizures (seen in 20 in 100 people with delirium), earlier delirium or seizures, older age, recent use of other depressant drugs, and other medical problems such as low potassium or magnesium. In the placebo groups of four trials from 1961 to 1980, tabulated in a 1997 review, 11 of 186 people in withdrawal, about 6 in 100, developed delirium (editors' sum), and one trial from 1969 supplied 130 of the 186 people and 8 of the 11 cases (Mayo-Smith, 1997; a practice guideline of a US medical society, ASAM, with no funding or conflict statement). The trials predate DSM-IV (the review says it kept only outcomes corresponding to DSM-IV definitions, without saying how it judged this) and the review does not describe their settings, the narrative review's figures are second-hand, and none of these sources measures how often delirium happens to people who stop drinking outside hospital. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Delirium tremens, or the DTs, is sudden confusion during alcohol withdrawal: trouble paying attention and thinking clearly that comes and goes, together with withdrawal signs such as shaking or a fast pulse. A review says it usually starts about 3 days after withdrawal begins and lasts 2 or 3 days, that 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get it, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who were given dummy pills developed delirium; most of these people were in one large trial from 1969. The review names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs that it is more likely. These figures are old or passed on by one review, and none measures how often it happens outside hospital.
population: People in alcohol withdrawal: people with alcohol use disorder who cut down or stop (figures relayed by a narrative review), patients in hospital for withdrawal (relayed), and the placebo groups of four trials published 1961 to 1980
exposure: Stopping or cutting down heavy, prolonged drinking; in the trials, placebo instead of a benzodiazepine
comparator: None for the definition and frequencies; the placebo groups are described on their own
outcome: DSM-5 alcohol withdrawal delirium (its definition), how often it occurs, when it starts and how long it lasts, case fatality, and the predictors named by the review

statement: In people in alcohol withdrawal in placebo-controlled trials published from the 1960s to 1983 (the largest testing chlordiazepoxide; the three in the Cochrane review's seizure analysis, all randomized, tested chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam and diazepam), benzodiazepines compared with placebo reduced withdrawal seizures: in a Cochrane review searched to December 2009, 1 of 149 people given a benzodiazepine against 14 of 175 given placebo had a seizure in three trials (risk ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.69), about 1 against 8 in 100 in the review's illustration (13 against 80 per 1,000), graded moderate quality by the review (Amato et al., 2010; funded by a Rome health authority and the Italian medicines agency; no conflicts declared). An earlier review found 7.7 fewer seizures per 100 people treated (95% CI 3.5 to 12.0 fewer; five trials) and 4.9 fewer cases of delirium per 100 (0.7 to 9.0 fewer; four trials, 3 of 172 against 11 of 186 people, editors' sums) (Mayo-Smith, 1997; a practice guideline of a US medical society, ASAM, with no funding or conflict statement). The two reviews share three trials, and one trial from 1969 supplies most of the events, so they are not independent confirmation. Against other medicines pooled together (trials up to 2009; anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, clonidine, beta-blockers and others), benzodiazepines showed no clear difference in seizures (risk ratio 0.52, 0.21 to 1.31; 12 trials) or delirium (0.65, 0.21 to 1.98; 8 trials), and people on benzodiazepines tended to have adverse events more often (1.31, 0.99 to 1.72; 18 trials); against anticonvulsants alone the estimates leaned towards the anticonvulsants, also without a clear difference (seizures 1.70, 0.39 to 7.37; delirium 1.90, 0.43 to 8.38). Phenothiazine antipsychotics given alone did not reduce delirium compared with placebo (risk difference 0.0 per 100, −5.8 to +6.6) and were followed by more seizures (11.4 more per 100, 6.2 to 16.6) and more delirium (6.6 more per 100, 2.4 to 10.8) than benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. In the comparisons with other medicines, deaths occurred in 4 of the 32 trials in the mortality analysis. For people already in withdrawal delirium, a narrative review, citing a 2004 review, describes the treatment evidence as nine prospective controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 and later uncontrolled studies (Schuckit, 2014). Most trials did not report how allocation was concealed, events were few, the placebo-controlled trials predate DSM-IV, and people with severe liver, heart, lung or kidney disease, epilepsy or dependence on other drugs were often left out. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials from the 1960s to the 1980s, people going through alcohol withdrawal who were given a benzodiazepine, a calming medicine, had fewer seizures than people given dummy pills: about 1 in 100 against about 8 in 100. They also developed delirium less often, about 2 in 100 against 6 in 100. Other medicines were not clearly better or worse at preventing seizures or delirium, but one kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines. Most trials were small and old, and few looked at people who already had the DTs.
population: People in alcohol withdrawal in placebo-controlled trials published from the 1960s to 1983 and randomized trials up to 2009 comparing medicines, mostly in hospital wards, detoxification units and veterans' hospitals, mostly men; the trials often left out people with serious medical illness or other drug dependence
exposure: A benzodiazepine (mostly chlordiazepoxide in the placebo-controlled trials; also diazepam and lorazepam)
comparator: Placebo; other medicines (anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, clonidine, beta-blockers and others, pooled); phenothiazine antipsychotics against placebo and against benzodiazepines or paraldehyde
outcome: Withdrawal seizures and withdrawal delirium during the withdrawal episode; adverse events; deaths
magnitude: Amato et al. 2010 (Cochrane, search to December 2009): against placebo, seizures RR 0.16 (0.04 to 0.69), 3 trials, 324 participants, 1/149 against 14/175, I² 0%, GRADE moderate, illustrative 80 against 13 per 1000 (3 to 55); against other drugs, seizures RR 0.52 (0.21 to 1.31), 12 trials, 1228, 5/442 against 37/786; against anticonvulsants 1.70 (0.39 to 7.37), 7 trials, 523; delirium RR 0.65 (0.21 to 1.98), 8 trials, 893, I² 52%; against anticonvulsants 1.90 (0.43 to 8.38), 5 trials, 342; at least one adverse event RR 1.31 (0.99 to 1.72), 18 trials, 919, GRADE low; deaths in 4 of the 32 trials of the mortality analysis (2 with benzodiazepines, 5 with other drugs, editors' sum). Mayo-Smith 1997: risk difference, benzodiazepine against placebo, delirium −4.9 per 100 (−9.0 to −0.7), 4 trials, 3/172 against 11/186; seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), 5 trials, 1/182 against 17/196 (editors' sums from Table 2); phenothiazine against placebo, delirium 0.0 (−5.8 to +6.6), seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9); phenothiazine against benzodiazepine or paraldehyde, delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8), seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6).

risk_of_bias.note: Allocation concealment was unclear in 2 of the 3 trials in the Cochrane seizure pool (the review's own reason for moderate) and adequate in 13 of 64 trials overall; the 1997 review appraised no trial (sc_mayo_smith_1997: AMSTAR 2 critically low); in the largest trial the seizure outcome appears to be counted only in those who stayed; the placebo-controlled trials predate DSM-IV (the 1997 review says their outcomes corresponded to DSM-IV definitions, without saying how; sc_mayo_smith_1997).

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by either review; with few small trials it cannot be judged. Not rated down, recorded as unknown.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Rated down for risk of bias (unclear concealment, an unappraised older pool, placebo trials from before DSM-IV) and imprecision (few events), giving low; the Cochrane review rated the seizure result moderate, downgrading only for concealment. 'Reduces' is used for the placebo comparison because the evidence is randomized and the intervals exclude no effect; the comparisons with other medicines show no clear difference either way and are not claimed as equivalence. Overlap: three trials (Kaim 1969, Sellers 1983, Naranjo 1983) are in both reviews' seizure pools, with different counts for Naranjo 1983 (0/21 against 1/20 in the Cochrane review, 0/15 against 2/15 in the 1997 review), so the two reviews are counted once. Status replicated: several independent trials point the same way, though no single trial was significant on its own. No regimens or doses are given (the reviews' dosing comparisons are left out).

statement: In adults with alcohol dependence treated as outpatients in double-blind trials, mostly after detoxification and with counselling or another psychosocial treatment in both groups, naltrexone tablets at the dose used in most trials compared with placebo reduced return to heavy drinking (in most trials 5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) during treatment: across 19 trials of 12 to 24 weeks (17 of them of 12 weeks) pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 728 of 1,593 people on naltrexone (46 in 100) and 698 of 1,282 on placebo (54 in 100) returned to heavy drinking (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared). Its 2023 update, also for the agency (no conflicts declared), found a risk ratio of 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90; 23 trials, 3,170 people) (McPheeters et al., 2023), and a Cochrane review of naltrexone in any form, mostly the same tablets, found 0.83 (0.76 to 0.90; 28 trials, 4,433 people) (Rösner, Hackl-Herrwerth, Leucht, Vecchi, et al., 2010; funded by the German education and research ministry; two of its six authors declare fees from drug companies). The effect on staying off alcohol completely was small or unclear: risk difference −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002) in 2014, risk ratio 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99) in 2023 and 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00) in the Cochrane review. In the 2023 review, people on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100 (−5.1 percentage points, −7.16 to −3.04) and drank heavily on about 4 fewer (−4.3, −7.60 to −0.91). With naltrexone at any dose (the 2023 review assessed harms for all doses together), nausea (risk ratio 1.73, 1.51 to 1.98), dizziness (1.99, 1.47 to 2.69) and vomiting (1.53, 1.23 to 1.91) were more common; about 1 more person in 48 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 48, 30 to 112), and serious adverse events were not more frequent (risk difference −0.02, −0.05 to 0.00; 9 trials). A higher oral dose and a long-acting injection were each tested in only 2 trials for return to heavy drinking, without a clear effect. Head to head, naltrexone and acamprosate did not differ (return to heavy drinking risk ratio 1.02, 0.93 to 1.11; 4 trials), but more than half of the people in this comparison were in one US trial (COMBINE, 612 of 1,141, editors' arithmetic), whose naltrexone group took the higher oral dose. Evidence on deaths, injuries and quality of life is insufficient. The three reviews share most of their trials and are one body of evidence, not three. Across the 2023 review's trials of all medicines, mean age was typically 40 to 49 and most trials that reported race and sex enrolled mostly White men; most participants had moderate to severe dependence and had stopped drinking before starting, and effects in people still drinking, with mild disorder or without counselling are uncertain. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials lasting mostly 3 months, people with alcohol dependence who took naltrexone tablets went back to heavy drinking less often than people on dummy pills: about 46 in 100 against 54 in 100. Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely. People on it drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common, and about 1 more person in 48 stopped because of side effects. Naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same when compared directly, though most people in that comparison were in one trial. Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and also had counselling.
population: Adults with alcohol dependence (DSM-III-R, DSM-IV or ICD-10) treated as outpatients in double-blind randomized trials (12 to 24 weeks, mostly 12, for the main 2014 estimates; 4 weeks or more in the Cochrane review), mostly after detoxification or a few days without alcohol and with a psychosocial co-intervention in both groups; in the 2023 review's trials of all medicines, mostly White men in their 40s; more trials in the US than elsewhere
exposure: Naltrexone tablets at the dose used in most trials (analysed apart from a higher oral dose and from the long-acting injection in the AHRQ reviews; any form, mostly the same tablets, in the Cochrane review)
comparator: Placebo with the same co-intervention; acamprosate in head-to-head trials
outcome: Return to heavy drinking and to any drinking during treatment; percentage of drinking days and of heavy drinking days; side effects, stopping a trial because of them, and serious adverse events; deaths and other health outcomes
magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (oral naltrexone, main dose group, against placebo): return to heavy drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials of 12 to 24 weeks (17 of 12 weeks), 2875 participants, I² 43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 728/1593 (45.7%) against 698/1282 (54.4%) (editors' arithmetic from Figure 3); return to any drinking RD −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, 2347, NNT 20 (11 to 500); percentage of drinking days WMD −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2); heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61); withdrawal from trials because of adverse events NNH 48 (30 to 112), 17 trials, 2743. McPheeters et al. 2023: return to heavy drinking RR 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90), 23 trials, 3170, moderate; return to any drinking 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99), 16 trials, 2347, moderate (the Table's counts; the forest plot lists more trials, a reporting issue on the study card); percentage of drinking days −5.1 (−7.16 to −3.04), 15 trials; heavy drinking days −4.3 (−7.60 to −0.91), 7 trials; any dose, return to heavy drinking 0.86 (0.80 to 0.93), 27 trials, 4645; higher oral dose 0.93 (0.84 to 1.01), 2 trials, and injection 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 2 trials, both low; nausea RR 1.73 (1.51 to 1.98), dizziness 1.99 (1.47 to 2.69), vomiting 1.53 (1.23 to 1.91), all naltrexone doses together; acamprosate against naltrexone, return to any drinking 1.03 (0.96 to 1.10), 3 trials, 800, return to heavy drinking 1.02 (0.93 to 1.11), 4 trials, 1141, of whom 612 in COMBINE, its naltrexone arm in the higher-dose group (editors' arithmetic from Jonas et al., 2014, Figure 3); deaths 1 against 2 (6 trials, 1738), insufficient. Rösner et al. 2010 (Cochrane): return to heavy drinking RR 0.83 (0.76 to 0.90), 28 trials, 4433, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); return to any drinking 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00), 27 trials, 4693 (fixed effect 0.95, 0.92 to 0.98); drinking days MD −3.89 (−5.75 to −2.04); nausea RD 0.10 (0.07 to 0.13); serious adverse events RD −0.02 (−0.05 to 0.00), 9 trials; drop-out because of adverse events RR 1.60 (1.15 to 2.23), 22 trials.

risk_of_bias.note: Few trials were at low risk of bias: 4 of 53 naltrexone studies in Jonas et al.; allocation concealment adequate in 3 of 50 and missing binary data adequately handled in 11 of 40 in the Cochrane review; drinking was self-reported. The reviews' own AMSTAR 2 ratings are critically low (Jonas; McPheeters) and low (Rösner), mainly for documentation.

inconsistency.note: Moderate heterogeneity (I² 43.7% in 2014, 58.7% in 2023) with most trials on the same side; the Cochrane review's approximate prediction interval (RR 0.61 to 1.12, editors' calculation on its study card) shows that single trials may find no effect, which the statement allows for.

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations (detoxified, mostly treatment-seeking adults with moderate to severe dependence, with counselling) and durations (mostly 12 weeks in the main 2014 pools); the uncertainty outside them is stated.

imprecision.note: Thousands of participants and intervals that exclude no effect for return to heavy drinking.

publication_bias.note: Funnel plots and Begg's or Egger's tests showed no clear asymmetry in two reviews, and industry and non-profit trials gave similar estimates; the 2023 review did not assess publication bias.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down one level for risk of bias, giving moderate, as both AHRQ reviews graded return to heavy drinking. 'Reduces' applies to return to heavy drinking; the effect on any drinking is small and depends on the review and model (significant in 2014 and 2023, not in the Cochrane random-effects model), and the claim says so. The duration is given as in the pooled trials (12 to 24 weeks, mostly 12, in the 2014 pools), not as the 12 to 52 weeks of all the review's studies. Overlap: the 2023 review updates the 2014 one (81 of its 118 trials carried over), the Cochrane review covers largely the same trials to January 2010, and COMBINE is in all three, so they are counted as one body of evidence; COMBINE also supplies more than half of the head-to-head comparison with acamprosate, with its higher-dose naltrexone group. Status replicated: that body holds many independent trials pointing the same way. The higher oral dose and the injection are named only as tested in 2 trials each for return to heavy drinking; no doses are given.
