statement: In people with alcohol dependence, mostly adults treated as outpatients, in double-blind trials, most of them European and most after detoxification, acamprosate compared with placebo is associated with fewer people returning to any drinking during treatment: across 16 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 1,968 of 2,576 people on acamprosate (76 in 100) and 1,893 of 2,271 on placebo (83 in 100) drank again (crude totals and a crude difference of 7 in 100, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit), with large differences between trials (I² 80.8%) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared); its 2023 update, also for the agency, gives a risk ratio of 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93; 20 trials, 6,380 people) (McPheeters et al., 2023), and a Cochrane review 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91; 24 trials) (Rösner, Hackl-Herrwerth, Leucht, Lehert, et al., 2010; funded by the German education and research ministry, with individual patient data from a database part-funded by the manufacturer; three of its six authors declare fees from drug companies, two of them from makers or marketers of acamprosate). In the Cochrane review abstinent days rose by about 11 in every 100 days (10.94 percentage points, 5.08 to 16.81; I² 94%), and in 7 trials fewer people on acamprosate had returned to drinking 3 to 12 months after treatment ended (risk ratio 0.91, 0.87 to 0.96). Acamprosate did not reduce return to heavy drinking (risk ratio 0.99, 0.94 to 1.05; 7 trials). In the 4 trials at low risk of bias the difference was not clear (risk difference −0.02, −0.09 to 0.05); the two of them with by far the most events, both in the US and one of them COMBINE, found no benefit, while most of the other 15 trials were European and recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes. The 2014 authors list population differences, other heterogeneity, chance or 'no true association between acamprosate and return to drinking' as possible explanations. Of the Cochrane review's 24 trials, 17 were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, though industry-run and non-profit trials gave similar estimates (risk ratios 0.88 and 0.88). Diarrhoea was more common (11 more in 100; risk difference 0.11, 0.09 to 0.13), and in the 2014 review so were anxiety (2 trials) and vomiting (4 trials); more people stopped because of side effects in the Cochrane review (risk ratio 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80), but not significantly more in the 2014 review. Head to head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ (return to any drinking risk ratio 1.03, 0.96 to 1.10; 3 trials, 612 of whose 800 people were in COMBINE, whose naltrexone group took the higher oral dose; editors' arithmetic). The three reviews share most of their trials. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
plain: In trials, mostly in Europe, fewer people with alcohol dependence who took acamprosate drank again during treatment than people on dummy pills: about 76 in 100 against 83 in 100. It did not cut heavy drinking. The most carefully run trials, including the two largest of them, both in the US, found no clear difference, and most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker. Diarrhoea was more common: about 11 more people in every 100. In one review, more people stopped taking it because of side effects. Acamprosate and naltrexone did about the same when compared directly.
population: People with alcohol dependence, mostly adults, in double-blind trials of 8 weeks to one year, mostly of outpatients, mostly after detoxification and with psychosocial treatment in both groups; most placebo-controlled trials in Europe (16 of 22 in Jonas et al.; 19 of 24 in the Cochrane review)
exposure: Acamprosate tablets as given in the trials
comparator: Placebo with the same co-intervention; naltrexone in head-to-head trials
outcome: Return to any drinking during treatment and 3 to 12 months after it; abstinent days; return to heavy drinking; side effects and stopping because of them
magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (against placebo, trials at low or medium risk of bias): return to any drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, 4847, I² 80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 1968/2576 (76.4%) against 1893/2271 (83.4%), a crude difference of 7.0 percentage points (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2); by risk of bias, post hoc: high or unclear −0.13 (−0.20 to −0.06), 3 trials, 757; medium −0.11 (−0.16 to −0.06), 12 trials, 3438; low −0.02 (−0.09 to 0.05), 4 trials, 1409; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials, 2496; percentage of drinking days WMD −8.8 (−12.8 to −4.8), 13 trials; deaths 7 against 6 (8 trials, 2677), insufficient; withdrawal from trials because of adverse events not significantly different from placebo; anxiety NNH 7 (5 to 11; 2 trials), diarrhoea NNH 11 (6 to 34; 12 trials), vomiting NNH 42 (24 to 143; 4 trials). McPheeters et al. 2023: return to any drinking RR 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93), 20 trials, 6380, moderate (I² 77.6%); return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05), 7 trials, moderate (no effect); percentage of drinking days −8.3 (−12.2 to −4.4), 14 trials; diarrhoea RR 1.58 (1.27 to 1.97). Rösner et al. 2010 (Cochrane): return to any drinking RR 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91), 24 trials, 6172, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); abstinent days MD 10.94 percentage points (5.08 to 16.81), 19 trials, I² 94%; after treatment RR 0.91 (0.87 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1986; return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.04), 6 trials, 2132; diarrhoea RD 0.11 (0.09 to 0.13), 16 trials; drop-out because of adverse events RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80), 19 trials; by funding, fully industry-sponsored 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), 11 trials, partly industry-supported 0.84 (0.78 to 0.89), 6 trials, non-profit 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96), 7 trials. COMBINE: acamprosate main effect on percent days abstinent 78.4 against 77.6 (P=.61); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15), the paper's main-effect hazard ratio, whose basis is unclear (study card sc_anton_2006).

risk_of_bias.note: Most trials were at medium risk of bias and the low-risk trials show no clear effect; allocation concealment was adequate in 3 of the Cochrane review's 24 trials; 17 of 24 trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, and several outcomes came from manufacturer reports, and the review's individual patient data came from a database part-funded by the manufacturer (study card sc_rosner_2010b). Industry and non-profit trials gave similar estimates, so funding is not rated separately.

inconsistency.note: Large unexplained heterogeneity for the main outcome (I² 80.8% in 2014, 77.6% in 2023; 94% for abstinent days) and a split between mostly European trials that found benefit and the largest US trials that did not; the explanations offered (recruitment, severity) were not tested. The crude difference (7 in 100) is smaller than the pooled 9 because the random-effects model gives the two large US trials about 16% of the weight for about 25% of the participants (editors' arithmetic on sc_jonas_2014, Figure 2).

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations (detoxified adults with alcohol dependence, mostly in Europe).

imprecision.note: The pooled intervals exclude no effect; the low-risk subgroup is imprecise, which is part of the inconsistency rating and not counted twice.

publication_bias.note: Not detected (funnel plots and Begg's or Egger's tests in two reviews); the 2023 review did not assess it.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias and for inconsistency, giving low, below the reviews' moderate grades, because the effect is not seen in the trials at low risk of bias and the 2014 authors name bias as one possible explanation. Worded as an association, as the 2014 review words it, because the randomized design would support causal wording but the evidence leaves open whether the pooled effect is real. Overlap: the three reviews share most trials, and COMBINE and Mason 2006 are in all of them, so they are counted once. Status mixed: trials point both to a modest benefit (mostly European) and to none (the largest low-risk US trials), with no adequate explanation; the critique comes from inside the review itself, and the claim does not take a side beyond the low certainty.

statement: In adults with alcohol use disorder in double-blind outpatient trials of at least 12 weeks, mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention, other medicines compared with placebo, as pooled in a 2023 review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (McPheeters et al., 2023; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared): topiramate is associated with fewer drinking days (−7.2 percentage points, 95% CI −14.3 to −0.1; 8 trials, 1,080 people), fewer heavy-drinking days (−6.2, −10.9 to −1.4; 9 trials) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days (−2.0, −3.1 to −1.0; 7 trials), each graded moderate strength of evidence by the review, with more tingling (risk ratio 3.08, 2.11 to 4.49), changes in taste (3.01, 1.70 to 5.34) and problems with thinking (2.37, 1.58 to 3.55); baclofen with fewer people returning to any drinking (risk ratio 0.83, 0.70 to 0.98; 8 trials), though not with its other drinking outcomes, and gabapentin with fewer returning to heavy drinking (0.90, 0.82 to 0.98; 3 trials), both graded low, with more drowsiness, sleepiness or dizziness and, with gabapentin, problems with thinking (2.76, 1.51 to 5.06). Disulfiram showed no clear difference in return to any drinking in blinded trials (risk ratio 1.03, 0.90 to 1.17; 3 trials; low), although no trial tested taking it under supervision, which the earlier review says may underestimate its benefit (Jonas et al., 2014). A long-acting injection of naltrexone showed no clear difference in return to any or heavy drinking (2 trials each; low) but was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days (−4.68 percentage points, −8.63 to −0.73; 3 trials; low). In the earlier review, nalmefene was associated with 2 fewer heavy-drinking days a month (−2.0, −3.0 to −1.0; 2 trials), and about 1 more person in 12 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 12, 7 to 50). Deaths were too few to judge (8 with baclofen against 3 with placebo in 4 trials). The 2023 review updates the 2014 one and shares most of its trials, and it reports results only for medicines with at least low strength of evidence for benefit. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Several other medicines have been compared with dummy pills. Topiramate was linked to fewer drinking days (about 7 fewer in every 100) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days, but tingling, changes in taste and trouble thinking were more common. Baclofen and gabapentin were linked to small benefits, but the evidence is weak. In blinded trials, disulfiram showed no clear benefit; no trial tested taking it with someone watching. A long-acting naltrexone injection showed no clear effect on going back to drinking, though it was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days. Most of these medicines were tested in only a few trials.
population: Adults with alcohol use disorder (mostly alcohol dependence) in double-blind outpatient trials of at least 12 weeks, mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention; mostly White men in their 40s
exposure: Topiramate, baclofen, gabapentin, disulfiram, injectable naltrexone and nalmefene, as given in the trials
comparator: Placebo
outcome: Drinking days, heavy-drinking days, drinks per drinking day, return to any or heavy drinking; side effects and stopping a trial because of them; deaths
magnitude: McPheeters et al. 2023, against placebo: topiramate, percentage of drinking days WMD −7.2 (−14.3 to −0.1), 8 trials, 1080; heavy drinking days −6.2 (−10.9 to −1.4), 9 trials, 1210; drinks per drinking day −2.0 (−3.1 to −1.0), 7 trials, 922; all moderate; paraesthesia RR 3.08 (2.11 to 4.49), taste abnormalities 3.01 (1.70 to 5.34), cognitive dysfunction 2.37 (1.58 to 3.55). Baclofen, return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98), 8 trials, 995, low; drowsiness 1.46 (1.15 to 1.86), dizziness 1.89 (1.40 to 2.55), sleepiness 1.81 (1.11 to 2.97); deaths 8 against 3 (4 trials, 660), insufficient. Gabapentin, return to heavy drinking 0.90 (0.82 to 0.98), return to any drinking 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02), 3 trials, 522, low; cognitive dysfunction 2.76 (1.51 to 5.06), dizziness 1.70 (1.24 to 2.32). risk_of_bias.note: Per-trial risk of bias is not shown in the 2023 review, whose AMSTAR 2 rating is critically low; in 2014 most trials were rated medium risk of bias, and drinking was self-reported.

inconsistency.note: Not rated separately; the review downgraded baclofen for inconsistency, which the claim reports as the review's low grade.

indirectness.note: Worded for the trial populations; disulfiram's untested supervised use is stated.

imprecision.note: Most findings rest on 2 to 9 trials; the topiramate drinking-days interval reaches −0.1 points; the baclofen and gabapentin intervals reach close to no effect, and the review's Results text calls the gabapentin heavy-drinking result not significant although its interval does not include 1 (reporting issue on sc_mcpheeters_2023); the disulfiram null rests on 3 trials; deaths are too few to judge.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the 2023 review; with few trials per medicine it cannot be judged.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias and imprecision, giving low for the claim as a whole; the review's own grades (moderate for topiramate's drinking outcomes, low for the others) are reported, not adopted. The claim gathers several medicines with different directions (topiramate, baclofen and gabapentin linked to less drinking; disulfiram to no clear difference; the injection to no clear difference in return to drinking but to fewer heavy-drinking days), so it is worded as an association rather than a single effect. Overlap: the 2023 review updates the 2014 one, so the two are counted once. Status replicated: each finding rests on more than one trial in the same direction. Medicines for which the review reported nothing (ondansetron, varenicline, prazosin) are not claimed; no doses are given.

statement: In adults with alcohol dependence at 11 US academic centres who had stopped drinking 4 to 21 days earlier (COMBINE, 1,383 people randomized, 2001 to 2004; Anton et al., 2006; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, with medicines and placebos donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals, a maker of acamprosate, and several authors reporting fees or grants from drug companies), adding up to 20 sessions of a specialist talking therapy (combined behavioural intervention) to medicine and nine medical-support visits did not detectably improve drinking during 16 weeks of treatment, while with placebo pills the therapy was linked to more days without alcohol. With naltrexone, the combination was no better than either alone: abstinent days were 77.1 in 100 with naltrexone and the therapy, 80.6 with naltrexone alone, 79.2 with the therapy and placebo naltrexone and 75.1 with placebo naltrexone alone (each group pooled over acamprosate or its placebo; naltrexone × therapy interaction P = 0.009), and only naltrexone alone differed clearly from placebo naltrexone alone (Cohen d 0.22, 97.5% CI 0.03 to 0.40; therapy with placebo 0.17, −0.02 to 0.35; both 0.07, −0.11 to 0.25). Averaged over all the pill groups, abstinent days were 78.2 against 77.8 in 100 (d 0.01, −0.12 to 0.14), an interval that excludes more than a small gain, and the chance of a first heavy-drinking day was not clearly lower (hazard ratio 0.81, 0.60 to 1.10, the paper's main-effect estimate, which by its interval may compare only two single groups), an interval that does not rule out a sizeable benefit; the authors say these averages must be read with caution because of the interaction. Among people given only placebo pills and medical support, those who also had the therapy had more abstinent days (79.8 against 73.8 in 100; P = 0.04 in a corrected post hoc comparison), and the authors read the results as the therapy helping when naltrexone was not given. More people had a good overall outcome at the end of treatment with naltrexone (74 in 100), the therapy (71) or both (74) than with placebo pills and medical support alone (58), a secondary outcome with more missing data than the main ones. People given the therapy without pills or medical management had fewer abstinent days (66.6 in 100) than either group on placebo pills and medical support. In the year after treatment the pattern changed: the combination no longer lagged (interaction P = 0.27; abstinent days 61.4 in 100 with placebo naltrexone alone, 66.2 with naltrexone, 66.6 with the therapy and 67.3 with both), and none of the differences was clear (the therapy averaged over the pill groups 66.9 against 63.8, P = 0.08). The trial had low power for combinations (0.40 to 0.50), the therapy could not be hidden from participants, drinking was self-reported to staff who knew who had the therapy, and people needing psychiatric medicines or with other recent drug use disorders (except nicotine or cannabis) were left out. In most other trials of medicines both groups received some psychosocial treatment, so those trials show what medicines add to it (Jonas et al., 2014). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In one large US trial, adults with alcohol dependence who took naltrexone and had nine short check-ins with a health worker did as well as those who also had up to 20 sessions of specialist talking therapy: combining the two added nothing. For people on dummy pills, adding the therapy was linked to more days without alcohol in one comparison. On an overall measure of doing well, naltrexone, the therapy or both were each better than dummy pills alone. People who had the therapy without pills or the medicine check-ins had fewer days without alcohol. In the year after treatment, no difference between the groups was clear. The trial was not built to test combinations, and drinking was reported by the people themselves.
population: 1,383 adults with DSM-IV alcohol dependence, treatment-seeking volunteers recruited by advertisement and referral at 11 US academic sites, 4 to 21 days abstinent at entry, without other substance use disorders (except nicotine or cannabis) or psychiatric disorders requiring medication
exposure: A combined behavioural intervention (up to twenty 50-minute sessions with a specialist) added to medical management (nine visits with a health care professional) and naltrexone, acamprosate, both or placebo pills
comparator: The same pills and medical management without the therapy; for the no-pill group, placebo pills with medical management, with or without the therapy
outcome: Percent days abstinent and time to the first heavy drinking day during 16 weeks of treatment (coprimary); a composite good clinical outcome; the same measures in the year after treatment
magnitude: Anton et al. 2006 (COMBINE), during treatment: CBI main effect on percent days abstinent 78.2 against 77.8 (P=.82), Cohen d 0.01 (97.5% CI −0.12 to 0.14); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10); naltrexone × CBI cells (pooled over acamprosate): placebo, no CBI 75.1; naltrexone, no CBI 80.6; CBI with placebo 79.2; naltrexone with CBI 77.1 (interaction P=.009); against placebo without CBI, d 0.22 (0.03 to 0.40), 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35) and 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25); good clinical outcome 58% (placebo, medical management), 74% (naltrexone), 71% (CBI with placebo), 74% (naltrexone with CBI), NNTs as printed 6, 7 and 7; CBI without pills or medical management 66.6 against 73.8 (placebo, medical management) and 79.8 (placebo, medical management and CBI); 79.8 against 73.8, P=.04, corrected post hoc. Year after treatment: 61.4, 66.2, 66.6 and 67.3 (interaction P=.27); CBI main effect 66.9 against 63.8 (P=.08). Power for interactions 0.40 to 0.50.

statement: In women in the general population who were pregnant or had recently given birth, any alcohol use during pregnancy, as reported in studies published from 1984 to mid-2014 (328 studies with data from 50 countries; studies of special populations, such as Indigenous women, adolescents and women with an alcohol use disorder, left out, although the review notes that drinking in pregnancy can be much higher in some such groups), was estimated in one systematic review with meta-analysis and modelling (Popova et al., 2017; funded by the authors' institute, with no external funding sought; no competing interests declared) at 9.8% worldwide (95% CI 8.9% to 11.1%), about 10 in 100 pregnant women, in estimates labelled 2012 and weighted by live births. By WHO region it was 10.0% (8.5% to 11.8%) in the African region, 11.2% (9.4% to 12.6%) in the Americas, 0.2% (0.1% to 0.9%) in the Eastern Mediterranean, 25.2% (21.6% to 29.6%) in the European region, about 25 in 100, 1.8% (0.9% to 5.1%) in South-East Asia and 8.6% (4.5% to 11.6%) in the Western Pacific; country estimates ran from 0% (five countries, all by prediction) to 60.4% (42.8% to 76.8%), and the five highest were all in the European region. Most of these figures are model estimates, not measurements: studies were pooled for 29 countries, and the other 158, including 21 of the 50 countries with data (editors' arithmetic), were given a value predicted from national income, women's average alcohol consumption and WHO region. The data are self-reports, which the authors say may undercount drinking; the amount and frequency of drinking, and so binge drinking, were not analysed because the studies reported them inconsistently or not at all, timing in pregnancy was not analysed either, and no drink size is defined; and studies published over three decades are pooled into one set of figures labelled 2012 (editors' observation). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: One large review estimated that about 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide drank some alcohol during pregnancy, from under 1 in 100 in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean region to about 25 in 100 in the European region. Only 29 countries had enough studies to pool; the figures for the other 158 countries came from a model. Women reported their own drinking, so it may be undercounted, and the review did not look at how much or when women drank. Groups who may drink more, such as adolescents or women with an alcohol use disorder, were left out, and the studies span 30 years.
population: Women in the general population of each country who were pregnant or had recently given birth, in studies published from January 1984 to June 2014 (328 studies, 50 countries in all six WHO regions); studies of special populations (for example Indigenous women, adolescents, women of low socioeconomic status, women with HIV or with an alcohol use disorder) and studies that left out women who did not drink were excluded; estimates for 187 WHO member states
exposure: Any alcohol use at any time in pregnancy, as reported by the women (mostly questionnaires or interviews); amount, frequency, binge drinking and timing not analysed; no drink size defined
comparator: None (a prevalence: the share of pregnant women who drank)
outcome: Prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy (%), by country, WHO region and worldwide, weighted by live births and labelled 2012
magnitude: Popova et al. 2017, Table (any alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population, 2012, weighted by live births; 95% CI by Monte Carlo simulation): worldwide 9.8% (8.9–11.1); WHO African region 10.0% (8.5–11.8); Americas 11.2% (9.4–12.6); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1–0.9); European 25.2% (21.6–29.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9–5.1); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5–11.6). The five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 46.6% (42.4–50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9–61.2), Ireland 60.4% (42.8–76.8), Russia 36.5% (18.7–56.4), UK 41.3% (lower limit 32.9; upper limit misprinted); 0% (predicted) in Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Pooled by random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries; predicted by fractional response regression for 158. As counts: about 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide and about 25 in 100 in the European region (editors' rounding).

The companion FASD review (Lange et al., 2017) builds on these drinking estimates and is not independent evidence for them. The paper's 2017 correction concerns only its two maps, from which no figure here is taken.

statement: In children and youth in the general population (special populations, such as children in care, left out of the estimates), fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), the umbrella term for the effects of alcohol before birth, which includes fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), partial FAS and alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder, was estimated in one systematic review with meta-analysis and modelling (Lange et al., 2017; 24 studies, 1,416 children and youth with FASD aged 0 to 16, from 8 countries; no funding statement; no conflicts declared) at 7.7 per 1,000 worldwide (95% CI 4.9 to 11.7), about 8 in 1,000, and FAS alone, in a companion review by the same team (Popova et al., 2017; 62 studies from 19 countries; funded by the authors' institute; no competing interests declared), at 14.6 per 10,000 people (9.4 to 23.3), about 1.5 in 1,000 (editors' conversion). By WHO region, FASD per 1,000 and FAS per 10,000 were 7.8 and 14.8 in the African region, 8.8 and 16.6 in the Americas, 0.1 and 0.2 in the Eastern Mediterranean, 19.8 and 37.4 in the European region, 1.4 and 2.7 in South-East Asia, and 6.7 and 12.7 in the Western Pacific. These world and regional figures are mostly calculated, not counted: FASD was pooled from studies for 6 countries and FAS for 7, and for every other country (181 and 180 of 187) the reviews divided the estimated share of women who drank during pregnancy, itself mostly predicted (see the answer on drinking in pregnancy), by a fixed ratio from a few countries, 13 women who drank per child with FASD and 67 per child with FAS, so the world figures are close to the world drinking figure of 9.8% divided by 13 and by 67 (editors' arithmetic). No FASD or FAS study came from the Eastern Mediterranean or South-East Asia regions, so the two lowest regional figures are wholly calculated. These ratios are averages across countries, not the chance for any one pregnancy, and neither review could examine the amount, pattern or timing of drinking. In the 24 FASD studies, figures ranged from 0.1 per 1,000 in a national Australian study and 0.4 to 5.6 per 1,000 in three French clinic studies of newborns to 63.9 to 207.5 per 1,000 in six studies of school-age children in South Africa's Northern and Western Cape in which researchers sought out and examined children; pooled national estimates were 53.3 per 1,000 for Croatia, 45.0 for Italy and 111.1 for South Africa. In nine select studies of special populations (adopted children or children in care, including one orphanage, a correctional population, Indigenous populations, a low-income rural population, people in psychiatric care), FASD figures ran from 40.0 to 521.1 per 1,000. The authors say the diagnostic systems used differ and lack reliability, that studies were often done where many cases were expected, and that self-reported drinking may be undercounted. The two reviews' ratios imply about 5 children with FASD for each child with FAS (67 / 13, editors' arithmetic), while the FAS review cites a ratio of about 9 or 10. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: FASD is the name for the range of effects of alcohol on a child before birth; FAS is one of the diagnoses within it. Two reviews by one team estimated that about 8 in 1,000 children and youth worldwide have FASD, and about 1.5 in 1,000 people have FAS; for FASD, from about 0.1 in 1,000 in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean region to about 20 in 1,000 in the European region. But FASD had been counted in only 8 countries, none of them in the regions with the lowest figures. For most of the world, the team took the estimated share of women who drank in pregnancy and divided it by one fixed number from a few countries; that number is an average, not the chance for any one pregnancy. Where researchers did count, figures ranged from under 1 to about 208 in 1,000 children, depending on the place and the method, and the ways of diagnosing FASD differ.
population: Children and youth (aged 0 to 16.4 years) in the general population: for FASD, 24 studies from 8 countries (Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, Norway, South Africa, USA) published November 1973 to June 2015, using active case ascertainment or clinic-based methods with a stated diagnostic guideline or case definition; for FAS, 62 general-population studies from 19 countries, the primary analysis using active case ascertainment or clinic-based studies with a stated guideline or case definition; estimates for 187 WHO member states, most of them predicted; select studies of special populations reported separately (FASD)
exposure: Not studied directly; for predictions, each country's prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy (self-reported, mostly itself predicted; Popova et al., 2017)
comparator: None (a prevalence); special populations set against the global FASD estimate as multiples
outcome: Prevalence of FASD per 1,000 children and youth and of FAS per 10,000 people in the general population, by country, WHO region and worldwide, weighted by live births and labelled 2012
magnitude: Lange et al. 2017 (FASD per 1,000 children and youth, Table 2; 95% CI by Monte Carlo simulation): worldwide 7.7 (4.9–11.7); WHO African region 7.8 (5.4–10.7); Americas 8.8 (6.4–13.2); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1–0.5); European 19.8 (14.1–28.0); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6–5.3); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5–11.7). Five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 36.6 (23.7–53.2; predicted), Croatia 53.3 (30.9–81.2; meta-analysis), Ireland 47.5 (28.0–73.6; predicted), Italy 45.0 (35.1–56.1; meta-analysis), South Africa 111.1 (71.1–158.4; meta-analysis); 76 of 187 countries above 10 per 1,000 (1%), almost all by prediction. Study level (Table 1, per 1,000): Australia 0.1 (national; 92 cases in 1,533,333) and 1.7; Canada 5.3; Croatia 40.8 and 66.8; France 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 in newborns and 66.0 on Réunion Island (75 cases in 1,320, which is 56.8, editors' arithmetic); Italy 40.5 and 47.1; Norway 1.1; South Africa 63.9 to 207.5; USA 5.1 to 33.5. Ratio: 1 FASD case per 13 women who drank in pregnancy, which the authors turn into about 630,000 children born with FASD each year. Special populations (Figure 2 legend, per 1,000): 40.0 to 521.1 in nine select studies (including a Brazilian orphanage, 170.2), 5.2 to 67.7 times the global estimate. Popova et al. 2017 (FAS per 10,000 people, Table): worldwide 14.6 (9.4–23.3); African 14.8 (8.9–21.5); Americas 16.6 (11.0–24.0); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2–0.9); European 37.4 (24.7–54.2); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3–8.1); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7–19.4). Five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 69.1 (42.1–103.5; predicted), Croatia 115.2 (34.8–236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4–142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1–134.6), South Africa 585.3 (430.7–761.7). Ratio: 1 FAS case per 67 women who drank in pregnancy (from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA), which the authors turn into about 119,000 children born with FAS each year by applying the prevalence per 10,000 people to 81,536,534 live births. The FAS review cites an earlier estimate (Abel, 1995; not read) of 4.3% FAS among children born to women who drank heavily in pregnancy (on average two or more drinks a day, or five to six at a time; no drink size in grams). Editors' arithmetic: 14.6 per 10,000 is 1.5 per 1,000; 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1,000 and 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000; 67 / 13 = 5.2 FASD cases per FAS case.

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews are AMSTAR 2 critically low on their cards (sc_lange_2017, sc_popova_2017): protocols registered after the searches, no lists of excluded studies, heterogeneity reported only in the supplements, publication bias tested but not discussed (FAS) or dismissed in advance (FASD). In the primary studies, diagnostic systems differ and, the authors say, lack reliability; studies were often done where high prevalence was expected; an inclusion rule was not applied strictly (an Australian study partly based on passive surveillance), and one row of the FASD table is misprinted (Réunion Island). Counted once.

inconsistency.note: Counted FASD runs from 0.1 to 207.5 per 1,000 across studies and from 0.4 to 66.0 within France; age, setting and method explain the spread only in part, and neither article reports heterogeneity statistics. The two reviews' ratios imply about 5 FASD cases per FAS case, against the 9 or 10 the FAS review cites.

indirectness.note: The world and regional figures are not measurements but drinking-in-pregnancy prevalences (self-reported and mostly predicted) divided by one ratio from a few countries and applied to all others (181 and 180 of 187 countries); FAS is counted per 10,000 people in samples of children of various ages, and the yearly birth figures apply it to live births; one set of figures labelled 2012 pools studies from 1974 to 2013; and a study could count FASD or any combination of its diagnoses (sc_lange_2017, inclusion criteria), so some study figures may cover only part of the spectrum.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately: the intervals are wide (FASD 4.9 to 11.7 per 1,000; FAS 9.4 to 23.3 per 10,000) and are reported; they come from Monte Carlo simulation and leave out the error in the ratios themselves, which is counted under indirectness.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: test results are only in the supplements (not read).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (a prevalence): it starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, which is below the floor, so very low. Status single study: each figure rests on one review (FASD on Lange et al., FAS on Popova et al.); the two share their team and their FAS search, and the FASD predictions are built on the FAS review's drinking estimates, so they are not independent, and they estimate different things, so they neither replicate nor contradict each other. FASD and FAS are kept in one claim because a person asks one question, FAS is part of FASD, and only together do the figures show that both world estimates are the same drinking figure divided by two different ratios. The most solid numbers are the pooled national estimates from active case-finding studies (Croatia, Italy, South Africa), which describe those countries' study areas, not the world. The Brazilian orphanage study is counted among the nine special-population studies, but its figure is not quoted on its own: the FAS review gives FAS there as 3191 per 10,000 and the FASD review gives FASD in the same orphanage as 170.2 per 1,000, which cannot both be right.

statement: In eight unrelated children (five girls and three boys; three Native American, three Black and two White; aged 3 to 57 months when their development was tested) evaluated by two physicians of a dysmorphology unit in Seattle and born to mothers who met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism (for more than 2 to 23 years, mean 9.4; delirium tremens in 5 of the 6 with a record, two of them in hospital with it during the pregnancy) and who drank heavily throughout pregnancy (no amounts recorded; none known to be dependent on another drug), a report that its authors call apparently the first to link a mother's alcoholism with abnormal development of the child's body (Jones et al., 1973; funded by US federal maternal and child health and National Institutes of Health grants and the National Foundation–March of Dimes; no conflict statement) describes a shared pattern: growth deficiency starting before birth in all eight (mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation, against a mean of 38 weeks; birth weights 1,550 to 2,500 g) with no catch-up later, even with adequate food during hospital stays for six of them or in foster care for three (after age 1, growth in length 65% and weight gain 38% of normal); short palpebral fissures (eye openings) in all eight; developmental delay in all eight (IQ or developmental index 57 to 83 in six and below 50 in one; none in the normal range, as the authors judged it); a small head in seven; an underdeveloped upper jaw in seven; altered palm creases in six; joint anomalies in five; heart anomalies in five (three of them murmurs that went away, taken to be septal defects that had closed); and folds of skin at the inner corner of the eye in four. The paper, published on 9 June 1973, does not use the name fetal alcohol syndrome and refers to the pattern only as a syndrome; its introduction credits a 1972 paper by one of its authors with having already noted growth deficiency and developmental delay in such children, and the two prevalence reviews read for this page date the first description of FAS to November 1973, one of them citing a later 1973 paper by two of the same authors with the name in its title, which was not read. This is a description of eight selected children, not a measure of how often the pattern follows heavy drinking in pregnancy or of what causes it: four children were recognised first, two more were found because they had the same features and two because their mothers had alcoholism, possibly milder cases were left out on purpose, there was no comparison group and no count of children of mothers with alcoholism who were unaffected, the examiners knew the mothers' histories, the amount of drinking was not recorded and its timing only as drinking throughout pregnancy, smoking and other drug use were not reported, nutrition was only partly recorded (four of the six mothers with data lost weight during the pregnancy), and poverty could not be separated out (all the families were on welfare); the authors nonetheless concluded that their data establish that maternal alcoholism can cause serious abnormal development before birth. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In 1973, a team in Seattle described eight young children, five girls and three boys, born to mothers who had had alcoholism for years and drank heavily all through pregnancy. All eight were small before and after birth and did not catch up, had short eye openings and were behind in development; seven had small heads, and many had a small upper jaw, unusual palm creases, joint problems or heart problems. The paper did not yet use the name fetal alcohol syndrome. It describes selected children: some were chosen because they had these signs, milder cases were left out, there was no comparison group, and the amount of drinking was not recorded. Four of the six mothers with a record lost weight during pregnancy, and the study could not separate nutrition from alcohol. So it cannot show how often these signs follow heavy drinking in pregnancy, or what caused them.
population: Eight unrelated children (five girls, three boys; three Native American, three Black, two White) evaluated at the Dysmorphology Unit, Department of Pediatrics, University of Washington, Seattle, aged 3 to 57 months at developmental testing; four recognised first as sharing a pattern, two ascertained because they had its features and two because their mothers had chronic alcoholism
exposure: Born to mothers who met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism (2+ to 23 years, mean 9.4) and drank excessively throughout pregnancy, as the paper puts it; no amounts, beverages or timing recorded
comparator: None (no comparison group); measurements set against published norms for growth, head size, eye-opening length and development
outcome: Physical features (growth before and after birth, head size, eye openings, face, joints, palm creases, heart) and development (mental, motor and social), as present or absent in each child and as test scores
magnitude: Jones et al. 1973 (descriptive counts; no comparison group, no statistical tests). Table II, features present out of 8: developmental delay 8, microcephaly 7, prenatal growth deficiency 8, postnatal growth deficiency 8, short palpebral fissures 8, maxillary hypoplasia with relative prognathism 7, epicanthal folds 4, joint anomalies 5, altered palmar crease pattern 6, cardiac anomaly 5 (three presumed ventricular septal defects that closed). Table I: maternal alcoholism 7, 3, 4, 11, 2+, 10, 23 and 15 years (mean 9.4); delirium tremens 5 of 6 with data; maternal age at the birth 22 to 40 (mean 31.7); gestational age 34 to 44 weeks (mean 38); birth weight 1,550 to 2,500 g (mean 2,034); birth length 38 to 47 cm (mean 43.6); breech presentation 3 of 8. Growth: mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation; after 1 year of age, linear growth 65% and weight gain 38% of normal; mean daily weight gain 9 g against 26.6 g in upper-middle-class Seattle children and 24.4 g in high-risk children in a local programme; head circumference below the 3rd percentile at birth in 7 of 8 and at 1 year in 5 of 6 with data. Table III (age at testing 3 to 57 months): IQ or mental development index 59, 83, 75, 57, 79, 70 and below 50 (one child not scored); fine motor dysfunction in 5 of 6 tested; repetitive self-stimulating behaviour in 5.

evidence.extracted: All eight had prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency: with a mean gestational age of 38 weeks, mean birth length and weight were at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation. statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected people took part), the 27,616 adults who had ever drunk were asked how old they were when they first started drinking, not counting tastes or sips: lifetime DSM-IV alcohol-dependence criteria were met by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled starting at 14 or younger, 16.6% of those who started at 18 and 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older (with a rise to 14.7% and 13.6% at 23 and 24), and lifetime abuse without dependence by up to 13.8% (a first drink at 14) against 2.5% (25 or older). After adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking, the odds of lifetime dependence were 14% lower, and of abuse 8% lower, for each later year of the first drink, with no confidence intervals or unadjusted estimates given. The age of the first drink was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses, often decades later; conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, family environment and other drug use were not taken into account in this analysis, which does not establish whether each was measured in the survey; two of the adjustments (current or former drinking, and the duration of drinking up to the last drink) may themselves follow from the disorder; and people who had died, were in institutions or were homeless were not sampled. The authors call the age of the first drink a powerful predictor and ages 16 and younger a particularly vulnerable period, but their closing paragraph says that the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors may explain the link and that a prospective study is needed to tell (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In general-population cohorts that recorded the age of the first drink during adolescence, an earlier first drink went with more adult drinking or alcohol problems in some analyses and not in others, and the association often shrank when other risk factors were taken into account. A systematic review found only four such cohorts up to January 2013 (two in the USA and two in Norway; 447 to 1,311 people each; five reports; no meta-analysis; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card): in an Oslo school cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21, with control only for parents' and peers' influence; in a US community cohort, a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, depending on where the first drink happened, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) but not after adjustment for further risk factors, while feeling drunk at the first drink remained a predictor; in the Young in Norway cohort, drinking by 13 to 14, compared with a later first drink, went with frequent intoxication (odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9) and with an AUDIT score of 8 or more, a screen for risky drinking (1.6, 1.3 to 2.1), at 26 to 27, adjusted for gender, both falling to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) when conduct problems in adolescence were also taken into account; in a Seattle cohort of people who started drinking before 21, the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with alcohol dependence at any follow-up, but, compared with a first drink at 11 to 14, a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the interviews held every 3 years from 21 to 33 (odds ratio 1.68) and, in a later report, with more chronic dependence, essentially unchanged across four adjusted models. The review's abstract says that rigorous adjustment markedly weakens or removes such associations, which its own Seattle summary contradicts; the authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems, and found that feeling drunk at the first drink and the start of regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In a Minnesota cohort of twins born 1977 to 1984 (1,512 twins at about age 11; drinking reported at the assessment planned for age 14, held at a mean age of 14.8; outcomes at about 25), twins who had drunk without their parents' permission by that assessment already differed beforehand from twins who had not, notably in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; after weighting for 29 characteristics of the twins and their families measured at about 11, early drinking was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score (standardized coefficient 0.57, SE 0.06), and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking the association was a little over a third as large but remained (0.21, SE 0.09, in all pairs; 0.22, SE 0.10, in identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family; the estimates for identical and fraternal pairs did not differ significantly), whereas within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14) (Irons et al., 2015). Twin comparisons remove what co-twins share, not differences between them such as their own early use of tobacco or other drugs. The same survey's analysis for other drugs is in the answer on starting to use drugs young (Grant & Dawson, 1998). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does drinking young lead to alcohol problems later? This is not known. In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who remembered starting to drink at 14 or younger had had alcohol dependence at some time, against 8 in 100 of those who started at 25 or older; but they were remembering back many years, and the survey could not tell whether early drinking itself, or something that leads to both, explains the link. In the few studies that followed young people over time, in the US and Norway, drinking early went with more drinking problems as an adult in some studies, but in others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems in adolescence, were taken into account. Feeling drunk at the first drink and starting to drink regularly went with later problems more strongly than the age of the first drink. In US twins, the twin who had drunk without their parents' permission by about age 15 drank more as an adult than the twin who had not, even in identical twins, though the difference was smaller than when all the young people in the study were compared; in identical twins, early drinking was not clearly linked to later symptoms of an alcohol disorder. Twin studies cannot rule out other differences between twins, such as smoking or other drug use. See the contested question.
population: US adults who had ever drunk alcohol, in a 1992 national household survey (27,616), recalling their first drink; and young people in general-population cohorts followed from adolescence into adulthood: four cohorts in the USA and Norway in a systematic review (447 to 1,311 people each) and Minnesota twins born 1977–1984 (1,512 at about age 11)
exposure: An earlier first drink: in the survey, the recalled age at which drinking started, not counting tastes or sips; in the cohorts, a first drink (more than a few sips; definitions differed, from before 11 to by 13–14) recorded in adolescence; in the twin study, drinking without parental permission, or being intoxicated, by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8)
comparator: People who started drinking later (in the survey, by each later year of age; in the Rutgers cohort, a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering; in the Seattle cohort, a first drink at 11 to 14); in the twin study, twins who had not, including their own co-twin
outcome: Lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence and abuse reported at the survey interview, at 18 or older; adult drinking, alcohol problems and alcohol dependence in the cohorts and twins (consumption indices, problem scales, AUDIT, DSM-IV symptom counts or diagnoses, at 18 to about 33)
magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Grant & Dawson (1997), NLAES 1992, 27,616 people who had ever drunk, weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV alcohol dependence by recalled age at first drink (SE): 12 or younger 40.6% (2.1), 13 47.3% (2.7), 14 40.8% (1.9), 15 38.7%, 16 30.6%, 17 24.5%, 18 16.6%, 19 16.5%, 20 11.4%, 21 10.0%, 22 9.5%, 23 14.7%, 24 13.6%, 25 or older 7.9% (0.6); lifetime abuse without dependence 8.3% to 13.8% for a first drink at 16 or younger and 2.5% at 25 or older; adjusted odds 14% lower for dependence and 8% lower for abuse per later year of the first drink (odds ratios about 0.86 and 0.92, editors' conversion on the study card), no intervals, p values or unadjusted estimates. Maimaris & McCambridge (2014), four cohorts, no pooling: Oslo (n = 522) structural coefficients −3.465 for debut age on consumption and −13.828 on a problem index (p < 0.0001), with parental and peer control only; Rutgers (n = 447, people with data at every wave) first drink before 11, OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10–5.20) at a family gathering and 5.75 (1.53–21.54) elsewhere, both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 31, not significant in the fully adjusted model (coefficient −0.0631), feeling drunk at the first drink 0.3848 (p < 0.0001); Seattle (n = 808 who started drinking before 21), against a first drink at 11–14, for a first drink before 11, at 15–17 and at 18–20: misuse at any follow-up ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64, dependence at any follow-up 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 (all p > 0.05); first drink before 11 and the number of interviews (every 3 years from 21 to 33) with a past-year dependence diagnosis OR 1.68 (p < 0.05; no intervals), later report (n = 706) chronicity β 0.44 unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models; Young in Norway (n = 1,311), drinking by 13–14 against later, adjusted for gender: frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2–1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more 1.6 (1.3–2.1); both 1.2 (0.9–1.6) with conduct problems added. Irons et al. (2015), drinking without parental permission by the age-14 assessment (mean age 14.8), standardized β (SE): adult alcohol-use index, weighted 0.57 (0.06), within all discordant pairs 0.21 (0.09), identical pairs 0.22 (0.10), fraternal pairs 0.20 (0.14) (within-pair estimates 0.37 and 0.39 of the weighted one, editors' calculation; zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms, weighted 0.36, all pairs 0.24 (0.11), identical 0.17 (0.14), fraternal 0.34 (0.16); intoxication by the age-14 assessment and alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms within all pairs 0.29 (0.15). The twin study's printed p-values are not used (card reporting issue).

risk_of_bias.note: The 1992 survey recalled the age of the first drink in the same interview as the diagnoses, measured none of the main shared causes except family history of alcoholism, and adjusted for two variables that may follow from the disorder (card sc_grant_1997: ROBINS-E, high); the cohorts adjusted for different, incomplete sets of confounders (only one for family history; none for genetic liability), some possibly on the causal path; confidence in the review is critically low (card sc_maimaris_2014: AMSTAR 2, no protocol, no list of excluded studies, single-reviewer screening); in the twin study, confounders not shared by co-twins, such as their own early tobacco or drug use, were not taken into account in this analysis, and 12% were not seen at about 25 (card sc_irons_2015: ROBINS-E, some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The association survived adjustment in some analyses (the 1992 survey, with limited adjustment; Seattle chronicity; within twin pairs for adult drinking) and not in others (Rutgers, Young in Norway, Seattle misuse and any dependence; identical pairs for abuse or dependence symptoms).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one US national survey (1992), four cohorts in the USA and Norway and one Minnesota twin cohort, with outcomes from drinking scores to symptom counts and chronic dependence, all stated.

imprecision.note: The survey is large but gives its per-year estimates without intervals; cohorts of 447 to 1,311 people with small exposure groups (a first drink before 11); no intervals for the Seattle estimates; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs (editors' estimate on the study card), with standard errors close to the estimates.

publication_bias.note: The review judges publication bias a profound threat but could not test it; not rated down separately, since the certainty is already at its floor.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Counted once: the two Seattle reports share one cohort (four cohorts, not five studies). The twin study's printed p-values are not valid (card reporting issue), so significance is judged from coefficients and standard errors. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the association of an earlier first drink with more adult drinking in several cohorts is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. Grant & Dawson (1997), the cross-sectional survey usually cited as the starting point, read in full, adds a steep association between a recalled early first drink and lifetime dependence (40.6% to 47.3% for a first drink at 14 or younger against 7.9% at 25 or older; 14% lower adjusted odds per later year); it describes what US adults reported in 1992 but cannot separate cause from shared liability, as its authors say, so the certainty about cause does not change. The same survey's analysis for other drugs (Grant & Dawson, 1998) is in the answer on starting drugs young. Status contested: credible analyses point both ways and the review's own authors say the answer is not known, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does drinking at a young age cause alcohol problems in adulthood, or do the same family, genetic and personal factors lead both to early drinking and to later problems?
debate.evidence_yes: In a 1992 US national survey of 27,616 adults who had ever drunk, lifetime alcohol dependence was reported by 40.6% to 47.3% of those who recalled a first drink at 14 or younger against 7.9% of those who started at 25 or older, and the odds of dependence were 14% lower for each later year of starting after adjustment for sex, race, age group, family history of alcoholism, duration of drinking and current or former drinking (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In the Seattle cohort, a first drink before 11 went with more chronic alcohol dependence to age 33, and the association was essentially unchanged after adding peer, school, behavioural and substance-use factors in four models (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted), with none of the three alternative explanations tested supported; in the Oslo cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21 (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In Minnesota twins, drinking without parental permission by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8), recorded at that assessment, was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score after weighting for 29 childhood characteristics (0.57) and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking (0.21), including identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family (0.22, SE 0.10); across all discordant pairs it was also associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.24, SE 0.11). The authors read the within-pair results as supporting an effect of early drinking, while noting that confounders not shared by co-twins could explain them (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.evidence_no: In two of the four general-population cohorts the association did not survive adjustment: in the Rutgers cohort a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) only before adjustment for further risk factors, and in the Young in Norway cohort drinking by 13 to 14 went with frequent intoxication and risky drinking at 26 to 27 (1.5 and 1.6, adjusted for gender) only until adolescent conduct problems were taken into account (both 1.2, 0.9 to 1.6); in the Seattle cohort the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with dependence at any follow-up; the Oslo estimate controlled only for parents' and peers' influence; feeling drunk at the first drink and starting regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink; and the review's authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). The authors of the 1992 survey themselves say that other factors associated with an early start more likely explain its link with later disorders, and call for a prospective study to tell whether an early start is a risk factor that can be changed or a marker (Grant & Dawson, 1997). In the twin study, twins who drank by the assessment planned for age 14 already differed beforehand in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; for the adult alcohol-use score the within-pair association was a little over a third of the weighted one (0.21 against 0.57, ratio 0.37; editors' calculation); and within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14), nor was intoxication by that assessment across all pairs (0.29, SE 0.15) (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.neither_can_show: No randomized evidence exists, since the age of a first drink cannot be assigned at random. A survey that asks adults to recall their first drink in the same interview as their diagnoses can show how strong the association is in the population surveyed, but not what causes it, and it misses people who died, were in institutions or were homeless. The cohorts recorded the first drink in adolescence, which avoids recalling it decades later, but they can adjust only for what they measured: only one adjusted for family history of alcohol problems, none controlled for genetic liability, and adjusting for peers or behaviour that early drinking may itself change can remove part of a real effect. In two of the four cohorts the first drink of late starters was not recorded in adolescence or 3 years before the outcome. Co-twin comparisons remove everything twins share (all genes in identical pairs, half in fraternal pairs, and the family they grew up in) but not what differs between them, such as their own early smoking, other drug use or friends, and random error in reporting early drinking shrinks within-pair estimates on its own; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs, so a non-significant result there is not evidence of no effect. Both twin exposures were yes-or-no, so nothing is known about how much the young people drank.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). An earlier first drink goes with much more lifetime alcohol dependence in a large US survey that relied on recall (Grant & Dawson, 1997), and with more adult drinking in several cohorts (Irons et al., 2015; Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014), and part of that link may reflect differences that were there before the first drink, such as behaviour problems and family drinking (Irons et al., 2015; Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014): in two of four cohorts the link was no longer statistically clear after adjustment (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014), and in twins it was a little over a third as large within pairs as in the comparison weighted for childhood characteristics (Irons et al., 2015). Within identical twins, early drinking still went with more adult drinking, which leaves room for an effect of early drinking itself, but it was not clearly linked to symptoms of alcohol use disorder, and the twin design cannot exclude differences between co-twins (Irons et al., 2015). The evidence read here cannot say whether delaying the first drink would reduce adult alcohol problems; in the review, feeling drunk at the first drink and early regular drinking were more strongly linked to adult problems than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014).
debate.what_would_settle_it: Pooled analyses of identical twin pairs who differ in early drinking across several twin registries, large enough to estimate effects on alcohol use disorder precisely, with early drinking recorded repeatedly (age, amount, intoxication) and the twins' own earlier behaviour and substance use measured; harmonized analyses of several large birth or school cohorts with the first drink recorded as it happens and the same confounders; and natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person, such as changes in minimum legal drinking ages.

statement: In 9 healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6) in a Swedish laboratory, each given the same small amount of alcohol (0.30 g per kg of body weight, diluted to 20% in orange juice and drunk within 15 minutes; study conditions) on five occasions at least a week apart in random order (Jones et al., 1997), drinking a few minutes after a breakfast of about 3,000 kJ, compared with drinking after a 10-hour overnight fast, reduced the peak blood alcohol concentration and the area under the blood-alcohol curve over 210 minutes by roughly half: peaks were 16.6, 17.7 and 13.3 mg/dl after breakfasts rich in fat, carbohydrate and protein, against 30.8 mg/dl after fasting (43 to 57 in 100 of the fasting peak; editors' calculation), and the areas 1,767, 1,619 and 1,270 against 3,210 mg/dl·min (40 to 55 in 100); the same dose infused into a vein gave a peak of 54.3 mg/dl. No test of each breakfast against fasting is printed, but by the editors' estimate each difference is several times its standard error. The three breakfasts did not differ significantly, but that comparison had little power (0.22 and 0.25, and the authors call for caution), and the protein-rich breakfast, which also had about 9 to 10 in 100 more energy, gave peaks 20 to 25 in 100 lower than the other two (editors' calculation), so the study cannot show whether the kind of food matters. After the fat- and carbohydrate-rich breakfasts the peak came 30 to 90 minutes after the start of drinking (30 to 60 after the protein-rich one and after fasting), and after food it varied more between men (coefficients of variation 24 to 40 in 100, against 14 after fasting). The authors explain the lower values by slower emptying of the stomach letting the liver break down more alcohol before it reaches the blood, or by part of the alcohol being held by the meal; neither was measured, and their statement that alcohol left the blood 1 to 2 hours sooner after food rests on the curves rather than a quantified meal-versus-fasting elimination estimate. The editors' approximate reading of Figure 1 f gives a fed–fasting gap of less than one hour, with the fasting end partly extrapolated; the larger reported gap also includes intravenous dosing. The study gave one small amount, to young men only, measured no impairment, and did not test larger amounts, women, other meals or longer gaps between eating and drinking. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In a small laboratory study, 9 young men drank the same small amount of alcohol on different days. When they had eaten a breakfast just before, the highest level of alcohol in their blood was about half of what it was when they had eaten nothing since the night before (13 to 18 against 31 mg per 100 ml). The kind of breakfast made no clear difference, but the study was too small to tell. Larger amounts, women, other meals and how drunk people felt were not studied.
population: 9 healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6 years, SD 4.8; mean weight 75.8 kg) in a laboratory in Linköping, Sweden
exposure: Drinking 0.30 g of alcohol per kg (20% v/v in orange juice, finished within 15 minutes) a few minutes after a breakfast of about 2,900 to 3,200 kJ rich in fat, carbohydrate or protein, eaten in 15 minutes (study conditions)
comparator: The same men drinking the same amount after a 10-hour overnight fast; the same dose infused into a vein over 30 minutes
outcome: Venous blood alcohol: peak concentration, time to peak and area under the concentration–time curve from 0 to 210 minutes
magnitude: Jones et al. (1997), n = 9, mean (SD): peak mg/dl, fat-rich 16.6 (4.0), carbohydrate-rich 17.7 (7.1), protein-rich 13.3 (4.0), fasting 30.8 (4.3), intravenous 54.3 (6.4); AUC 0–210 min, mg/dl·min, 1,767 (549), 1,619 (760), 1,270 (406), 3,210 (527), 4,786 (446). Five conditions: F = 98.7 (peak) and 88.9 (AUC), P < 0.001; three meals: F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05, post hoc power 0.22 and 0.25. Time to peak 30–90 min (fat- and carbohydrate-rich), 30–60 min (protein-rich, fasting), 30 min (intravenous). Coefficients of variation: peak 24–40% after meals, 14% fasting; AUC 31–47% and 16%. Editors' calculations: meal peaks 43–57% and AUCs 40–55% of the fasting values; protein-rich peak about 20% and 25% lower than fat- and carbohydrate-rich, AUC about 28% and 22% lower; each meal–fasting difference about 5 to 9 times its approximate standard error (five-condition residual SD, assuming sphericity).

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_jones_1997, RoB 2 some concerns: how the order was randomized and which order each man had are not reported, and the planned meal-against-fasting tests are not printed. Not rated down: the outcome is blood alcohol measured by a validated method, each man was his own comparison, carryover after a week is implausible, and the difference is large beside its variation, so bias is unlikely to explain it.

inconsistency.note: One study; the paper cites earlier fed-against-fasting studies, not read, as pointing the same way.

indirectness.note: Nine young men, one small dose, breakfast eaten just before drinking, blood alcohol only: larger amounts drunk over longer times, women, other meals and gaps, and impairment were not studied.

imprecision.note: Nine men; no meal-against-fasting test or interval printed (the editors' estimate is approximate); the comparison of meals was underpowered.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: A randomized within-person crossover with an objective outcome starts high; rated down for indirectness (nine young men, one small dose, breakfast just before drinking) and imprecision (nine men, no printed meal-against-fasting test): low. 'Reduces' concerns the peak and area of the blood-alcohol curve after a meal compared with fasting, under these conditions; whether the kind of food matters is left open, because that comparison had little power and the meals differed in energy. The mechanism and the faster elimination after food are the authors' explanations, not measurements. Reported as conditions, not advice: no amount, meal or timing is recommended. Status single study: earlier fed-against-fasting studies are cited by the paper and a later study of food and elimination rates (Ramchandani et al., 2001) is on the reading list; none was read.

statement: In laboratory experiments that told people they were drinking alcohol or not, and separately gave them alcohol or not, believing they had drunk alcohol increased drinking: in one experiment it doubled how much men drank in a short taste test, and the three such studies of drinking or wanting to drink pooled by a meta-analysis all pointed the same way, while the alcohol actually drunk did not detectably change drinking. The same meta-analysis found that the alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, physical sensations, mood and coordination; it also found more sexual arousal, on average, in people who believed they had drunk alcohol, but this result varied widely between studies. These were laboratory experiments: the meta-analysis did not report doses, and in the taste-test experiment the task lasted 15 minutes and estimated blood alcohol averaged under 0.1%, so they say little about higher amounts or drinking outside the laboratory. In the taste-test experiment, in Madison, Wisconsin (published 1973), 64 men, 32 with a history of alcohol problems who were still drinking (treatment admissions, repeated drunkenness arrests, or past membership of Alcoholics Anonymous or a rehabilitation programme; the study's 'alcoholic' group) and 32 social drinkers, were randomly assigned within each group to be told that their drinks were vodka and tonic or tonic only, and to be given one or the other; men told vodka drank about twice as much in a 15-minute taste test as men told tonic (about 18.8 against 9.1 fluid ounces, from the table; the text prints 17.77 for the first; d about 1.1, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.7, editors' calculation), whatever was in the glass and in both groups, while receiving vodka made no detectable difference (13.2 against 14.7 ounces when given tonic; difference −1.5 ounces, 95% CI −5.8 to +2.8, editors' calculation: an increase of more than about a third of a standard deviation is unlikely, but a moderate decrease cannot be ruled out, and among the men with alcohol problems alone, −1.2 ounces, 95% CI −7.2 to +4.8, a moderate increase cannot be ruled out either). Drinking, as estimated from sips in each 3-minute block, was mostly highest in the first 3 minutes and then fell, with no sign of drinking getting out of control; blood alcohol at the end, estimated rather than measured, averaged 0.031% to 0.093%; each of the eight groups formed by problem history, instructions and drink held 8 men (implied by the degrees of freedom); the men with alcohol problems were older (mean age 46.75 against 37.19 years); and the authors could not rule out that men told the drinks held vodka drank more in order to taste for it (Marlatt et al., 1973). The 1986 meta-analysis of 36 such experiments published before September 1985 found significant pooled effects of believing one had drunk alcohol on sexual arousal (mean g 0.31, 9 studies, ranging from −0.25 to 1.21, more variation than chance would explain) and on drinking or wanting to drink (0.52, 3 studies, all in the same direction, this experiment included), none on memory-related information processing, mood, physical sensations, motor performance or bodily arousal, and a non-significant effect in the opposite direction on aggression (−0.13); the alcohol itself impaired information processing (0.53, 5 studies) and motor performance (0.64, 3 studies), changed physical sensations (0.64) and improved mood (0.21), and did not detectably change drinking (−0.04) or sexual arousal (−0.02). The sizes from that analysis are rough: about 35% to 45% of effects of unknown size were set to zero, studies were not weighted, no confidence intervals were given, and doses and participants were not extracted; for the 1973 experiment it averaged three measures (amount drunk, number of sips and amount per sip), giving 0.66 where the effect on the amount drunk alone was about 1.1. In 18 of 20 experiments that did not first ask participants which drink they had received, the alcohol itself changed what they believed they had drunk, so the design seldom tests alcohol without the belief; the authors answer that no measure showed significant effects of both alcohol and belief, and conclude from this that the effects of alcohol were not effects of belief (Hull & Bond, 1986). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Does believing you've had alcohol change how you act? In lab studies, partly yes. In one experiment, 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass; real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking and, on average, more sexual arousal, though that varied a lot between studies; the alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, and blood alcohol stayed low.
population: Adults in balanced-placebo laboratory experiments published 1973–1985: 64 men with and without a history of alcohol problems in one taste-test experiment in Madison, Wisconsin (Marlatt et al., 1973); participants of 36 experiments whose characteristics and doses the meta-analysis did not extract (Hull & Bond, 1986)
exposure: Being told the drink contained alcohol (against being told it did not), crossed with actually receiving alcohol (against a drink without alcohol), at doses the meta-analysis did not report (estimated blood alcohol averaging 0.031% to 0.093% in the 1973 experiment; study conditions)
comparator: Participants told they were not drinking alcohol; participants given a drink without alcohol
outcome: Amount drunk in a 15-minute taste test; in the meta-analysis, sexual arousal, drinking or desire to drink, aggression, mood, memory-related information processing, motor performance, physical sensations and bodily arousal
magnitude: Marlatt et al. (1973), fluid ounces drunk in 15 minutes: told vodka about 18.8 (Table 1; 17.77 in the text) vs told tonic 9.12, F = 20.59, df 1/56, p < .01, d about 1.13 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.66 by the exact noncentral-t method, 0.63 to 1.64 treating the SD as known; editors' calculations); given vodka 13.19 vs given tonic 14.69, F = .50, difference −1.5 oz (95% CI −5.8 to +2.8; d −0.18, −0.68 to 0.33; editors' calculation), within the men with alcohol problems −1.2 oz (−7.2 to +4.8; editors' calculation); cell means, men with alcohol problems told tonic 10.94 and 10.25, told vodka 23.87 and 22.13; social drinkers 9.31 and 5.94, 14.62 and 14.44; estimated end-of-task blood alcohol .031% to .093%. Hull & Bond (1986), mean g (unweighted; effects of unknown size set to zero; no intervals), expectancy vs alcohol: sexual arousal 0.306 (Z = 2.861; study values −0.25 to 1.21, heterogeneity chi-square(8) = 20.64, p < .01) vs −0.017; drinking or desire to drink 0.523 (Z = 2.870; study values 0.66, 0.52, 0.39) vs −0.040; aggression −0.131 vs 0.255 (p < .10); information processing −0.002 vs 0.5344; physical sensations 0.0450 vs 0.6440; motor performance 0.1230 vs 0.6360; mood 0.061 vs 0.209; bodily arousal 0.046 vs −0.225 (not significant). For Marlatt et al. the meta-analysis averages amount drunk, number of sips and amount per sip (0.66), lower than the effect on the amount drunk alone (about 1.1).
