risk_of_bias.note: The 1973 experiment assigned men at random within each group, but sequence generation and concealment are not reported, the experimenter who mixed the drinks and gave the instructions knew each assignment, and no standard deviations are printed (card sc_marlatt_1973: RoB 2 some concerns); the meta-analysis has critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (undescribed search, effects of unknown size set to zero, unweighted means without intervals, primary studies' randomization not appraised, experimenters blind in only 7 of 36 studies; card sc_hull_1986), and the outcomes other than drinking are seen only through it.

inconsistency.note: The three drinking studies point the same way (0.66, 0.52, 0.39; heterogeneity chi-square(2) = 0.32). The expectancy effect on sexual arousal varied more than chance would explain (chi-square(8) = 20.64; study values −0.25 to 1.21); the statement reports it as a variable average, not as an established effect, so it does not lower the rating of what the claim asserts, but read as an established effect that part alone would rate very low. Expectancy effects on other behaviours differ by type, which the statement reports type by type.

indirectness.note: Blood alcohol estimated at 0.03% to 0.09% in the drinking experiment (the meta-analysis reports no doses), a 15-minute taste test and laboratory measures, in samples from the 1970s and early 1980s; the meta-analysis's outcomes other than drinking are second-hand, and its drinking category mixes desire to drink with amounts drunk and, for the 1973 experiment, averages amount drunk with two sip measures.

imprecision.note: The effect of belief on the amount drunk is precise enough for its direction (d 1.13, 0.60 to 1.66 by the exact method, editors' calculation); the absence of an effect of alcohol on drinking is imprecise and is stated as such, with the direction each interval leaves open; the meta-analysis gives no intervals, so its sizes are called rough.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the meta-analysis (published studies only); with three drinking studies, small-study effects cannot be judged.

grade.reasoning: Randomized factorial experiments start high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. 'Increases' rests on random assignment of the instructions within the experiments and applies to the laboratory conditions stated; whether belief changes drinking at higher doses or outside a laboratory is not claimed. The comparison of men with and without alcohol problems is not randomized (they differed in age and social class) and is not used for any causal statement. Status replicated: the three balanced-placebo studies of drinking or desire to drink, as coded by Hull & Bond (1986), point the same way; the 1973 experiment is one of them and the other two were not read. The meta-analysis's conclusions that alcohol and expectancy rarely interact (7 of 137 tests significant) and that the design is no longer needed are not used: a count of significant tests cannot show that interactions are absent (card interpretation gap). The authors' answer to the confounding of alcohol with belief (no measure with significant effects of both, p. 358) is reported as theirs; like their interaction count, it rests on which tests reached significance. Doses appear only as study conditions.

statement: In 11 white men aged 36 to 64 who had drunk alcohol heavily for many years (a severe and lasting history of excessive drinking, DSM-III-R criteria for alcoholism, the paper's term, and alcohol-related disease at necropsy, most with liver cirrhosis), whose brains were examined after death at Danish hospitals in 1986–1990, long-term heavy drinking compared with no history of heavy drinking (11 men aged 34 to 67 without a history or tissue signs of heavy drinking, matched as groups for age and height) was not associated with a detectable difference in the total number of neurons (nerve cells) in the neocortex, the brain's outer layer, counted by design-based stereology in one hemisphere of each brain: 23.4 billion in the heavy-drinking group and 23.2 billion in the comparison group (coefficient of variation 0.12 in each; p = 0.86), with no difference in the frontal, temporal, parietal or occipital lobe (Jensen & Pakkenberg, 1993). By the editors' calculation from the printed means and coefficients of variation, the difference was +0.2 billion (95% CI −2.3 to +2.7 billion), about −10% to +12% of the comparison group's mean, so these data exclude a loss larger than about a tenth, while the comparison had 80% power only for a difference of about 15%; smaller losses, and losses confined to particular areas or layers, could not be detected. Neurons were not counted in the hippocampus, the subcortical limbic structures or the cerebellum, which was removed with the brainstem before sampling. The 11 men were the only ones among 55 consecutively collected brains of people with chronic heavy drinking who met the criteria, which excluded women, men over 67, and men with a history of Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens or withdrawal seizures, hepatic coma lasting more than 5 days, signs of infarction or other neurological disease, medicines acting on the nervous system, diabetes, disseminated cancer, severe lung disease or severe head injury; nobody had been given thinking tests in life. White-matter volume was 9% lower in the heavy-drinking group but not significantly (459 against 502 cm³, p = 0.21); only white-matter volume divided by brain weight was significantly lower (0.16 against 0.18, called 11%, p = 0.013), which the summary presents as confirming that white matter is lost; the same ratio for the archicortex, a region that includes the hippocampus and that the authors call hard to delimit, was lower (0.011 against 0.014, p = 0.028; called 30%, about 21% from the printed means by the editors' calculation), while its raw volume was not significantly lower (30.7 against 38.6 cm³, p = 0.053); 16 group comparisons were reported without correction for multiple testing (editors' count). The comparison men died mostly of heart attacks and the heavy-drinking group mostly of complications of drinking; the amount and duration of drinking are not reported, nor whether the person counting knew each brain's group. A single comparison after death cannot show change within a person, and the authors' suggestion that preserved nerve-cell bodies might let lost connections recover after prolonged abstinence or treatment was not tested. Funded by three Danish foundations; the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a Danish study, scientists counted the nerve cells in the brain's outer layer (the neocortex) after death in 11 men who had drunk alcohol heavily for years and in 11 men who had not. Both groups had about 23 billion; in these men, the numbers rule out a loss of more than about a tenth (editors' calculation), but not a smaller one. Other areas, such as the hippocampus, were not counted, and women and men who had had an alcohol-related brain illness, the DTs or withdrawal fits were left out. The brain's wiring (white matter) was not clearly smaller; only its share of brain weight was lower. One comparison after death cannot show what drinking did to each man's brain over time.
population: 11 white men aged 36 to 64 (mean 46.8) with a severe and lasting history of excessive drinking, DSM-III-R criteria for alcoholism (the paper's term) and alcohol-related disease at necropsy (most with liver cirrhosis and oesophageal varices), whose brains were examined after death; the only 11 of 55 brains collected consecutively in 1986–1990 from 18 Danish hospitals that met the criteria, which excluded women, men over 67, and men with Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, hepatic coma over 5 days, signs of infarction or other neurological disease, medicines acting on the nervous system, diabetes, disseminated cancer, severe lung disease or severe head injury; none had been tested neuropsychologically in life
exposure: Long-term heavy drinking, from history and pathology at necropsy; amounts, duration and time since the last drink not reported
comparator: 11 white men aged 34 to 67 (mean 46.9; 9 died of a heart attack, 1 violently; where their brains came from is not stated) without a history or tissue signs of heavy drinking, selected with the same exclusions and matched as groups for age and height; their drinking was not quantified

evidence.extracted: The study set out to estimate total neocortical neuron number by stereological counting in people with chronic heavy drinking and to test the popular belief that such drinking costs neocortical neurons; the authors note that earlier counts had been two-dimensional. 55 brains of people with chronic heavy drinking were collected consecutively over 4 years (1986–1990) from 18 Danish hospitals, each with a complete necropsy including histology. Inclusion: a known severe and lasting history of excessive drinking, the DSM-III-R criteria for alcoholism (the paper's term) and pathoanatomical evidence of alcohol-related disease at necropsy; most had liver cirrhosis and oesophageal varices, and ascites, pancreatitis and alcoholic cardiomyopathy were also found.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors report no neocortical neuron loss although the men were severely affected and all but 2 died of the consequences of their drinking. They name two limitations: a total count may overlook small, localised losses in subdivisions of neocortical areas or in particular layers, although the almost identical totals at least exclude any major loss, and cells were not counted in the subcortical limbic structures or the hippocampus; and telling the largest glial cells from the smallest neurons is not a trivial problem (several criteria were used), with doubtful cells (under 3% in both groups) left out. Brain weight did not differ, unlike in earlier studies, which the authors relate to a much smaller sample than the 545 necropsies in which a 2% difference was found; the 26% larger ventricles were not significant, and the biological variation in ventricular volume between individuals together with the small number of brains did not allow this to be clarified.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_jensen_1993 (ROBINS-E, first pass): overall high, from selection: only 11 of 55 consecutively collected brains were used, and the criteria removed women and men with Wernicke-Korsakoff psychosis, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, prolonged hepatic coma or other neurological disease, a selection related both to drinking and to brain damage that would bias towards finding no loss. Also: blinding of the person counting is not reported; causes of death differ (complications of drinking against heart attacks); the amount and duration of drinking, and the comparison men's drinking, are not quantified; nothing is adjusted beyond group matching for age and height.

inconsistency.note: One study; not assessable.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for what was measured (neocortical neuron totals in a selected group of Danish men with long-term heavy drinking who died in hospital) and states what was not counted (the hippocampus, the subcortical limbic structures, the cerebellum) and who was excluded; it is not worded as 'alcohol does not kill brain cells'.

imprecision.note: 11 brains per group. By the editors' calculation the 95% interval runs from a 10% deficit to a 12% excess of neocortical neurons, which excludes a large loss but not a smaller one, and the study had 80% power only for a difference of about 15%; losses confined to areas or layers cannot be detected with a total count.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from one study.

grade.reasoning: An observational comparison of brains after death starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (11 of 55 brains chosen by criteria that removed the men with alcohol-related neurological illness, in the editors' reading the men in whom a loss would be most expected; counting blind to group not reported) and one for imprecision (11 per group; the data exclude only a loss larger than about a tenth): very low, the floor. 'Does not detectably change' is used within the study's detection limit: no difference in neocortical neuron totals was detected, and the claim states the size of loss the data exclude (about 10%) and what could not be detected (smaller or localised losses, other regions). The claim does not say that drinking spares every brain cell: the hippocampus, the subcortical limbic structures and the cerebellum were not counted, women and men with alcohol-related neurological illness were excluded, and one comparison after death cannot show change within a person. The white-matter result is reported as measured, a lower volume-to-brain-weight ratio with a raw volume that did not differ significantly, and the authors' readings (white-matter 'loss', possible recovery after abstinence, dementia not due to neocortical neuron death) are given as theirs. Status single study: no replication of the stereological count is among the sources read. The editors' interval and power calculations, from the printed means and coefficients of variation, are approximate and are for the second reader to recompute.

statement: In 527 UK civil servants of the Whitehall II cohort without alcohol dependence (a CAGE score below 2 at every study phase recorded; 75 lacked CAGE data at one phase or more), 424 men and 103 women (editors' arithmetic from Table 2), aged 43 on average when the cohort began in 1985–88, who reported their weekly drinking at up to six study phases until 2011–12 and had one brain MRI scan in Oxford in 2012–15, drinking more alcohol on average across the phases, counted in UK units of 8 g of alcohol, compared with averaging less than 1 unit a week (37 people) is associated with higher odds of hippocampal atrophy on that single scan, defined as any visual rating above zero on the 4-point Scheltens scale, agreed by three clinicians. On the right side, the study's groups gave 13 of 37 people averaging under 1 unit a week (35 in 100), 67 of 140 at 1 to <7 units (48 in 100), 87 of 165 at 7 to <14 (53 in 100), 63 of 97 at 14 to <21 (65 in 100), 39 of 57 at 21 to <30 (68 in 100) and 24 of 31 at 30 or more (77 in 100), with adjusted odds ratios against the under-1-unit group of 1.5 (95% CI 0.7 to 3.4), 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4), 3.4 (1.4 to 8.1), 3.6 (1.4 to 9.6) and 5.8 (1.8 to 18.6); on the left side only 30 or more units differed (5.7, 1.5 to 21.6); because the rating was common, the crude risk ratio at 14 to <21 units is about 1.85, not 3.4 (editors' calculation) (Topiwala et al., 2017). The odds ratio of 3.4 is given here for 14 to <21 units a week, as in Table 2, the abstract and the Discussion; the Results text attaches it to 7 to <14 units, whose own estimate in Table 2 (2.0, 0.9 to 4.4) did not differ significantly, and 14 to <21 units counts as moderate only for men under the paper's own definitions (moderate: 7 to <14 units a week for women, 7 to <21 for men). More than half of all participants were rated atrophic on the right (293 of 527) and two thirds on the left (351 of 527), including 13 and 19 of the 37 people averaging under 1 unit (editors' arithmetic). Automatically measured hippocampal volume was smaller with more drinking (per 10 units a week, −0.19, 95% CI −0.30 to −0.08, after adjustment, in the paper's squared percentage of intracranial volume), grey-matter density was lower in both hippocampi, and white-matter integrity was lower in the front of the corpus callosum. Of three thinking tests repeated from 1991–93 onwards, only lexical fluency (words beginning with a given letter in one minute) declined faster than in the under-1-unit group, by 0.5%, 0.8% and 0.6% more of the starting score a year at 7 to <14, 14 to <21 and more than 21 units (overall p = 0.006); semantic fluency (words in a category) and recall of a 20-word list did not differ after correction for three tests, and no test given at the time of the scan, among them the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, trail making and a verbal learning test, was related to drinking. People averaging 1 to <7 units did not differ significantly from the under-1-unit group in atrophy ratings or cognitive decline, the only analyses that compared these groups (right side 1.5, 0.7 to 3.4, an interval that excludes neither a modest benefit nor a modest harm). The odds ratios come from tests the authors call post hoc; each brain was scanned once, so 'atrophy' is a rating at one time, not observed shrinkage; drinking was self-reported; the 37 people averaging under 1 unit are not described as lifelong abstainers or as people who had stopped; people above the pre-2016 UK limits were more often smokers and had a higher estimated IQ (more were men, 86% against 79%, but not significantly), and smoking entered the brain models only within a stroke risk score; and the sample is of survivors, mostly educated, middle-class men, with only 14 women averaging 14 units or more and none 30 or more. The authors cite one earlier study, in which drinking was measured once, that reported a protective association of moderate drinking with hippocampal size compared with abstinence, which they say conflicts with their results (not read here). Funded by the UK Medical Research Council and two charitable trusts; the authors declare no other relevant ties. Being observational, the study shows associations only, not that drinking caused these differences. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a UK study of 527 government workers, mostly men, who reported how much alcohol they drank for about 30 years and then had one brain scan around age 70, those who drank more on average more often had a hippocampus, an area involved in memory, rated as shrunken. The rating counted any sign of shrinkage at all and was common: 35 in 100 people who averaged less than 1 UK unit a week got it on the right side, against 65 in 100 of those averaging 14 to under 21 units, the group behind the paper's 'three times the odds'. For people averaging 7 to under 14 units, and 1 to under 7, the study was too small to tell whether the odds differed. Measured hippocampal size was smaller, and the brain's wiring at the front looked less intact, in people who drank more. Of three thinking tests repeated over the years, only one, naming words that start with a given letter, fell slightly faster, and no test at the time of the scan differed. Each brain was scanned once, drinking was self-reported and people who drank more also differed in other ways, so the study shows links, not that alcohol caused them.
population: 527 UK civil servants (424 men, 103 women; editors' arithmetic from Table 2) from the Whitehall II cohort (10,308 recruited at phase 1, 1985–88), mean age 43.0 (SD 5.4) at phase 1 (1985–88) and about 70 at the scan (the age the paper uses for its typical participant), without alcohol dependence by the CAGE questionnaire at every phase recorded (75 lacked CAGE data at one phase or more) and safe for MRI; from a random list of 1380 phase 11 or phase 10 pilot participants sampled across socioeconomic groups, 550 were scanned in Oxford in 2012–15 and 23 excluded (brain abnormality, poor images or missing data); 511 in the diffusion analyses; mostly educated, middle-class men
exposure: Average self-reported weekly alcohol intake across up to six study phases (1985–88 to 2011–12), in UK units of 8 g of alcohol: grouped as 1 to <7, 7 to <14, 14 to <21, 21 to <30 and 30 or more units a week for the atrophy ratings (7 to <14, 14 to <21 and more than 21 for cognitive decline) and used as a continuous measure in the imaging and volume analyses; medians across the phases 11.5 units a week for men (IQR 6.2 to 18.8) and 6.4 for women (2.8 to 11.9)
comparator: People averaging less than 1 unit a week across the phases (37: 22 men, 15 women), not described as lifelong abstainers or as people who had stopped; lower continuous intake in the imaging analyses
outcome: Hippocampal atrophy on one MRI scan (any visual Scheltens rating above zero, right and left; post hoc), automatically measured hippocampal volume, grey-matter density (voxel-based morphometry) and white-matter microstructure (tract-based spatial statistics); decline in lexical and semantic fluency and 20-word recall over repeated testing; thinking tests at the time of the scan
magnitude: Topiwala et al. (2017), Table 2, right hippocampal atrophy, number rated atrophic / number in group and adjusted odds ratio (95% CI) against under 1 unit a week (13/37): 1 to <7 units 67/140, 1.5 (0.7 to 3.4), p = 0.3; 7 to <14 87/165, 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4), p = 0.1; 14 to <21 63/97, 3.4 (1.4 to 8.1), p = 0.007; 21 to <30 39/57, 3.6 (1.4 to 9.6), p = 0.009; 30 or more 24/31, 5.8 (1.8 to 18.6), printed p < 0.001 (about 0.003 from the interval, editors' calculation). Left: 19/37; 89/140, 1.3 (0.6 to 3.0); 107/165, 1.4 (0.6 to 3.2); 68/97, 1.9 (0.8 to 4.6); 41/57, 1.9 (0.7 to 4.9); 27/31, 5.7 (1.5 to 21.6), p = 0.01. Men, right: 3.2 (1.1 to 9.3), 3.9 (1.3 to 12.0) and 5.2 (1.4 to 19.0) at 14 to <21, 21 to <30 and 30 or more; women: no estimate significant (14 to <21: 4.2, 0.6 to 28.8). Editors' arithmetic: rated atrophic on the right 293/527 (56%), on the left 351/527 (67%); right-side shares by group 35%, 48%, 53%, 65%, 68% and 77%; crude risk ratio at 14 to <21 against under 1 unit 1.85. Table 3: hippocampal volume (squared, % of intracranial volume) per 10 units a week −0.26 (−0.37 to −0.15) unadjusted and −0.19 (−0.30 to −0.08) adjusted, both p < 0.001. Lexical fluency fell faster than in the under-1-unit group by 0.5%, 0.8% and 0.6% of the starting score a year at 7 to <14, 14 to <21 and more than 21 units (Wald χ² 14.4, p = 0.006); semantic fluency χ² 10.0, p = 0.04, and recall χ² 9.8, p = 0.04, not significant after correction for three tests (threshold p < 0.017); no association with any test at the scan.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Design, Setting and Participants (p. 1); Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph (p. 2, left column); Fig 2 (p. 15)
evidence.extracted: Observational cohort study with weekly alcohol intake and cognitive performance measured repeatedly over 30 years (1985–2015) and one multimodal MRI at the study endpoint (2012–15), in community-dwelling adults of the Whitehall II imaging substudy. Whitehall II, established in 1985, recruited 10,308 non-industrial civil servants (phase 1 ran 1985–88); measures were repeated about every five years (phase 1 1985–88, phase 3 1991–93, phase 5 1997–99, phase 7 2003–04, phase 9 2007–09, phase 11 2011–12). For the imaging substudy a random list of 1380 people who had taken part in phase 11 or the phase 10 pilot and had consented was drawn, sampled from high, intermediate and low socioeconomic groups. Fig 2: 6306 phase 11 participants; 1380 on the list; 550 with a structural scan; 23 excluded for structural abnormality or missing alcohol or confounder data, leaving 527 in all analyses except diffusion imaging; 16 more without usable diffusion images, leaving 511. Mean age at baseline 43.0 (SD 5.4); none 'alcohol dependent' by the CAGE questionnaire; all safe for MRI.

evidence.extracted: The authors state that the sample may not represent the UK population: most participants were educated, middle-class men; the atrophy associations held in men but not in women, possibly from lower power, as few women drank heavily; the study is observational because long-term drinking cannot be randomised; drinking was self-reported and may be underestimated; 75 participants (14.2%) had CAGE data missing at one phase or more, so some people dependent at times may have been included, and some reported heavy drinking while screening negative; the MRI analyses were cross-sectional, so a confounding variable could explain the associations, and residual confounding from unmeasured sources is conceivable; they judge it unlikely, but cannot exclude, that people with hippocampal atrophy at baseline drank more; for lexical decline, P values of 0.015 to 0.004 pass a Bonferroni threshold of P < 0.017; the structural equation model was defined post hoc. risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_topiwala_2017 (ROBINS-E, first pass): overall high, from selection of the reported result (post hoc odds ratios, many uncorrected comparisons across groups, sides and sexes, the right side emphasised in the abstract). Further concerns: a single scan, so no observed change; residual confounding (smoking only within the Framingham score, diet and genotype not measured, several covariates measured at the scan; people above the limits were more often smokers and had higher IQ, while the excess of men was not significant); a reference group of 37 whose history (lifelong abstainers or people who stopped) is not stated; a survivor cohort; visual ratings without reported blinding to drinking; self-reported intake.

inconsistency.note: One cohort. Its authors report that the only earlier study of hippocampal findings in non-dependent drinkers (Den Heijer and colleagues; drinking measured once, hippocampus traced by hand) found a protective association of moderate drinking, which conflicts with theirs. That study has not been read, so this is rated down second-hand, as for another answer on this site whose trial reported conflicting studies, and is to be revisited when the study is on file.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: worded for this cohort (mostly male UK civil servants without dependence, scanned once around age 70), for a visual rating above zero rather than measured shrinkage, and for the study's groups in UK units; few women drank heavily, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: 37 people in the reference group (15 women): intervals are wide (14 to <21 units: 1.4 to 8.1; 30 or more: 1.8 to 18.6), and at 1 to <7 and 7 to <14 units they include both no association and a doubling of the odds; the lexical-fluency differences are under 1 percentage point a year.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one cohort; the imaging substudy has a published protocol, not read.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the crude risk ratio at 14 to <21 units is about 1.85, and odds ratios overstate risk ratios for so common an outcome; the evidence is also already rated down.

dose_response.note: The odds rise across the groups (1.5, 2.0, 3.4, 3.6, 5.8), but the analyses are post hoc, the intervals overlap widely, and confounders that also rise with drinking (male sex, smoking, IQ) could produce a gradient; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; rated down one level each for risk of bias (post hoc, selectively emphasised analyses; one scan; residual confounding; an undefined reference group of 37), inconsistency (an earlier study reported the opposite association, known only second-hand) and imprecision (wide intervals around a small reference group): very low, the floor. Rated as worded: an association, in this cohort, between higher average self-reported drinking and a common visual rating of hippocampal atrophy on one scan, smaller hippocampal volume, lower white-matter integrity, and a slightly faster decline on one of three repeated thinking tests; not that moderate drinking shrinks the brain or harms thinking, since no change in brain structure was observed and no test at the scan differed. For the odds ratio of 3.4 the claim follows Table 2 (14 to <21 units a week), with which the abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusions agree and with which the Results' own last sentence on right-sided risk above 14 units is consistent; the Results text's attribution to 7 to <14 units is treated as a mislabel, because that group's estimate in the table is 2.0 (0.9 to 4.4). Absolute shares are given beside the odds ratios because the outcome was common (35 in 100 of the under-1-unit group on the right). The gradient is not used to rate up (see the dose-response note). The groups are reported as the study's groups of average intake, not as limits or advice. Status single study. The editors' arithmetic (totals by sex, shares, the crude risk ratio, the p value implied by the interval for 30 or more units, the compounding of 0.8% a year) is for the second reader to recompute.

statement: In healthy, mostly white adults in their twenties, N-acetylcysteine (NAC) capsules, an over-the-counter supplement, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking, compared with identical dummy capsules taken by the same people in another session, did not detectably change next-morning hangover symptoms in a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of 49 completers (median total symptom score 10 against 13 on a 0 to 52 scale, P = 0.45), nor headache, nausea or weakness separately; comparing women with men, women's scores were lower on NAC than on placebo and men's higher (P = 0.04), a subgroup comparison among several uncorrected tests (Coppersmith et al., 2021). Evidence is insufficient to say whether NAC prevents or eases hangover: only medians were reported, without intervals; one low dose range and one timing were tested; drinking after the session was not controlled; and the difference between women and men needs testing in a trial designed for it. Side effects were few and mild with both NAC and placebo. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, capsules of N-acetylcysteine (NAC), sold as a supplement, did not ease next-morning hangover symptoms compared with dummy capsules. Women seemed to do a little better on NAC and men a little worse, but that may be chance. Side effects were few and mild with both.
population: 49 healthy adults (31 men, 18 women; predominantly white, mostly aged 20 to 30) without alcohol use disorder who completed both sessions, at one US hospital
exposure: N-acetylcysteine capsules at low doses, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking (doses and timing are on the study card)
comparator: Identical lactose placebo capsules taken by the same people during another session with the same drinking target
outcome: Next-morning Hangover Symptoms Scale total score; headache, nausea and weakness; side effects

Difference scores by sex (NAC minus placebo): women −3.5, men +2 (P = 0.04); nausea P = 0.05, weakness P = 0.03, headache P = 0.32. Side effects after NAC: gastrointestinal 4, headache 2, rash 1, muscle twitches 1, insomnia 1; after placebo: headache 3, gastrointestinal 1.

statement: In adults with a hangover, whether drinking water prevents or relieves it had not been tested in any experimental study up to July 2024, as described in a narrative review (Mackus et al., 2024). In the review authors' own re-analysis of 176 people with a hangover on a long walk, those who drank more water had worse hangovers, but the amount drunk was not related to how much their hangover or their thirst changed during the day; in student surveys, water was the most used remedy and was rated about 5 to 6 out of 10 for how well it worked. After a night of heavy drinking, thirst was clearly raised only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day, and small old studies found mild, short-lived changes in fluid balance, which the authors read as dehydration and hangover being separate effects of drinking. Evidence is insufficient to say whether water helps; the figures are second-hand or the authors' own re-analysis. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Nobody had tested whether drinking water stops or cures a hangover; thirst faded by late morning, but the hangover stayed.
population: Adults with a hangover: 176 walkers in Crete (authors' re-analysis), Dutch students (surveys) and small groups of men in old laboratory studies
exposure: Drinking water during a hangover day (amount self-reported) or as a remedy during or after drinking (survey ratings)
comparator: People who drank less water on the same walk (correlation); no untreated comparison in the surveys
outcome: Hangover severity and thirst ratings and their change during the day; perceived efficacy of water; markers of dehydration
magnitude: Water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk: r = 0.176, 0.243 and 0.229 (p from 0.019 to below 0.001); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst and change in thirst |r| no more than 0.061, none significant. Survey efficacy ratings for water 5.2 to 5.8 out of 10. Thirst above an alcohol-free day only at the 09:30 and 10:30 ratings; hangover above it at every rating to 15:30.

statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023 (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, did not detectably change how much people said they drank (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, a step not described as planned); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, all outcomes were self-reported and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those effects cannot be credited to the strategies. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
plain: In 15 trials, mostly with US college students, teaching bundles of safety habits for drinking made very little difference: students drank very slightly less often, but the amount they drank did not clearly change, and no trial tested any one habit on its own. In surveys, students who said they used more safety habits also said they drank less, but most asked about both at the same time, and day by day students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the 2013 review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. So whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
population: College students and young adults: 15 randomized trials (2007 to 2023), 13 at US universities, one at a Swedish university and one Australian pilot, mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 (15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed, editors' calculation); and college students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
exposure: Protective behavioural strategies taught or prompted in randomized trials, as bundles (limiting or stopping drinking, manner of drinking such as pacing, harm reduction such as a designated driver), alone or within multi-component interventions, mostly brief and digital; and self-reported use of strategies in observational studies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
comparator: In trials: assessment only, no intervention, education or other active or attention controls, or the same intervention without a strategies booster; in observational studies: students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional), days without a given strategy (within people, two studies), control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized, and no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (quantity, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol), alcohol-related problems and reported strategy use
magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).

risk_of_bias.note: Trials (card sc_van_nhat_2026): 14 of 15 at some concerns or high risk of bias by the review's RoB 2 figure, mainly from deviations from the intended interventions and missing outcome data; every outcome self-reported; attrition up to 95%; no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias. Observational studies (card sc_pearson_2013): strategies and outcomes self-reported, nearly always at the same sitting, mostly cross-sectional, unappraised, the review's author a co-author of 7 of the 62 studies.

inconsistency.note: The trial estimates for drinking and problems agree (I² 0% to 22%). The observational findings point different ways by strategy and design (less drinking between people, more on days with some strategies), which the status 'mixed' records; the very heterogeneous effect on reported strategy use (I² 98%) is not a drinking outcome. Not rated down, because the graded finding rests on the trials.

indirectness.note: No trial isolated a single strategy: strategies were taught in bundles, often with personalized normative feedback, against a mix of controls, so the effect of the strategies themselves, or of strategies people choose on their own, is not measured; almost all participants were young US university students.

imprecision.note: The intervals for quantity, frequency and problems are narrow and exclude more than a small effect (none goes beyond −0.19); the problems estimate reaches no difference.

publication_bias.note: No funnel asymmetry in any pool, though with 6 to 9 trials the tests have little power; English-language peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature. Not rated down.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk, self-reported outcomes) and indirectness (bundles taught with other components, not single strategies; US students), giving low for what the trials show: teaching bundles of strategies changed reported drinking very little. The relation stays insufficient evidence for the claim's question, whether the strategies themselves lower drinking or harms: no trial tested any single strategy, the bundles' effects are very small and partly attributable to other components, and the observational associations, which by themselves would be very low (narrative review only), point different ways by design. The meta-analysis is AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional: its list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read), searched English-language peer-reviewed reports only, and its abstract leads with estimates made after dropping a trial; its PRISMA counts do not add up (564 records by database against 514 printed). Counted once: Larimer et al. (2007) and Sugarman and Carey (2009), described in the 2013 review, are among the meta-analysis's trials. Status mixed: the observational findings differ in direction by strategy and design, with only the review author's untested explanation, while the trials show very small or no effects. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review.
